items.ex: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states (or the people) powers not delegated to the United States, such as education and marriage licensing.
w: The Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause gives Congress implied powers; it does not grant powers to states.
The Supremacy Clause
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme over conflicting state law.
The Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause gives Congress power over interstate commerce.

alt.q: The Tenth Amendment states: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." This amendment most directly supports
alt.a: federalism
alt.ex: By reserving undelegated powers to the states, the Tenth Amendment protects the state side of the federal system.
w: judicial review
Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws.
separation of powers
Separation of powers divides federal power among three branches.
equal protection
Equal protection (Fourteenth Amendment) bars unfair discrimination by states.

alt.q: Which power is concurrent, meaning it is held by both the national and state governments?
alt.a: Levying taxes
alt.ex: Both Congress and the states may tax and borrow; these are concurrent powers.
w: Coining money
Only Congress may coin money; Article I, Section 10 forbids states to do so.
Declaring war
Declaring war is a delegated power of Congress alone.
Making treaties
Treaty-making belongs to the President with Senate consent; states are barred from it.

items.q: A state passes a law that directly conflicts with a valid federal law. Under the Constitution, which law controls?
items.a: The federal law, under the Supremacy Clause
items.ex: Article VI makes the Constitution and federal laws made under it 'the supreme Law of the Land,' so valid federal law prevails over conflicting state law.
w: The state law, under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth reserves undelegated powers but does not let states override valid federal law.
Whichever of the two laws was passed most recently
Timing does not decide federal-state conflicts; the Supremacy Clause does.
Whichever law the state's voters approve
Voter approval cannot make a state law override valid federal law.

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court held that Maryland could not tax the Second Bank of the United States. This ruling strengthened which side of federalism?
alt.a: National power over conflicting state action
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall upheld the bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause and ruled that, under the Supremacy Clause, a state cannot tax a federal institution ('the power to tax involves the power to destroy').
w: State power to regulate national institutions
This states the opposite of the holding; Maryland's tax was struck down.
Individual rights against state interference
The case concerned national versus state power, not individual rights.
Judicial power over presidential decisions
The case did not involve the President; it involved Congress's bank and a state tax.

alt.q: Article VI states: "This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof... shall be the supreme Law of the Land." In a federal system, this clause is needed mainly to
alt.a: settle conflicts between national and state laws
alt.ex: Because federalism creates two levels of lawmaking, the Supremacy Clause tells courts that valid federal law wins when the two conflict.
w: divide power among the three federal branches
That is separation of powers (Articles I-III).
reserve unlisted powers to the individual states
That is the Tenth Amendment.
guarantee each state a republican government
That is the Guarantee Clause of Article IV.

items.q: Which statement best describes individual liberty as a principle of American democracy?
items.a: People may speak, believe, and act as they choose within the law
items.ex: Individual liberty means freedom from unjust government control over personal, political, and religious life, protected especially by the Bill of Rights.
w: People must follow the religion chosen by their state government
An established church requiring belief is the opposite of religious liberty.
People's freedoms depend on approval by the majority of voters
Basic liberties are protected even from majorities.
People receive freedoms only as rewards for service to the nation
Liberty is treated as a natural right, not a reward.

alt.q: The First Amendment begins: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." These two clauses together protect
alt.a: freedom of belief and worship from government control
alt.ex: The Establishment Clause bars an official church and the Free Exercise Clause protects practicing one's faith; together they secure religious liberty.
w: the right to petition officials to correct wrongs
That is the Petition Clause, later in the First Amendment.
the freedom of reporters to publish without censorship
That is freedom of the press.
equal treatment of people regardless of race
That is equal protection (Fourteenth Amendment).

alt.q: Amish parents refuse, for religious reasons, to send their children to school after eighth grade, and the state prosecutes them. In Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972), the Supreme Court ruled that
alt.a: the Free Exercise Clause protected the parents' choice
alt.ex: Yoder held that requiring Amish children to attend school past eighth grade violated the parents' free exercise of religion.
w: the Establishment Clause required the state to fund Amish schools
The case was about free exercise; no school funding was ordered.
the state's interest in schooling outweighed the parents' beliefs
That is the right case with the wrong holding; the Court sided with the parents.
the Equal Protection Clause required the same rules for everyone
The ruling rested on religious freedom, not equal protection.

items.q: Students wear black armbands to school to protest a war, and the school suspends them even though no disruption occurred. Which case and principle apply?
items.a: Tinker v. Des Moines; students keep free speech rights in school
items.ex: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Court held that students do not 'shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate'; armbands were protected symbolic speech.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier; schools may edit school-sponsored papers
Hazelwood (1988) allowed censorship of a school-sponsored newspaper, not personal expression.
Engel v. Vitale; public schools may not lead official prayers
Engel (1962) is an Establishment Clause case about school prayer.
Texas v. Johnson; burning the U.S. flag is protected speech
Johnson (1989) protected flag burning as symbolic speech, but not in a school setting.

alt.q: Which case held that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate"?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969)
alt.ex: Tinker protected students' armbands protesting the Vietnam War as symbolic speech absent substantial disruption.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988)
Hazelwood let schools control school-sponsored publications.
Engel v. Vitale (1962)
Engel struck down official school prayer under the Establishment Clause.
Texas v. Johnson (1989)
Johnson protected flag burning as political expression.

alt.q: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), what did the Supreme Court decide about students' black armbands?
alt.a: They were protected symbolic speech that caused no real disruption
alt.ex: The Court held schools may limit student expression only if it would substantially disrupt school; silent armbands did not.
w: They could be banned because schools control all student expression
The Court rejected total school control over student speech.
They were protected only because the students wore them off campus
The armbands were worn at school, and they were still protected.
They were school-sponsored speech that officials could freely edit
That is the Hazelwood (1988) standard for school newspapers.

items.q: Which example best illustrates political liberty rather than religious liberty?
items.a: Criticizing the President at a peaceful public rally
items.ex: Political liberty is the freedom to take part in public life and dissent: speech, press, assembly, petition, and voting.
w: Choosing not to attend any house of worship
Choosing whether to worship is religious liberty.
Praying privately during the lunch period at a public school
Private student prayer is free exercise of religion.
Refusing to salute a flag for reasons of faith
Faith-based refusal to salute (Barnette, 1943) involved religious objections.

alt.q: The First Amendment protects "the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances." These freedoms are most important to democracy because they
alt.a: let citizens criticize leaders and influence policy
alt.ex: Speech, press, assembly, and petition allow citizens to debate, organize, and pressure government: the core of political liberty.
w: prevent the government from setting up an official church
That is the Establishment Clause.
guarantee accused persons a fair and speedy trial
That is the Sixth Amendment.
keep soldiers from being housed in private homes
That is the Third Amendment.

alt.q: A group of residents gathers peacefully outside city hall and delivers a signed request asking the council to repair local roads. Which First Amendment freedoms are they exercising?
alt.a: Assembly and petition
alt.ex: Gathering peacefully is assembly; formally asking government to act is petitioning 'for a redress of grievances.'
w: Press and free exercise
Press concerns publishing; free exercise concerns religion.
Religion and the press
Neither religion nor publishing is involved.
Due process and speech
Due process concerns fair procedures before government takes liberty or property.

items.q: In Federalist No. 39, Madison defines a republic as "a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior." Which form of government does this describe?
items.a: Rule by elected officials
items.ex: Madison's definition describes representative democracy, or republicanism: power from the people, exercised by officials serving limited terms or during good behavior.
w: Rule by citizens in person
Citizens governing in person is direct democracy, as in Athens.
Rule by a hereditary king
Hereditary rule is monarchy; Madison's offices are held for limited periods.
Rule by a wealthy few
Rule by a wealthy few is oligarchy, not power from 'the great body of the people.'

alt.q: Article IV, Section 4 states: "The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government." This clause requires every state to have
alt.a: a government whose leaders are chosen by the people
alt.ex: The Guarantee Clause requires representative (republican) government in every state, with no monarchy or hereditary rule.
w: a government in which citizens vote on every single law
That is direct democracy, which the clause does not require.
a government led by a governor who serves for life
Life rule would contradict republican government.
a government whose laws match those of every other state
States may have different laws; Full Faith and Credit concerns honoring other states' records.

alt.q: Citizens of a country elect a legislature, which makes laws on their behalf; there is no monarch. Which term best describes this country?
alt.a: A republic
alt.ex: A republic is a government in which citizens elect representatives to make laws, with no hereditary ruler.
w: A direct democracy
In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves rather than through a legislature.
A constitutional monarchy
A constitutional monarchy keeps a monarch with limited powers.
An oligarchy
An oligarchy is rule by a small, privileged group.

items.q: Madison argued in Federalist No. 10 that "a pure democracy, by which I mean a society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person, can admit of no cure for the mischiefs of faction." Which conclusion did Madison draw?
items.a: A large republic with elected representatives can best control factions
items.ex: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), Madison argued that representation and a large republic with many competing interests would keep any single faction from dominating.
w: Factions should be eliminated entirely by restricting freedom of opinion
Madison said removing the causes of faction would destroy liberty, a cure 'worse than the disease.'
Small democracies best protect minorities from majority factions
Madison argued the opposite: small democracies are most easily dominated by a majority faction.
States should stay independent instead of forming a strong union
That is closer to the Anti-Federalist view (e.g., Brutus No. 1).

alt.q: Which Federalist essay argues that a large republic is the best cure for the 'mischiefs of faction'?
alt.a: Federalist No. 10
alt.ex: Madison's Federalist No. 10 explains how a large republic with representation controls the effects of faction.
w: Federalist No. 51
No. 51 explains checks and balances and separation of powers ('Ambition must be made to counteract ambition').
Federalist No. 78
No. 78 (Hamilton) defends an independent judiciary and judicial review.
Brutus No. 1
Brutus No. 1 is an Anti-Federalist essay arguing a large republic could not work.

alt.q: A framer argues that elected representatives will "refine and enlarge the public views" by filtering out the passions of the moment better than a crowd of voters could. This is an argument for
alt.a: republicanism over direct democracy
alt.ex: Madison (Federalist No. 10) argued that passing public views 'through the medium of a chosen body of citizens' improves decisions: the case for a republic.
w: states' rights over national power
The argument concerns representation, not the balance between states and nation.
judicial review over legislative power
The argument concerns elected representatives, not courts.
a monarchy over representative rule
The argument favors elected representatives, not a monarch.

items.q: In the founders' view of republicanism, why was civic virtue important?
items.a: Citizens had to put the common good ahead of private interests
items.ex: Classical republicanism, drawn from Rome, held that a republic survives only if citizens and leaders place the public good above self-interest.
w: Citizens had to obey a hereditary ruler without question
Unquestioning obedience to a hereditary ruler describes monarchy.
Citizens had to vote directly on every single law the state passed
Voting directly on laws is direct democracy, not republican civic virtue.
Citizens had to belong to the official church of their state
Required church membership conflicts with religious liberty.

alt.q: George Washington was praised as a 'modern Cincinnatus' for giving up command of the army in 1783 and returning to private life. This praise reflects the republican value of
alt.a: civic virtue, placing public service above personal power
alt.ex: Like the Roman Cincinnatus, who gave up emergency power to return to his farm, Washington resigned his commission (December 1783), modeling republican virtue.
w: popular sovereignty, letting voters elect the army's leaders
Washington was appointed by Congress, not elected by voters, and the praise is about giving up power.
federalism, letting each state command its own militia
The praise concerns personal restraint, not state-national power.
natural rights, protecting each soldier's private property
The praise is about giving up power, not protecting property.

alt.q: Which Roman figure, who gave up emergency power and returned to his farm, became a symbol of republican virtue for the founders?
alt.a: Cincinnatus
alt.ex: Cincinnatus was named dictator to save Rome, then resigned and returned to his farm; the Society of the Cincinnati and the city of Cincinnati honor him.
w: Julius Caesar
Caesar took power as dictator for life, helping to end the Republic.
Augustus
Augustus became Rome's first emperor, replacing the Republic.
Cicero
Cicero was an orator who defended the Republic, but he is not known for giving up emergency power.

items.q: Which statement best describes constitutionalism?
items.a: Government's powers are defined and limited by a supreme fundamental law
items.ex: Constitutionalism means government operates under, and is limited by, a constitution that ranks above ordinary laws and can be changed only by a special process (Article V).
w: Government's powers are divided between the nation and the states
That is federalism.
Government's powers come from the consent of the governed
That is the social contract and popular sovereignty.
Government's powers are exercised by the citizens' elected representatives
That is republicanism.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 78, Hamilton writes: "The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts. A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges, as a fundamental law." Hamilton's argument supports
alt.a: courts treating the Constitution as superior to ordinary laws
alt.ex: Hamilton argued that judges must prefer the Constitution over conflicting statutes, foreshadowing judicial review in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: Congress overriding the court rulings by a simple majority vote
Hamilton argued courts protect the Constitution against the legislature, not the reverse.
states deciding for themselves which federal laws are valid
That is nullification, which Federalist No. 78 does not support.
the President interpreting the laws without judicial review
Hamilton assigns interpretation to the courts, not the executive.

alt.q: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Supreme Court declared part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 void. This reinforced constitutionalism by establishing that
alt.a: a law conflicting with the Constitution cannot stand
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall held that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act unconstitutionally expanded the Court's original jurisdiction, so the Constitution controls over ordinary law.
w: the President may ignore any Supreme Court ruling
The case asserted courts' power to say what the law is, not presidential defiance.
states may nullify unconstitutional federal laws
Nullification was a states' rights theory (Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions), not the holding.
Congress may expand the Court's original jurisdiction
That is exactly what the Court said Congress could not do.

items.q: A new majority in Congress wants to extend House members' terms from two years to six without changing the Constitution. Why can't Congress simply pass a law to do so?
items.a: The Constitution sets the term, and only an amendment can change it
items.ex: Article I sets two-year House terms; ordinary laws cannot change constitutional provisions, which require the Article V amendment process.
w: The President alone decides the length of congressional terms
The President has no power over congressional terms.
Each state legislature sets the terms of its own U.S. representatives
House terms are set by the Constitution, not by states.
The Supreme Court must approve all laws before they take effect
Courts review laws only in actual cases after passage; they do not pre-approve laws.

alt.q: Which feature most clearly makes the U.S. Constitution a higher law than ordinary statutes?
alt.a: It can be changed only through the special amendment process
alt.ex: Article V requires supermajorities (two-thirds to propose, three-fourths of states to ratify), so the Constitution cannot be altered by ordinary legislation.
w: It can be changed by a simple majority vote in both houses of Congress
That describes ordinary statutes, not the Constitution.
It was written by members of the Continental Congress
It was written at the Constitutional Convention of 1787; authorship does not make it supreme.
It must be renewed by the states every twenty years
The Constitution has no renewal requirement.

alt.q: A state constitution says the governor may serve only two terms. A popular governor's supporters in the legislature pass a statute allowing a third term, and a court strikes it down. The court's reasoning rests on
alt.a: constitutionalism: a constitution limits ordinary lawmaking
alt.ex: A statute cannot override the constitution that creates and limits the legislature; changing the term limit requires amending the constitution.
w: federalism: states may ignore national term limits
The term limit here is in the state constitution; no federal-state conflict exists.
popular sovereignty: voters may choose any candidate they want
Popular sovereignty would not let a statute override the constitution the people adopted.
majority rule: the legislature speaks for the people
Majority rule is limited by the constitution, which is why the statute fails.

items.q: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice Marshall wrote: "It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is." Which power did this decision establish?
items.a: Judicial review
items.ex: Marbury established judicial review, the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional, reinforcing the Constitution as supreme law.
w: Judicial restraint
Judicial restraint is a philosophy that judges should defer to elected branches; it is not a power Marbury created.
Implied powers
Implied powers were upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Selective incorporation
Selective incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to states through the Fourteenth Amendment, case by case.

alt.q: Which case first established judicial review, the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
alt.ex: In Marbury, Chief Justice John Marshall struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing judicial review.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
McCulloch upheld implied powers and barred state taxation of the national bank.
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
Dred Scott was only the second time the Court struck down a federal law, but it did not establish the power.
Baker v. Carr (1962)
Baker held that legislative apportionment can be challenged in federal court.

alt.q: A federal court rules that a statute passed by Congress violates the First Amendment and cannot be enforced. The court is exercising
alt.a: judicial review
alt.ex: Striking down a law as unconstitutional is judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: executive privilege
Executive privilege is a presidential confidentiality claim.
senatorial courtesy
Senatorial courtesy is the custom of consulting home-state senators on nominations.
legislative oversight
Legislative oversight is Congress monitoring executive agencies.

items.q: In his First Inaugural Address (1801), Jefferson said: "though the will of the majority is in all cases to prevail, that will to be rightful must be reasonable; that the minority possess their equal rights, which equal law must protect, and to violate would be oppression." Jefferson is describing
items.a: majority rule limited by the rights of the minority
items.ex: Jefferson summarized the balance at the heart of American democracy: the majority governs, but it may not violate the equal rights of the minority.
w: unlimited majority rule over every question of rights
Jefferson said the majority's will 'to be rightful must be reasonable' and may not oppress the minority.
a minority's power to veto the decisions of the majority
Jefferson said the majority's will is 'in all cases to prevail'; minorities keep their rights, not a veto.
the people's right to abolish a destructive government
That is the right of revolution in the Declaration of Independence.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the principle of majority rule with minority rights?
alt.a: The majority decides, but it cannot violate the basic rights of the few
alt.ex: Decisions are made by majority vote, but constitutional rights limit what any majority may do to a minority.
w: The minority decides whenever the majority's choice is unwise
Minorities do not overrule majorities; they are protected in their rights.
Every public decision must have the unanimous approval of all the citizens
Unanimity is a different rule (the Articles required it for amendments).
The majority decides every question, including individual rights
Unlimited majority rule can become 'tyranny of the majority'; rights are protected.

alt.q: Voters in a town approve, by a large margin, a measure banning one small religious group from holding public meetings. A court strikes down the measure. This outcome illustrates
alt.a: that some rights are protected even against the majority
alt.ex: Free exercise and assembly rights cannot be voted away; courts protect minority rights from majority decisions.
w: that federal courts must follow local voters' wishes
The court overrode the voters, the opposite.
that the majority rules on all matters involving religion
The First Amendment removes religious freedom from majority control.
that towns hold powers reserved by the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers do not allow towns to violate constitutional rights.

items.q: In West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943), the Court wrote: "One's right to life, liberty, and property, to free speech, a free press, freedom of worship and assembly, and other fundamental rights may not be submitted to vote; they depend on the outcome of no elections." This means that
items.a: the Bill of Rights places certain rights beyond majority control
items.ex: Justice Jackson explained that the Bill of Rights places fundamental rights beyond the reach of majorities; the Court struck down a mandatory flag salute.
w: fundamental rights may be changed by a statewide voter referendum
The passage says the opposite: rights may not be submitted to vote.
the states, not voters, decide which rights are fundamental
The Court, applying the Constitution, protected the rights against the state.
elections are the main way to protect individual rights
The passage says rights depend on 'no elections'; courts protect them.

alt.q: Jehovah's Witness students refused, for religious reasons, to salute the flag as their public school required. In 1943, the Supreme Court ruled that
alt.a: the school could not force the students to salute
alt.ex: West Virginia v. Barnette (1943) held that compelling the flag salute violated the First Amendment, overruling Minersville v. Gobitis (1940).
w: the school could require the salute for national unity
That was the holding of Minersville v. Gobitis (1940), which Barnette overruled.
the students could be expelled only after a hearing
A hearing requirement is a due process idea; the Court protected the refusal itself.
the matter should be settled by a school board vote
Barnette held such rights 'may not be submitted to vote.'

alt.q: Which feature of the Constitution most directly protects minority rights from majority rule?
alt.a: The Bill of Rights, which limits what laws may say
alt.ex: The Bill of Rights restricts government even when a majority supports a law, protecting minorities' freedoms.
w: The Electoral College, which counts votes by state
The Electoral College selects the President; it does not protect individual rights.
The census, which apportions House seats by population
The census distributes representation by population, a majoritarian feature.
The House of Representatives, elected by population
The House is the most majoritarian branch.

items.q: The Constitution requires two-thirds of both houses of Congress to propose an amendment and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. Why require more than a simple majority?
items.a: To protect basic rules and minorities from a temporary majority
items.ex: Article V's supermajorities ensure that fundamental law changes only with broad agreement, limiting a temporary majority.
w: To let any single state block a national law that it strongly dislikes
One state could block amendments only under the Articles' unanimity rule, and Article V does not cover ordinary laws.
To give the President final control over amendments
The President has no formal role in the Article V process.
To ensure that the Supreme Court proposes all amendments
Amendments are proposed by Congress or a national convention, not the Court.

alt.q: Which action requires a supermajority rather than a simple majority under the Constitution?
alt.a: Overriding a presidential veto
alt.ex: Article I, Section 7 requires two-thirds of both houses to override a veto.
w: Passing an ordinary bill in the House
Ordinary bills pass by simple majority.
Impeaching an official in the House
Impeachment in the House takes a simple majority; conviction in the Senate takes two-thirds.
Electing the Speaker of the House
The Speaker is chosen by a majority of votes cast.

alt.q: A majority of senators wants to ratify a treaty, but fewer than two-thirds of senators present support it. What happens?
alt.a: The treaty is not ratified
alt.ex: Article II requires the consent of two-thirds of senators present for treaties, protecting against narrow majorities.
w: The treaty is ratified by majority vote
A simple Senate majority is not enough for treaties.
The House decides by majority vote
The House has no constitutional role in ratifying treaties.
The President may ratify it alone
Treaties require Senate consent; the President cannot ratify alone.

items.q: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) forbids any State to "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws." Relying on this clause, the Supreme Court rejected 'separate but equal' in public schools in which decision?
items.a: Brown v. Board (1954)
items.ex: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) unanimously held that school segregation violates the Equal Protection Clause: 'Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.'
w: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Plessy interpreted the same clause but upheld 'separate but equal'; Brown overturned it for public schools.
Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
Mapp applied the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule to the states.
Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
Miranda rests on the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.

alt.q: "We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." Which case does this come from?
alt.a: Brown v. Board (1954)
alt.ex: Chief Justice Warren wrote these words for a unanimous Court in Brown v. Board of Education, applying the Equal Protection Clause.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Plessy created the 'separate but equal' doctrine that this passage rejects.
Regents v. Bakke (1978)
Bakke concerned racial quotas in university admissions.
Shaw v. Reno (1993)
Shaw concerned racial gerrymandering of congressional districts.

alt.q: A state requires Black and white children to attend separate public schools, claiming the schools are equal. Under current law, which ruling and clause make this unconstitutional?
alt.a: Brown v. Board, under the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Brown (1954) held that state-mandated school segregation denies equal protection of the laws under the Fourteenth Amendment.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson, under the Equal Protection Clause
Plessy (1896) upheld segregation; it is the case Brown overturned.
Brown v. Board, under the First Amendment
Right case, wrong clause: Brown rested on equal protection, not the First Amendment.
Plessy v. Ferguson, under the Due Process Clause
Plessy upheld segregation, and Brown's holding rests on equal protection.

items.q: A state medical school reserved a fixed number of seats only for minority applicants. In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), the Supreme Court held that
items.a: racial quotas were unconstitutional, though race could be one factor
items.ex: Bakke struck down the school's fixed quota (16 of 100 seats) but allowed race as one factor in admissions. (Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 2023, later held race-conscious admissions programs unconstitutional.)
w: all consideration of race in admissions was fully permitted
Bakke struck down the quota, so it did not permit every use of race.
racial quotas were required to remedy past discrimination
The Court rejected the quota rather than requiring one.
universities could not consider any factor other than their test scores
Bakke said nothing limiting admissions to test scores.

alt.q: Which 1978 case struck down a medical school's racial quota but allowed race to be considered as one factor in admissions?
alt.a: Regents v. Bakke
alt.ex: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978) rejected fixed racial quotas while permitting race as one 'plus' factor.
w: Grutter v. Bollinger
Grutter (2003) upheld the University of Michigan Law School's holistic admissions; it came 25 years later.
Shaw v. Reno
Shaw (1993) concerned racially drawn congressional districts.
Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal' segregation.

alt.q: A university reviews applicants individually and considers race as one factor among many, without setting aside any seats. Under the 1978 Bakke decision, this approach was treated as
alt.a: permissible, unlike a fixed racial quota
alt.ex: Bakke distinguished quotas (unconstitutional) from considering race as one factor (allowed); in 2023, SFFA v. Harvard held race-conscious admissions unconstitutional.
w: unconstitutional, like any use of race
Under Bakke, race as one factor was allowed; only the quota was struck down.
required by the Equal Protection Clause
Bakke permitted race as a factor but did not require it.
a matter left only to state legislatures
The Court decided the issue under the Constitution and federal law.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Equal Protection Clause?
items.a: States must apply their laws equally and not discriminate unfairly
items.ex: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause (1868) forbids states from denying any person 'the equal protection of the laws.'
w: States must follow fair procedures before taking a person's liberty
That is the Due Process Clause.
States must honor the public records and court rulings of other states
That is the Full Faith and Credit Clause (Article IV).
States must provide every citizen with an equal amount of income
Equal protection concerns equal treatment under law, not equal income.

alt.q: A state draws an oddly shaped congressional district based almost entirely on race. In Shaw v. Reno (1993), the Court held that such a district
alt.a: may violate the Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Shaw v. Reno held that districts drawn mainly by race are subject to strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause.
w: is always required by the Voting Rights Act
The Court rejected the idea that the Voting Rights Act automatically justified such districts.
is a political question courts cannot review
Baker v. Carr (1962) had already made districting challenges reviewable.
violates the one-person, one-vote rule
One person, one vote concerns equal population, not racial line-drawing.

alt.q: The Equal Protection Clause appears in which amendment, ratified after the Civil War?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) contains the Citizenship, Due Process, and Equal Protection Clauses.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth (1865) abolished slavery.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.
The Fifth Amendment
The Fifth (1791) contains a due process clause limiting the federal government, not the Equal Protection Clause.

items.q: Which statement best distinguishes civil liberties from civil rights?
items.a: Liberties limit what government may do; rights guarantee equal treatment
items.ex: Civil liberties (speech, religion, fair trial) are freedoms protected from government interference; civil rights are guarantees of equal treatment and freedom from discrimination (equal protection, Civil Rights Act of 1964).
w: Liberties are granted by states; rights are granted by the national government
Both are protected at both levels; the difference is in what they protect.
Liberties apply only to citizens; rights apply to all persons in the country
Most liberties and rights protect 'persons,' not only citizens.
Liberties come from statutes; rights come only from court decisions
Liberties come mainly from the Bill of Rights; civil rights come from amendments, laws, and rulings.

alt.q: A restaurant refuses to serve customers because of their race, and the customers sue under federal law. This dispute is mainly about
alt.a: civil rights
alt.ex: Freedom from discrimination in public accommodations is a civil right, protected by Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
w: civil liberties
Civil liberties are protections against government interference, such as free speech.
natural law
Natural law is the philosophical basis of rights, not the legal category of this dispute.
reserved powers
Reserved powers (Tenth Amendment) belong to states, not individuals.

alt.q: A city arrests a person for criticizing the mayor in a letter to a newspaper. This dispute is mainly about
alt.a: a civil liberty protected by the First Amendment
alt.ex: Freedom of speech and press are civil liberties, limits on what government may do to individuals.
w: a civil right protected by the Civil Rights Act
The Civil Rights Act targets discrimination, not punishment for speech.
a reserved power protected by the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers belong to states; the issue is an individual freedom.
an equal protection claim under the Fourteenth
No unequal treatment of a group is described; the issue is punishment for speech.

items.q: Which statement best describes the original purpose of the Bill of Rights (1791)?
items.a: To limit the national government's power over individual freedoms
items.ex: Demanded by Anti-Federalists and drafted by Madison, the Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833); it was later applied to states through selective incorporation.
w: To limit state governments' power over individual freedoms
The amendments applied to states only later, through the Fourteenth Amendment.
To guarantee the right to vote regardless of race or sex
Those guarantees came in the Fifteenth (1870) and Nineteenth (1920) Amendments.
To divide powers between the national and the various state governments
That division is federalism, set up in the main body of the Constitution.

alt.q: In 1961, the Supreme Court ruled that evidence from an illegal police search could not be used in a state court. This case applied the Fourth Amendment to the states through
alt.a: the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause
alt.ex: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) incorporated the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule against the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause (selective incorporation).
w: the Fourth Amendment's own text, which names the states
The Bill of Rights originally limited only the federal government.
the Full Faith and Credit Clause of Article IV
That clause requires states to honor each other's records and judgments.
the Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article IV
That clause bars discrimination against citizens of other states.

alt.q: Why did Anti-Federalists insist on adding a Bill of Rights to the Constitution?
alt.a: They feared a strong national government would threaten liberties
alt.ex: Anti-Federalists such as George Mason argued the new, stronger central government needed written limits to protect individual freedoms.
w: They wanted the states to give up their reserved powers
Anti-Federalists wanted to protect state power, not reduce it.
They wanted to guarantee voting rights to all of the adult citizens
Universal suffrage was not part of the 1791 Bill of Rights.
They feared the Constitution gave Congress too little power
That was the Federalists' complaint about the Articles of Confederation.

items.q: Which law is an example of government protecting a civil right?
items.a: A 1964 law banning racial discrimination in public places
items.ex: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations and employment: a civil rights guarantee.
w: The First Amendment, barring laws that abridge the freedom of speech
Free speech is a civil liberty, a limit on government.
The Fourth Amendment, requiring warrants for most searches and seizures
Protection from unreasonable searches is a civil liberty.
The Tenth Amendment, reserving undelegated powers to the states
The Tenth Amendment concerns federalism, not individual rights.

alt.q: A worker is fired by a private employer because of their religion. Which federal law most directly protects them?
alt.a: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
alt.ex: Title VII bans employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, including by private employers.
w: The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment
The First Amendment limits government, not private employers.
The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
Equal protection limits state action, not private businesses.
The Voting Rights Act of 1965
The Voting Rights Act protects voting, not employment.

alt.q: Which pair correctly classifies the two protections: (1) freedom from unreasonable searches; (2) freedom from racial discrimination in hiring?
alt.a: (1) civil liberty; (2) civil right
alt.ex: Freedom from unreasonable searches limits government (Fourth Amendment), a civil liberty; freedom from job discrimination is equal treatment (Title VII), a civil right.
w: (1) civil right; (2) civil liberty
This reverses the categories.
(1) civil liberty; (2) civil liberty
Hiring discrimination involves equal treatment, a civil right.
(1) civil right; (2) civil right
Search protection limits government power, a civil liberty.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the Electoral College selects the President?
items.a: Each state gets electors equal to its House and Senate seats; 270 votes wins
items.ex: Under Article II, each state's electors equal its senators plus representatives; with D.C.'s 3 (Twenty-third Amendment, 1961) there are 538, and a majority of 270 is needed.
w: Each state gets electors equal to its House seats only, and a plurality wins
Electors also include each state's two Senate seats, and a majority, not a plurality, is required.
The candidate with the most popular votes nationwide automatically wins
The national popular vote does not decide the election; electoral votes do.
State legislatures choose the President directly by a majority vote
State legislatures decide how electors are chosen (today by popular vote), but they do not elect the President.

alt.q: Article II states: "Each State shall appoint, in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct, a Number of Electors, equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives to which the State may be entitled in the Congress." A state with 2 senators and 8 representatives has how many electors?
alt.ex: Electors equal senators plus representatives: 2 + 8 = 10.
w: That counts only House seats and leaves out the two senators.
That counts only Senate seats.
Electors are not double the House delegation; they equal the total congressional delegation.

alt.q: No presidential candidate wins a majority of electoral votes. Under the Twelfth Amendment, who chooses the President?
alt.a: The House, with one vote per state delegation
alt.ex: If no one has a majority of electoral votes, the House chooses among the top three, each state delegation casting one vote (as in 1824); the Senate chooses the Vice President.
w: The Senate, with one vote per senator
The Senate chooses the Vice President in this situation, not the President.
The Supreme Court, by majority vote
The Court has no constitutional role in choosing the President.
The House, with one vote per individual member
The House votes by state delegation, one vote per state, not one per member.

items.q: In 2016, one candidate won the most popular votes nationwide, but the other won the presidency. How is this possible?
items.a: The winner earned a majority of electoral votes by carrying key states
items.ex: The President is chosen by electoral votes, mostly awarded winner-take-all by state; popular-vote losers also won in 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016.
w: The House overturned the popular vote by a majority decision
The House chooses the President only if no candidate wins an electoral majority.
The Supreme Court awarded the victory after ordering a recount
In Bush v. Gore (2000) the Court halted a recount; it played no such role in 2016.
The Senate rejected the electors sent from several of the largest states
The Senate did not reject electors; the electoral count followed state results.

alt.q: Most states award all of their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state's popular vote. Which two states use a district-based method instead?
alt.a: Maine and Nebraska
alt.ex: Maine and Nebraska give two electors to the statewide winner and one to the winner of each congressional district.
w: Florida and Texas
Both use winner-take-all.
Iowa and New Hampshire
These states are known for early caucuses and primaries; both use winner-take-all.
California and New York
Both use winner-take-all.

alt.q: Which outcome is possible because most states award electoral votes on a winner-take-all basis?
alt.a: A candidate can lose the national popular vote and still win
alt.ex: Narrow wins in states with many electors can produce an electoral majority without a popular-vote plurality, as in 2000 and 2016.
w: A candidate can win without receiving any of the electoral votes
A candidate must win a majority of electoral votes (270).
A state can split its votes evenly among all candidates
Winner-take-all gives all of a state's votes to one candidate.
A candidate needs only a plurality of electoral votes
A majority of electoral votes is required; otherwise the House decides.

items.q: "The right of citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of age." Which amendment is this, and what did it do?
items.a: The 26th, lowering the voting age to 18 in 1971
items.ex: The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, driven by the argument that those drafted for Vietnam should be able to vote.
w: The 19th, giving women the vote in 1920
The Nineteenth bars denial of the vote 'on account of sex.'
The 24th, banning poll taxes in 1964
The Twenty-fourth bans poll taxes in federal elections.
The 15th, barring racial limits on voting in 1870
The Fifteenth bars denial 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.'

alt.q: In 1970, an 18-year-old who could be drafted to serve in Vietnam could not vote in most states. Which amendment changed this?
alt.a: The Twenty-sixth Amendment
alt.ex: Ratified in 1971, the Twenty-sixth Amendment set 18 as the minimum voting age in all elections.
w: The Nineteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth (1920) extended the vote to women.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The Twenty-fourth (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth (1870) barred racial discrimination in voting.

alt.q: Which statement best explains the main argument for the Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971)?
alt.a: People old enough to be drafted should be old enough to vote
alt.ex: During the Vietnam War, the slogan 'old enough to fight, old enough to vote' drove ratification of the amendment lowering the voting age to 18.
w: Women deserved the same voting rights that men already had
That was the argument for the Nineteenth Amendment (1920).
Poll taxes kept poor citizens from voting in federal elections
That was the argument for the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964).
Residents of the capital deserved electoral votes for President
That was the purpose of the Twenty-third Amendment (1961).

items.q: Which statement best describes the primary function of the Preamble to the U.S. Constitution?
items.a: It states the government's goals and the source of its authority
items.ex: The Preamble announces that “We the People” ordain the Constitution and lists six goals (union, justice, domestic tranquility, common defence, general welfare, liberty); it grants no powers by itself.
w: It grants Congress the specific powers it is allowed to exercise
Specific congressional powers are listed in Article I, Section 8, not the Preamble.
It lists individual rights that the government may never violate
That describes the Bill of Rights (1791), not the Preamble.
It explains the colonies' reasons for separating from Britain
That is the purpose of the Declaration of Independence (1776).

alt.q: A lawyer argues a federal law is valid only because it “promote[s] the general Welfare,” citing nothing but the Preamble. Why is this argument weak?
alt.a: The Preamble sets out goals but is not a grant of power
alt.ex: Courts treat the Preamble as a statement of purposes; a federal law must rest on a power granted elsewhere, such as Article I, Section 8.
w: The Preamble was repealed by a later constitutional amendment
No amendment has ever repealed or changed the Preamble.
The Preamble limits only the states, not the national government
The Preamble limits no one; it states the purposes of the national government.
The Preamble was not part of the text the states ratified
The Preamble was part of the Constitution ratified in 1787–1788.

alt.q: Which part of the Constitution lists aims such as to “establish Justice” and “insure domestic Tranquility”?
alt.a: The Preamble
alt.ex: These phrases are among the six goals named in the Preamble's single sentence.
w: Article I, Section 8
Article I, Section 8 lists Congress's enumerated powers, such as taxing and declaring war.
The Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people.
Article VI
Article VI contains the Supremacy Clause, oaths of office and the ban on religious tests.

items.q: “We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union…” The opening words of this excerpt most directly reflect which principle?
items.a: Popular sovereignty
items.ex: “We the People” signals that the government's authority comes from the people themselves, not from the states or a monarch: popular sovereignty.
w: Separation of powers
Separation of powers (Montesquieu) divides authority among three branches; it is built into Articles I–III.
Federalism
Federalism divides power between national and state governments; the phrase names the people as the source of power.
Judicial review
Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

alt.q: At Virginia's 1788 ratifying convention, Patrick Henry objected that the framers had written “We, the people” instead of “We, the states.” The wording he objected to emphasizes that the Constitution's authority comes from…
alt.a: The people of the nation as a whole
alt.ex: The Preamble grounds the Constitution in the people (popular sovereignty), which Anti-Federalists like Henry saw as creating a consolidated national government.
w: The state legislatures acting together
Authority from the states was the basis of the Articles of Confederation, which Henry preferred.
The Confederation Congress that called it
The Confederation Congress only forwarded the Constitution; it was not named as its source.
The convention delegates' own authority
The delegates claimed no authority of their own; the text points to the people.

alt.q: A government that rests on the consent of the governed is applying popular sovereignty. Which words of the Constitution most directly express this idea?
alt.a: “We the People of the United States”
alt.ex: The Preamble's opening words name the people as the ones who “ordain and establish” the Constitution.
w: “secure the Blessings of Liberty to ourselves”
This Preamble goal concerns protecting freedom, not the source of the government's authority.
“the supreme Law of the Land”
This phrase is from the Supremacy Clause of Article VI.
“a Republican Form of Government”
This is the Guarantee Clause of Article IV, promising each state a representative government.

items.q: Congress funds a national army and navy to protect the country against foreign attack. Which goal of the Preamble does this most directly serve?
items.a: “provide for the common defence”
items.ex: Protecting the nation from outside threats is the Preamble goal to “provide for the common defence.”
w: “insure domestic Tranquility”
Domestic tranquility means peace and order inside the country, such as stopping uprisings.
“promote the general Welfare”
General welfare refers to the overall well-being of the people, not military protection.
“secure the Blessings of Liberty”
This goal concerns protecting freedom for present and future generations.

alt.q: After Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787), many leaders wanted a national government able to keep order inside the states. Which Preamble goal best reflects this concern?
alt.a: “insure domestic Tranquility”
alt.ex: Shays' Rebellion was an internal uprising in Massachusetts; keeping peace at home is the goal to “insure domestic Tranquility.”
w: “provide for the common defence”
Common defence refers to protection from foreign enemies, not internal unrest.
“establish Justice”
Establishing justice refers to fair laws and courts.
“promote the general Welfare”
General welfare concerns the people's overall well-being.

alt.q: A federal court system that settles disputes under fair and equal laws best serves which Preamble goal?
alt.a: “establish Justice”
alt.ex: Fair laws and impartial courts serve the Preamble goal to “establish Justice.”
w: “insure domestic Tranquility”
Domestic tranquility means keeping peace and order at home.
“form a more perfect Union”
This goal refers to strengthening the bonds among the states beyond the Articles of Confederation.
“secure the Blessings of Liberty”
This goal concerns protecting freedom for the people and their descendants.

items.q: Which set of requirements does Article I set for members of the House of Representatives?
items.a: Age 25, a citizen for 7 years, an inhabitant of the state; 2-year term
items.ex: Article I, Section 2 requires Representatives to be at least 25, citizens for 7 years and inhabitants of their state, and sets two-year terms.
w: Age 30, a citizen for 9 years, an inhabitant of the state; 6-year term
These are the requirements and term for Senators (Article I, Section 3).
Age 35, natural-born citizen, 14 years a resident; 4-year term
These are the requirements and term for the President (Article II, Section 1).
Age 21, a citizen for 5 years, a resident of the district; 2-year term
Article I sets no age-21 rule and no district-residence requirement for the House.

alt.q: A 26-year-old who has been a U.S. citizen for 8 years and lives in Ohio wants to serve in Congress for Ohio. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: They may serve in the House but not yet in the Senate
alt.ex: They meet the House minimums (25 years old, 7 years a citizen) but not the Senate's (30 years old, 9 years a citizen).
w: They may serve in the Senate but not yet in the House
This reverses the rules; the Senate's requirements are stricter than the House's.
They may serve in neither chamber until they turn 30
Age 30 applies only to the Senate; the House minimum is 25.
They may serve in either chamber, since only citizenship matters
Both chambers have age and citizenship-length requirements.

alt.q: “No Person shall be a Representative who shall not have attained to the Age of twenty five Years, and been seven Years a Citizen of the United States…” A person who meets these requirements and wins a seat must face reelection…
alt.a: Every two years
alt.ex: Article I, Section 2 provides that House members are chosen “every second Year,” keeping the House closest to the people.
w: Every four years
Four-year terms belong to the President and Vice President.
Every six years
Six-year terms belong to Senators.
Every three years
No federal elected office has a three-year term.

items.q: Which feature did the framers give the Senate to make it more stable and less swayed by sudden shifts in public opinion than the House?
items.a: Six-year terms, with one-third of seats up every two years
items.ex: Article I, Section 3 sets staggered six-year terms; originally senators were also chosen by state legislatures, until the Seventeenth Amendment (1913).
w: Two-year terms, with every seat up for election at the same time
That describes the House of Representatives.
Seats divided among the states according to population
Population-based seats describe the House; each state has two senators.
Service for life during good behavior, like judges
Life tenure applies to federal judges under Article III, not to senators.

alt.q: Under the original Constitution of 1787, how were U.S. senators chosen?
alt.a: By the legislature of each state
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3 originally had senators “chosen by the Legislature thereof”; the Seventeenth Amendment (1913) switched to direct popular election.
w: By direct popular vote in each state
Direct election came only with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913.
By the Electoral College every 6 years
The Electoral College chooses the President and Vice President.
By the House of Representatives
The House plays no role in choosing senators.

alt.q: In any single federal election year, about how many Senate seats are on the ballot nationwide?
alt.a: About one-third of the seats
alt.ex: Senators are divided into three classes so roughly one-third of the Senate is elected every two years (Article I, Section 3).
w: All one hundred of the seats
Electing every seat at once describes the House, not the Senate.
About one-half of the seats
The Senate is divided into thirds, not halves.
About two-thirds of the seats
Only one class (one-third) is chosen in each two-year cycle.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Great (Connecticut) Compromise of 1787?
items.a: It based the House on population and gave states equal Senate votes
items.ex: Roger Sherman's compromise blended the Virginia Plan (population) and the New Jersey Plan (equality) into a bicameral Congress.
w: It counted three-fifths of enslaved people for House seats and taxes
That was the Three-Fifths Compromise.
It gave each state one vote in a single-chamber legislature
That describes the Articles of Confederation and the New Jersey Plan.
It based seats in both houses of Congress on state population
That was the Virginia Plan, which small states rejected.

alt.q: Small states feared being outvoted, while large states wanted power based on population. Which outcome settled this dispute at the Convention?
alt.a: A two-house Congress mixing population and equal votes
alt.ex: The Great Compromise created a House apportioned by population and a Senate with two members per state.
w: A one-house Congress with one vote for each state
That was the New Jersey Plan, favored by small states.
A two-house Congress with both houses based on population
That was the Virginia Plan, favored by large states.
A three-fifths ratio for counting the enslaved
The Three-Fifths Compromise settled a different, North–South dispute.

alt.q: Which delegate is most closely associated with proposing the Great Compromise?
alt.a: Roger Sherman of Connecticut
alt.ex: Roger Sherman (with Oliver Ellsworth) of Connecticut proposed the plan, which is why it is also called the Connecticut Compromise.
w: James Madison of Virginia
Madison drafted the Virginia Plan, which based both houses on population.
William Paterson of New Jersey
Paterson presented the New Jersey Plan of equal state votes.
Alexander Hamilton of New York
Hamilton proposed a plan with a lifetime executive and senate, which was not adopted.

items.q: “The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen by the Legislature thereof, for six Years…” This provision most directly reflects which demand at the Constitutional Convention?
items.a: Small states' demand for equal representation
items.ex: Equal Senate representation was the small states' half of the Great Compromise, carried over from the New Jersey Plan.
w: Large states' demand for seats based on population
Population-based seats were the large states' demand, met in the House.
Southern states' demand to count enslaved people
That demand was settled by the Three-Fifths Compromise in Article I, Section 2.
Anti-Federalists' demand for a written bill of rights
That demand was met by the Bill of Rights in 1791, not by Senate structure.

alt.q: The idea preserved in this provision, equal votes for every state, had been proposed at the Convention in which plan?
alt.a: The New Jersey Plan
alt.ex: William Paterson's New Jersey Plan kept one vote per state; the Great Compromise preserved that idea in the Senate.
w: The Virginia Plan
The Virginia Plan based representation in both houses on population.
The Hamilton Plan
Hamilton's plan proposed senators serving for life, not equal state votes as such.
The Albany Plan of Union
The Albany Plan of Union (1754) was Benjamin Franklin's colonial proposal, decades earlier.

alt.q: What special protection does Article V give the rule stated in this provision?
alt.a: No state can lose its equal Senate vote without its consent
alt.ex: Article V ends: “no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.”
w: It can be changed only through a national amendment convention
Article V names no such special route for this rule.
It can be changed by a simple majority of the states
Ordinary amendments need three-fourths of the states, and this rule needs the affected state's consent.
It can be changed by Congress through ordinary legislation
Constitutional text cannot be changed by statute.

items.q: “…which shall be determined by adding to the whole Number of free Persons… three fifths of all other Persons.” This clause of Article I most directly determined…
items.a: How many House seats each state would receive
items.ex: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of enslaved people when apportioning House seats and direct taxes, boosting Southern power in the House and Electoral College.
w: How many Senate seats each state would receive
Every state receives two senators regardless of population.
Which people were allowed to vote in federal elections
The clause concerned counting population, not voting; states set voter qualifications.
Which states could keep importing enslaved people
The slave-trade clause (Article I, Section 9) barred Congress from ending imports before 1808.

alt.q: What did the Three-Fifths Compromise decide?
alt.a: How enslaved people were counted for seats and taxes
alt.ex: Article I, Section 2 counted “three fifths of all other Persons” for apportioning representatives and direct taxes.
w: How many senators each state would send to Congress
Senate seats were fixed at two per state by the Great Compromise.
Whether Congress could end the slave trade before 1808
That was a separate compromise in Article I, Section 9.
Whether new western states could allow slavery
That issue arose later, e.g., the Missouri Compromise (1820).

alt.q: Which amendment replaced the three-fifths formula by apportioning House seats “counting the whole number of persons in each State”?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) changed apportionment to count the whole number of persons.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery but did not rewrite the apportionment formula.
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred denying the vote on account of race.
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) barred denying the vote on account of sex.

items.q: A majority of the House votes to approve articles of impeachment against a federal judge. What happens next under the Constitution?
items.a: The Senate holds a trial; conviction requires a two-thirds vote
items.ex: The House has “the sole Power of Impeachment” (Art. I, §2); the Senate has “the sole Power to try all Impeachments” and conviction needs two-thirds of members present (§3).
w: The judge is removed from office at once by the House's vote
Impeachment is only a formal accusation; removal requires Senate conviction.
The Supreme Court holds a trial and decides by majority vote
The Supreme Court has no role in impeachment trials.
The Senate holds a trial; conviction requires only a simple majority
Conviction requires two-thirds of senators present, not a simple majority.

alt.q: Who presides over the Senate trial when a President has been impeached?
alt.a: The Chief Justice of the United States
alt.ex: Article I, Section 3: “When the President of the United States is tried, the Chief Justice shall preside.”
w: The Vice President of the United States
The Vice President normally presides over the Senate but would gain from a President's removal.
The Speaker of the House of Representatives
The Speaker leads the House, which only brings the charges.
The President pro tempore of the Senate
The President pro tempore presides in the Vice President's absence, not in presidential trials.

alt.q: Which statement best describes “impeachment” as the Constitution uses the term?
alt.a: A formal accusation voted by the House
alt.ex: Impeachment is the House's charge; removal follows only if two-thirds of the Senate votes to convict.
w: Removal from office after a Senate vote to convict
That is conviction and removal, the step after impeachment.
A criminal trial held in a federal district court
Impeachment is a political process in Congress, not a criminal trial.
A recall election held by a state's voters
Recall is a state-level procedure; federal officials cannot be recalled.

items.q: “The House of Representatives shall chuse their Speaker and other Officers; and shall have the sole Power of Impeachment.” Which statement best explains the power in the second half of this sentence?
items.a: Only the House may formally charge federal officials
items.ex: The House alone impeaches (accuses); the Senate alone tries the case and decides on removal.
w: Only the House may remove federal officials from office
Removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the Senate.
Only the House may try impeached officials and rule on them
The Senate has “the sole Power to try all Impeachments.”
Only the House may approve the President's appointments
Approving appointments is the Senate's “Advice and Consent” power.

alt.q: Article II, Section 4 lists which grounds for removing a President after impeachment and conviction?
alt.a: Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors
alt.ex: Article II, Section 4: officers “shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.”
w: Treason, incompetence, or a loss of the public's confidence
Incompetence and unpopularity are not listed grounds.
Any felony conviction in a state or federal court
The Constitution does not tie impeachment to criminal convictions.
Abuse of office as defined by the Supreme Court
The Court does not define impeachable offenses; Congress decides.

alt.q: Andrew Johnson (1868), Bill Clinton (1998) and Donald Trump (2019 and 2021) share which outcome?
alt.a: Impeached by the House but acquitted by the Senate
alt.ex: Each was impeached by a House majority, but the Senate never reached the two-thirds needed to convict; no President has been removed.
w: Removed from office after a Senate conviction
No President has ever been convicted and removed.
Resigned before the full House could vote
That describes Richard Nixon in 1974.
Impeached by the Senate but acquitted by the House
This reverses the roles; the House impeaches and the Senate tries.

items.q: “All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives…” Why did the framers give this power to the House?
items.a: Its members were directly elected by the people
items.ex: The House was the only chamber chosen directly by voters, so the power to start tax bills was placed closest to the people (“no taxation without representation”).
w: Its members served longer and more stable terms
Longer, more stable terms describe the Senate (six years).
It represented the states as equal partners
Equal state representation describes the Senate.
It was smaller and could act on bills more quickly
The House has always been the larger chamber.

alt.q: A senator introduces a bill to raise federal income tax rates. Under Article I, what is the constitutional problem?
alt.a: Revenue bills must begin in the House
alt.ex: Article I, Section 7 (the Origination Clause) requires revenue bills to originate in the House, though the Senate may amend them.
w: Tax bills need the President's approval in advance
The President signs or vetoes bills after passage; there is no prior approval.
Only state governments may levy income taxes
The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) lets Congress tax incomes.
Tax bills need a two-thirds vote in the Senate
Tax bills pass by majority vote; two-thirds is for overrides and treaties.

alt.q: Which power belongs to the House of Representatives alone?
alt.a: Starting bills that raise revenue
alt.ex: Under the Origination Clause, only the House may introduce revenue bills (the House also has the sole power of impeachment).
w: Approving treaties with foreign nations
Treaty approval belongs to the Senate (two-thirds of senators present).
Confirming judges and ambassadors
Confirmation is the Senate's “Advice and Consent” role.
Trying officials who are impeached
The Senate has the sole power to try impeachments.

items.q: Which of the following is an expressed (enumerated) power of Congress listed in Article I, Section 8?
items.a: Declaring war
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power “To declare War,” along with powers such as taxing, coining money and regulating commerce.
w: Chartering a national bank
A national bank is an implied power, upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Issuing drivers' licenses
Licensing drivers is a reserved power of the states.
Granting federal pardons
Pardons belong to the President under Article II, Section 2.

alt.q: Congress passes a law establishing post offices and post roads. This action is best classified as…
alt.a: An expressed power written in Article I
alt.ex: Article I, Section 8 expressly lists the power “To establish Post Offices and post Roads.”
w: An implied power from the Elastic Clause
Implied powers are not written; the postal power is listed word for word.
A reserved power under the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers belong to the states; postal service was delegated to Congress.
A concurrent power shared with the states
States may not run a competing postal system; it is a federal power.

alt.q: Which list contains only powers expressly given to Congress?
alt.a: Coin money, declare war, regulate interstate trade
alt.ex: All three are listed in Article I, Section 8.
w: Coin money, declare war, negotiate foreign treaties
Treaties are made by the President with two-thirds Senate consent (Article II).
Levy taxes, declare war, set up public schools
Public schools are a reserved power of the states.
Raise armies, borrow money, veto bills it dislikes
The veto belongs to the President (Article I, Section 7).

items.q: Congress passes a law declaring a specific, named person guilty of disloyalty and seizing their property without any trial. Which constitutional limit does this violate?
items.a: The ban on bills of attainder
items.ex: Article I, Section 9 says “No Bill of Attainder or ex post facto Law shall be passed”; a bill of attainder punishes a named person or group without a trial.
w: The ban on ex post facto laws
An ex post facto law punishes conduct that was legal when it was done.
The ban on titles of nobility
That clause bars granting titles such as duke or lord.
The limit on suspending habeas corpus
Habeas corpus protects against being held without being brought before a judge.

alt.q: “No Bill of Attainder or ex post facto Law shall be passed.” A bill of attainder is best described as…
alt.a: A law that punishes a named person without a trial
alt.ex: A bill of attainder lets the legislature act as judge and jury, which Article I, Section 9 forbids.
w: A law that punishes acts done before it was passed
That is an ex post facto law, the other item in this sentence.
A court order to bring a prisoner before a judge
That is a writ of habeas corpus.
A law that grants a citizen a title of nobility
Titles of nobility are banned by a separate clause of Section 9.

alt.q: “The Privilege of the Writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it.” This clause primarily protects people from…
alt.a: Being jailed without going before a judge
alt.ex: Habeas corpus lets a prisoner demand that a court review the legality of their detention; Lincoln controversially suspended it during the Civil War.
w: Being punished under a law passed after the act
That protection is the ban on ex post facto laws.
Being punished by a legislature without a trial
That protection is the ban on bills of attainder.
Being searched by police without any warrant
Protection from unreasonable searches is in the Fourth Amendment.

items.q: A state legislature votes to print its own paper currency and sign a trade treaty with Canada. Under Article I, Section 10, these actions are…
items.a: Forbidden, since states may not coin money or make treaties
items.ex: Article I, Section 10: “No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation; … coin Money; emit Bills of Credit…”
w: Allowed, since they are reserved powers of the states
Reserved powers cannot include powers the Constitution expressly denies to states.
Allowed, since they are concurrent powers shared with Congress
Concurrent powers include taxing and borrowing, not coining money or treaties.
Forbidden only because the Senate did not ratify the treaty
Even Senate approval could not let a state make a treaty; states also cannot coin money.

alt.q: Which problem from the Articles of Confederation era does Article I, Section 10 most directly address?
alt.a: States printing their own paper money
alt.ex: Under the Articles, states issued their own paper money, causing confusion and inflation; Section 10 bars states from coining money or emitting bills of credit.
w: Congress lacking any power to collect taxes
The taxing problem was fixed by Article I, Section 8, which limits Congress, not states.
No national court system to settle disputes
The lack of national courts was fixed by Article III.
Amendments needing approval of all 13 states
The unanimity problem was fixed by Article V.

alt.q: Which of the following is a power the Constitution denies to the states?
alt.a: Coining money
alt.ex: Article I, Section 10 bars states from coining money; it is an exclusive national power.
w: Collecting taxes
Taxing is a concurrent power held by both states and the national government.
Establishing courts
Both levels of government create courts, making this concurrent.
Conducting elections
Running elections is largely a state power (Article I, Section 4).

items.q: The President vetoes a bill. Which statement best describes how the bill can still become law?
items.a: Two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to override
items.ex: Article I, Section 7 lets Congress override a veto by a two-thirds vote in each house.
w: A simple majority of both houses passes it a second time
A simple majority passes a bill originally, but an override needs two-thirds.
The Supreme Court reviews the bill and approves it
Courts review laws only in actual cases; they cannot enact a vetoed bill.
Three-fourths of the state legislatures approve it
Three-fourths of the states is the threshold for ratifying amendments.

alt.q: Congress passes a bill and then adjourns, and the President neither signs nor returns it within ten days (Sundays excepted). What is the result?
alt.a: The bill dies in what is called a pocket veto
alt.ex: Under Article I, Section 7, an unsigned bill becomes law after ten days unless Congress's adjournment prevents its return, in which case it does not become law.
w: The bill becomes law without the President's signature
That happens only if Congress is still in session after ten days.
The bill is sent to the Supreme Court for decision
The Supreme Court plays no role in the lawmaking process.
The bill passes to the next Congress automatically
Bills do not carry over; a new Congress must start again.

alt.q: The veto and the veto override are best described as examples of…
alt.a: Checks and balances between branches
alt.ex: The President checks Congress with the veto, and Congress checks the President with the override.
w: Federalism between nation and states
Federalism concerns national-state relations; the veto involves two federal branches.
Judicial review of acts of Congress
Judicial review is the courts' check, not the President's.
Popular sovereignty through elections
Popular sovereignty means power comes from the people.

items.q: Which person would be constitutionally eligible to serve as President?
items.a: A 36-year-old natural-born citizen who has lived in the U.S. 15 years
items.ex: Article II, Section 1 requires a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and 14 years a resident of the United States.
w: A 40-year-old naturalized citizen who has lived in the U.S. 30 years
Naturalized citizens are not eligible; the President must be natural-born.
A 33-year-old natural-born citizen who has lived in the U.S. 33 years
This person is younger than the minimum age of 35.
A 50-year-old natural-born citizen who has lived in the U.S. 10 years
This person falls short of the 14-year residency requirement.

alt.q: “…neither shall any Person be eligible to that Office who shall not have attained to the Age of thirty five Years, and been fourteen Years a Resident within the United States.” Which other requirement does Article II add for this office?
alt.a: Being a natural-born citizen
alt.ex: Article II, Section 1 also requires the President to be “a natural born Citizen” (or a citizen when the Constitution was adopted).
w: Owning property in one's home state
The Constitution sets no property requirement for any federal office.
Prior service in Congress or the military
No prior office or military service is required.
Being a citizen for at least nine years
Nine years of citizenship is the requirement for Senators.

alt.q: Which minimum ages, in order, does the Constitution set for Representative, Senator and President?
alt.ex: Article I sets 25 for the House and 30 for the Senate; Article II sets 35 for the President.
w: These numbers are each one step too low.
This reverses the House and Senate ages.
Eighteen is the voting age under the Twenty-sixth Amendment, not an office minimum.

items.q: How does Article II determine the number of presidential electors each state receives?
items.a: It equals the state's senators plus its representatives
