items.ex: Each state gets electors “equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives” it has in Congress.
w: It equals only the state's number of House seats
This leaves out the two electors that match each state's senators.
It is two per state, regardless of population
Two per state matches Senate seats only, not the full elector count.
It is set by each state's share of the national popular vote
Elector numbers are fixed by congressional seats, not vote totals.

alt.q: “Each State shall appoint, in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct, a Number of Electors…” Under this clause, who decides how a state's electors are chosen?
alt.a: The state's legislature
alt.ex: Article II, Section 1 leaves the method of choosing electors to each state legislature; today every state uses a popular vote.
w: The United States Congress
Congress sets the day electors are chosen, not the method.
The U.S. Supreme Court
The Court resolves disputes but does not set each state's method.
The national party conventions
Parties nominate candidates; the Constitution gives the choice of method to legislatures.

alt.q: If no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, who chooses the President?
alt.a: The House, with one vote per state delegation
alt.ex: Under Article II and the Twelfth Amendment (1804), the House picks the President with each state delegation casting one vote (as in 1800 and 1824).
w: The Senate, with one vote cast by each senator
The Senate chooses the Vice President in that situation.
The House, with one vote for each member
Votes are cast by state delegations, one per state.
The Supreme Court, by a majority of justices
The Court has no constitutional role in choosing the President.

items.q: “He shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur…” This clause best illustrates…
items.a: Power shared between the President and the Senate
items.ex: The treaty power is split: the President negotiates, and two-thirds of senators present must consent, a check and balance.
w: Exclusive executive control over all foreign affairs
The clause requires Senate consent, so control is not exclusive.
Cooperation between federal and state governments
States have no role in treaties; Article I, Section 10 bars them from making treaties.
The House's role in approving foreign agreements
The House has no formal role in approving treaties.

alt.q: The President negotiates a treaty with another nation. What must happen before the treaty takes effect for the U.S.?
alt.a: Two-thirds of senators present must consent
alt.ex: Article II, Section 2 requires the consent of two-thirds of the senators present.
w: A majority of both houses must approve it
Treaties go to the Senate only, and need two-thirds, not a majority.
Three-fourths of the states must ratify it
State ratification applies to constitutional amendments.
The Supreme Court must review it in advance
The Court does not pre-approve treaties.

alt.q: The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles (1919–1920) is an example of which constitutional check?
alt.a: The Senate's treaty-consent power
alt.ex: President Wilson signed the treaty, but it never won two-thirds approval in the Senate, so the U.S. never ratified it.
w: Congress's power to declare war
Declaring war was not at issue; the treaty ended a war.
The House's power over revenue bills
The House has no formal role in treaties.
Judicial review of executive actions
No court was involved in the treaty's defeat.

items.q: A President nominates someone to fill a Supreme Court vacancy. What must happen for the nominee to take the seat?
items.a: A majority of the Senate must confirm the nominee
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 gives the President the power to appoint judges “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate”; confirmation is by majority vote.
w: Two-thirds of the Senate must confirm the nominee
Two-thirds is the threshold for treaties, not appointments.
Both the House and the Senate must confirm the nominee
The House has no role in confirming appointments.
The sitting justices must vote to accept the nominee
Justices have no constitutional role in choosing colleagues.

alt.q: Which officials does Article II say the President appoints with the Senate's “Advice and Consent”?
alt.a: Ambassadors and Supreme Court justices
alt.ex: Article II, Section 2 lists “Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court” and other officers.
w: Senators and members of the House
Members of Congress are elected, not appointed.
State governors and state judges
State officials are chosen under state law.
The presidential electors of each state
Electors are chosen as each state legislature directs.

alt.q: Senate confirmation hearings for a cabinet nominee are an example of…
alt.a: The legislative branch checking the executive
alt.ex: Requiring Senate consent for executive appointments lets Congress check the President.
w: The judicial branch checking the legislative branch
Courts are not involved in confirmations.
The executive branch checking the judiciary
A cabinet post is executive; the check here comes from the Senate.
The states checking the national government
Confirmation is a power of the U.S. Senate, not the states.

items.q: “The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States…” Which war-related power did the framers give to Congress instead, dividing control over war?
items.a: The power to declare war
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power “To declare War” and to raise and fund armies, while the President commands them.
w: The power to direct military strategy
Directing the armed forces is part of the President's role as Commander in Chief.
The power to negotiate peace treaties
The President negotiates treaties, subject to Senate consent.
The power to pardon military deserters
Pardons belong to the President under Article II.

alt.q: The War Powers Resolution (1973) was Congress's attempt to address tension between which two constitutional provisions?
alt.a: The Commander in Chief power and Congress's war power
alt.ex: After the Vietnam War, Congress sought to limit how long a President could commit troops without a declaration of war or authorization.
w: The treaty power and the Supremacy Clause of Article VI
These concern treaties as law, not the commitment of troops.
Congress's war power and the Senate's treaty power
Treaties were not at issue; the Resolution targets presidential troop deployments without congressional approval.
The appointment power and Senate confirmation
These concern filling offices, not military action.

alt.q: Which statement best describes how the Constitution divides military power?
alt.a: Congress declares war and funds forces; the President commands them
alt.ex: Article I gives Congress the power to declare war and raise armies; Article II makes the President Commander in Chief.
w: The President declares war; Congress commands the military
This reverses the roles of the two branches.
Congress both declares war and directly commands the military forces
Command belongs to the President.
The states declare war; the President commands the military
Article I, Section 10 bars states from engaging in war unless invaded.

items.q: Congress created the U.S. Air Force in 1947, though Article I mentions only armies and a navy. This action is best classified as an example of…
items.a: An implied power
items.ex: The power comes from the listed powers to raise armies and maintain a navy, combined with the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: An expressed power
Expressed powers are written out; an air force is not mentioned in the text.
A reserved power
Reserved powers belong to the states under the Tenth Amendment.
A concurrent power
Concurrent powers are shared by state and national governments; states cannot raise air forces.

alt.q: Which statement best defines implied powers?
alt.a: Unlisted powers reasonably drawn from listed ones
alt.ex: Implied powers are not written in the Constitution but are reasonably inferred from enumerated powers through the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: Powers specifically written in Article I, Section 8
That defines expressed (enumerated) powers.
Powers kept by the states under the Tenth Amendment
That defines reserved powers.
Powers used by both national and state governments
That defines concurrent powers.

alt.q: Which clause of Article I is the main textual basis for implied powers?
alt.a: The Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: The final clause of Article I, Section 8 lets Congress make all laws “necessary and proper” for carrying out its listed powers.
w: The Interstate Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause is itself an enumerated power over trade.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme over conflicting state law.
The Origination Clause
The Origination Clause requires revenue bills to begin in the House.

items.q: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” According to this excerpt, who creates the federal courts below the Supreme Court?
items.a: Congress
items.ex: Article III creates only the Supreme Court and leaves lower federal courts to Congress, which first set them up in the Judiciary Act of 1789.
w: The President
The President nominates judges but does not create courts.
The Supreme Court
The Supreme Court decides cases; it does not establish other courts.
The states
States create their own courts, not federal courts.

alt.q: Which statement about the federal court system is accurate under Article III?
alt.a: Only the Supreme Court is required; Congress sets up lower courts
alt.ex: Article III names one Supreme Court and lets Congress “ordain and establish” inferior courts.
w: The Constitution itself names every federal court that must exist
Only the Supreme Court is named; the rest are left to Congress.
States create the lower federal courts within their borders
Federal courts are created by Congress, not by states.
The President creates lower courts by executive order
Creating courts is a legislative power, not an executive one.

alt.q: Congress abolishes one federal appeals circuit and creates two new ones in its place. Under Article III, this action is…
alt.a: Permitted, since Congress establishes the lower courts
alt.ex: Congress may reorganize lower courts; for example, it split the Fifth Circuit in 1980, creating the Eleventh Circuit.
w: Forbidden, since only the Supreme Court can organize courts
The Supreme Court has no constitutional power to create or abolish courts.
Permitted only after the President issues an executive order
No executive order is needed; Congress acts by statute.
Forbidden, since Article III fixes the number of courts
Article III sets no number of lower courts.

items.q: “The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour…” The main purpose of this provision, along with protected salaries, is to…
items.a: Protect judges' independence from political pressure
items.ex: Tenure “during good Behaviour” (effectively life) and salaries that cannot be cut free judges from fear of the other branches and of voters.
w: Keep judges accountable to the voters who elect them
Federal judges are appointed, not elected, and life tenure reduces accountability to voters.
Let Congress remove judges who rule against it
Judges can be removed only by impeachment and conviction.
Give the President control over the courts' decisions
Life tenure means the President cannot fire judges after appointment.

alt.q: In practice, the “good Behaviour” clause of Article III means federal judges…
alt.a: Serve until death, resignation or removal
alt.ex: Federal judges have no fixed term; they leave office only by death, resignation, retirement, or impeachment and conviction.
w: Serve fixed terms of ten years each
Article III sets no fixed terms.
Must retire when they reach age 70
The Constitution sets no retirement age.
Face reconfirmation by the Senate periodically
Once confirmed, judges never face the Senate again.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 78, Alexander Hamilton defended life tenure for judges by arguing that the judiciary…
alt.a: Is “the least dangerous” branch and needs independence
alt.ex: Hamilton wrote that the judiciary “will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution,” having neither sword nor purse.
w: Commands the military and must be kept stable
The military belongs to the executive.
Holds the power of the purse and must be watched
The power of the purse belongs to the legislature.
Is elected by the people and must stay answerable to them
Federal judges are appointed, not elected.

items.q: Where does the federal courts' power of judicial review come from?
items.a: The ruling in Marbury v. Madison (1803)
items.ex: Judicial review is not stated in the Constitution; Chief Justice John Marshall established it in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: An explicit grant of power in Article III, Section 2
Article III defines jurisdiction but never mentions judicial review.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), on implied powers
McCulloch upheld the national bank and federal supremacy, not judicial review.
Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789
Marbury actually struck down part of Section 13 as unconstitutional.

alt.q: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” This sentence was written by which Chief Justice, in which case?
alt.a: John Marshall, in Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: Marshall wrote these words in Marbury v. Madison (1803), establishing judicial review.
w: John Marshall, in McCulloch v. Maryland
Right Chief Justice, wrong case; McCulloch (1819) concerned the national bank.
Roger Taney, in Dred Scott v. Sandford
Taney's Dred Scott opinion (1857) concerned slavery and citizenship.
John Jay, in Chisholm v. Georgia
Jay's era case (1793) concerned suits against states, leading to the Eleventh Amendment.

alt.q: A federal court rules that a law passed by Congress violates the First Amendment and cannot be enforced. The court is exercising…
alt.a: Judicial review
alt.ex: Judicial review is the power to declare laws or government acts unconstitutional, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
w: Original jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction is the power to hear a case first, not to void laws.
Executive privilege
Executive privilege is a President's claim to withhold information (U.S. v. Nixon, 1974).
Selective incorporation
Incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to the states; this was a federal law.

items.q: Texas sues New Mexico in a dispute over water from a river the two states share. Where does this case begin?
items.a: In the Supreme Court, under its original jurisdiction
items.ex: Article III, Section 2 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases “in which a State shall be Party,” so state-versus-state suits start there.
w: In a federal district court, followed by appeals
Most federal cases start there, but state-versus-state suits go straight to the Supreme Court.
In the Supreme Court, under its appellate jurisdiction
Appellate jurisdiction means reviewing a lower court; here no lower court is involved.
In the state courts of the defending state
A state court could not neutrally decide a dispute against another state.

alt.q: “In all Cases affecting Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, and those in which a State shall be Party, the supreme Court shall have original Jurisdiction.” Original jurisdiction means the Supreme Court…
alt.a: Hears the case first, acting as a trial court
alt.ex: In original jurisdiction cases, the Supreme Court is the first and only court to hear the dispute.
w: Reviews decisions already made by lower courts
That is appellate jurisdiction, which covers most of the Court's cases.
Chooses which appeals it will agree to hear
That is the certiorari process, a part of appellate review.
Gives advisory opinions when Congress asks
The Supreme Court does not issue advisory opinions.

alt.q: Most cases reach the U.S. Supreme Court under which type of jurisdiction?
alt.a: Appellate jurisdiction
alt.ex: Article III, Section 2 gives the Court appellate jurisdiction in “all the other Cases,” and nearly all of its cases arrive on appeal.
w: Original jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction covers only a few cases, such as those involving states or ambassadors.
Concurrent jurisdiction
Concurrent jurisdiction means two court systems may hear the same type of case.
Exclusive state jurisdiction
Cases solely under state law end in state courts.

items.q: “Treason against the United States, shall consist only in levying War against them, or in adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort.” Why did the framers define treason this narrowly?
items.a: To keep it from being used against political critics
items.ex: English rulers had used broad treason laws against opponents; Article III limits treason to two acts and requires two witnesses or a confession in open court.
w: To make treason easier to prosecute during times of war
A narrow definition and strict proof make treason harder, not easier, to prove.
To let Congress redefine treason as it chooses
The definition is fixed in the Constitution; Congress sets only the punishment.
To let each state try treason on its own terms
This clause defines treason against the United States.

alt.q: Which conduct would fit the Constitution's definition of treason?
alt.a: Secretly arming a country at war with the U.S.
alt.ex: Giving “Aid and Comfort” to enemies during war is one of the two forms of treason in Article III, Section 3.
w: Publicly criticizing the President's foreign policy
Criticism is protected speech, not treason.
Refusing to pay federal income taxes owed
Tax evasion is a crime but not treason.
Organizing a peaceful march against a war
Peaceful protest is protected by the First Amendment.

alt.q: A person is charged with treason. Under Article III, which evidence would be enough to convict?
alt.a: Two witnesses to the same overt act
alt.ex: Article III, Section 3 requires “the Testimony of two Witnesses to the same overt Act, or … Confession in open Court.”
w: One witness plus strong circumstantial evidence
The Constitution specifically requires two witnesses to the same act.
A confession made privately to police officers
A confession must be made in open court.
A grand jury indictment by itself alone
An indictment is only a formal charge, not proof for conviction.

items.q: A U.S. territory votes to seek statehood. Under Article IV, who has the power to admit it as a new state?
items.a: Congress
items.ex: Article IV, Section 3: “New States may be admitted by the Congress into this Union.”
w: The President
The President signs admission laws but cannot admit a state alone.
The Supreme Court
The Court has no role in admitting states.
Three-fourths of the states
Three-fourths of the states ratify amendments, not new states.

alt.q: Residents of one region of a state want to break away and form a new state. Article IV requires consent from…
alt.a: The state's legislature and Congress
alt.ex: No new state may be formed within another state without consent of the legislatures concerned and of Congress (Art. IV, §3); West Virginia (1863) is the classic case.
w: Only the residents of the breakaway region
Local residents alone cannot create a state.
Only Congress, acting by itself
The existing state's legislature must also agree.
The President and the Supreme Court
Neither has a role in forming new states.

alt.q: Which article of the Constitution deals with relations among the states and the admission of new states?
alt.a: Article IV
alt.ex: Article IV covers full faith and credit, privileges and immunities, extradition, new states and the republican-government guarantee.
w: Article I
Article I sets up Congress and its powers.
Article V
Article V describes the amendment process.
Article VI
Article VI covers supremacy, debts and oaths.

items.q: A state charges out-of-state residents a much higher fee than its own residents for a commercial fishing license, and the law is challenged. Which Article IV provision is most directly at issue?
items.a: The Privileges and Immunities Clause
items.ex: Article IV, Section 2 entitles citizens of each state to “all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States,” limiting discrimination against out-of-staters.
w: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause requires states to honor other states' public acts, records and court judgments.
Article IV's Republican Guarantee Clause
That clause promises each state a republican form of government.
The Extradition Clause
That clause requires states to return people who flee criminal charges.

alt.q: A person charged with a crime in Georgia flees to Alabama. Under Article IV, Alabama generally must…
alt.a: Return the person to Georgia on demand
alt.ex: Article IV, Section 2's Extradition Clause requires a fugitive to be delivered up on demand of the state they fled.
w: Try the person in Alabama's own courts
Crimes are tried in the state where they were committed.
Grant the person asylum if they request it
States may not shelter fugitives from other states.
Refer the matter to the Supreme Court first
Extradition is handled between the states' executives.

alt.q: “The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government…” This clause promises each state…
alt.a: A government run by elected representatives
alt.ex: The Guarantee Clause (Article IV, Section 4) promises republican, representative government and protection from invasion.
w: Equal representation in the United States Senate
Equal Senate representation is in Article I and protected by Article V.
Freedom from all forms of federal taxation
States receive no such protection.
A government chosen by the national political parties
Parties are not mentioned in the Constitution.

items.q: Which pair correctly describes the two ways Article V allows amendments to be proposed?
items.a: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention called at the request of two-thirds of the states
items.ex: Proposal: two-thirds of both houses, or a national convention on application of two-thirds of state legislatures; ratification: three-fourths of the states.
w: Three-fourths of both houses of Congress, or a convention called at the request of three-fourths of the states
Three-fourths is the ratification threshold, not the proposal threshold.
A majority of both houses of Congress, or a convention called at the request of a majority of the state governors
Article V requires two-thirds, and it gives governors no role.
Two-thirds of the Senate acting alone, or a national referendum called by the President of the United States
The House must also vote, and Article V has no national referendum or presidential role.

alt.q: After an amendment has been proposed, what does Article V require to ratify it?
alt.a: Approval by three-fourths of the states
alt.ex: Ratification requires the legislatures of, or conventions in, three-fourths of the states (38 of 50 today).
w: Approval by two-thirds of the states
Two-thirds is the threshold for proposing, not ratifying.
Approval by a majority of voters nationwide
The Constitution has no national referendum.
Approval by the President and the Supreme Court
Neither has a formal role in ratification.

alt.q: “The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution, or, on the Application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States, shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments…” Which statement about this process is accurate?
alt.a: Every amendment so far has been proposed by Congress
alt.ex: All 27 amendments were proposed by two-thirds of Congress; the convention route has never been used.
w: Most amendments were proposed by a national convention
No national convention for proposing amendments has ever been called.
The President must sign each proposed amendment
The President has no formal role in proposing amendments.
Amendments take effect once Congress proposes them
Proposed amendments must still be ratified by three-fourths of the states.

items.q: The Twenty-first Amendment (1933), which repealed Prohibition, is unique among the amendments because it was…
items.a: Ratified by state conventions, not legislatures
items.ex: Article V allows ratification by legislatures or conventions in three-fourths of the states; the Twenty-first is the only amendment ratified by conventions.
w: Proposed by a national convention, not by Congress
Congress proposed it; no amendment has come from a national convention.
Ratified by a national popular referendum
Article V provides no national referendum.
Adopted without the President's signature
No amendment needs a President's signature, so this is not unique.

alt.q: Thirty-five of the fifty states have ratified a proposed amendment. What is its status?
alt.a: Not yet ratified; 38 states are needed
alt.ex: Three-fourths of 50 states is 37.5, so 38 states must ratify.
w: Ratified, since two-thirds of the states approved
Two-thirds is the threshold for proposing, not ratifying.
Ratified, since a majority of the states approved
A simple majority of states is not enough.
Not yet ratified; 45 states are needed
Article V requires three-fourths (38), not 90 percent.

alt.q: The amendment process is often described as “federal” in character because…
alt.a: Both national and state bodies take part
alt.ex: Congress (or a convention) proposes and the states ratify, so both levels of government participate.
w: Only the national government may change it
Ratification requires action by three-fourths of the states.
Only the states may propose any change
Congress has proposed every amendment so far.
The Supreme Court must approve each change
The Court has no formal role in amending the Constitution.

items.q: Why did the framers make amending the Constitution difficult but still possible?
items.a: To allow change but guard against hasty changes
items.ex: Supermajority thresholds (two-thirds to propose, three-fourths to ratify) make change deliberate, while avoiding the Articles' unanimity rule.
w: To prevent the Constitution from ever being changed
Article V exists precisely so the Constitution can change.
To let Congress alone update it whenever needed
The states must ratify every amendment.
To make sure no group of states could block a change
Just 13 of the 50 states can block ratification, since 38 are needed.

alt.q: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation did Article V correct?
alt.a: Amendments needed all thirteen states' approval
alt.ex: Under the Articles, amendments required unanimity, so one state could block reform; Article V lowered this to three-fourths.
w: Congress could not regulate trade among the states
Trade was fixed by the Commerce Clause in Article I.
No national executive existed to enforce the laws
That was fixed by Article II.
Each state had one vote in the Congress
That was addressed by the Great Compromise in Article I.

alt.q: Supporters of a balanced-budget amendment, frustrated with Congress, urge state legislatures to apply for a convention. Which Article V route are they using?
alt.a: A convention on application of two-thirds of the states
alt.ex: Article V lets two-thirds of state legislatures require Congress to call a convention to propose amendments; this route has never been completed.
w: A proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress
That is the congressional route these supporters are bypassing.
Ratification by conventions in three-fourths of the states
That is a ratification method, used only after an amendment is proposed.
A national referendum called by the state governors
Article V provides no referendum and no role for governors.

items.q: “…no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.” This clause most directly means that…
items.a: Federal officials cannot be required to hold a faith
items.ex: Article VI bars religious qualifications for federal office, at a time when many states required officeholders to hold Christian beliefs.
w: Congress may not establish an official national church
That is the First Amendment's Establishment Clause.
People may freely practice any religion they choose
That is the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause.
States must keep organized prayer out of public schools
That comes from Engel v. Vitale (1962) under the Establishment Clause.

alt.q: Before the Bill of Rights was added, which part of the Constitution addressed religion and government office?
alt.a: Article VI, banning religious tests
alt.ex: The original Constitution's main reference to religion is Article VI's ban on religious tests for federal office.
w: Article I, barring a national church
The ban on an established church is in the First Amendment (1791).
Article III, protecting free worship
Article III concerns the courts; free exercise is in the First Amendment.
The Preamble, invoking God's blessing
The Preamble does not mention God or religion.

alt.q: A federal agency requires applicants for a senior post to swear that they believe in God. Which provision of the original Constitution does this most directly violate?
alt.a: Article VI's ban on religious tests
alt.ex: Requiring a profession of belief as a condition of federal office is exactly what Article VI forbids.
w: Article I's ban on titles of nobility
That clause bars granting noble titles, not religious oaths.
Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause protects out-of-state citizens from discrimination by states.
Article II's presidential oath of office
The President's oath has no religious requirement and does not govern other posts.

items.q: A newly elected state legislator takes an oath of office. Under Article VI, that oath must include a promise to…
items.a: Support the Constitution of the United States
items.ex: Article VI requires federal and state legislators, executives and judges to be bound “by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution.”
w: Support only the constitution of their own state
State officials must also support the U.S. Constitution.
Support the policies of the current President
Oaths run to the Constitution, not to any officeholder.
Support the platform of their political party
The Constitution never mentions political parties.

alt.q: “…the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution…” Why is it significant that state officials are included?
alt.a: It binds state officials to the national Constitution
alt.ex: Requiring state officers to swear to support the Constitution reinforces federal supremacy within the states.
w: It lets state officials overrule federal laws they oppose
Article VI does the opposite, making federal law supreme.
It makes state officials employees of the federal government
State officials remain state officers; the oath binds them to the Constitution.
It requires state officials to belong to a religious faith
Article VI forbids religious tests for federal office.

alt.q: Which promise in Article VI reassured creditors and foreign nations in 1787?
alt.a: Debts from before the Constitution remained valid
alt.ex: Article VI: “All Debts contracted and Engagements entered into, before the Adoption of this Constitution, shall be as valid against the United States…”
w: States could print money to repay their debts
Article I, Section 10 bars states from coining money or emitting bills of credit.
Congress would cancel all Revolutionary War debts
The Constitution kept those debts valid.
Creditors could sue the President for repayment
No such provision exists.

items.q: “The Ratification of the Conventions of nine States, shall be sufficient for the Establishment of this Constitution between the States so ratifying the Same.” Why did the framers adopt this rule instead of requiring all thirteen states?
items.a: Unanimity had made the Articles nearly unamendable
items.ex: Because amending the Articles required all 13 states, the framers let nine states put the Constitution into effect; New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788.
w: Nine states already held a majority of the population
Population was not the basis for the rule; it counted states.
Rhode Island had already promised to ratify it
Rhode Island boycotted the Convention and ratified last, in 1790.
Only nine states had sent delegates to Philadelphia
Twelve states sent delegates; only Rhode Island did not.

alt.q: Which state's ratification in June 1788 made it the ninth, putting the Constitution into effect?
alt.a: New Hampshire
alt.ex: New Hampshire ratified on June 21, 1788, the ninth state; Virginia and New York followed soon after.
w: Delaware
Delaware ratified first, in December 1787.
Massachusetts
Massachusetts ratified sixth, in February 1788.
Rhode Island
Rhode Island ratified last, in May 1790.

alt.q: Article VII called for ratification by special state conventions rather than by state legislatures. The main reason was to…
alt.a: Base its authority directly on the people
alt.ex: Conventions elected for the purpose reflected popular sovereignty and bypassed legislatures that might resist losing power.
w: Let state legislatures keep control of the decision
Using conventions deliberately took the decision away from legislatures.
Speed approval by avoiding any public debate
Ratification produced intense public debate, such as the Federalist Papers.
Allow Congress to choose the convention delegates
Delegates were chosen in the states, not by Congress.

items.q: Both Florida and the national government collect taxes and run court systems. These are examples of…
items.a: Concurrent powers
items.ex: Concurrent powers are held by both levels of government at the same time, such as taxing, borrowing and establishing courts.
w: Reserved powers
Reserved powers belong to the states alone under the Tenth Amendment.
Implied powers
Implied powers are unlisted federal powers drawn from the Necessary and Proper Clause.
Enumerated powers
Enumerated powers are those listed for the national government, mainly in Article I, Section 8.

alt.q: Which power is best described as concurrent?
alt.a: Borrowing money
alt.ex: Both the states and the national government may borrow money, so it is a concurrent power.
w: Declaring war
Declaring war is an expressed power of Congress alone.
Coining money
Coining money is national only; Article I, Section 10 denies it to states.
Issuing marriage licenses
Marriage licensing is a reserved power of the states.

alt.q: Which statement best defines concurrent powers?
alt.a: Powers both levels of government may use
alt.ex: Concurrent means held at the same time by both levels, such as taxing and making laws.
w: Powers that are kept only by the states
That defines reserved powers.
Powers drawn from listed powers by implication
That defines implied powers.
Powers that are denied to both levels entirely
These are prohibited powers, such as granting titles of nobility.

items.q: “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” Which action is an example of the powers described?
items.a: A state setting rules for drivers' licenses
items.ex: The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers, such as licensing drivers, to the states.
w: Congress setting rules for trade with Mexico
Regulating foreign commerce is a power delegated to Congress.
The national government printing paper money
Coining and printing money is a delegated national power.
A state signing a defense pact with Canada
Treaties and alliances are prohibited to the states by Article I, Section 10.

alt.q: Which amendment is the basis for the states' reserved powers?
alt.a: The Tenth Amendment
alt.ex: The Tenth Amendment (1791) reserves powers not delegated to the national government to the states or the people.
w: The Ninth Amendment
The Ninth protects unlisted rights retained by the people, not state powers.
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth limits the states (due process, equal protection).
The Eleventh Amendment
The Eleventh limits federal-court lawsuits against states.

alt.q: A state creates a public school system, sets graduation requirements and licenses its teachers. Which type of power is it using?
alt.a: Reserved powers
alt.ex: Education is not delegated to the national government, so it falls to the states under the Tenth Amendment.
w: Delegated powers
Delegated powers are those given to the national government.
Implied powers
Implied powers are unlisted federal powers drawn from listed ones.
Concurrent powers
Running a school system is not a power shared with the national government.

items.q: A state law directly conflicts with a valid federal statute that Congress passed under its commerce power. A court will most likely rule that…
items.a: The federal statute controls under Article VI
items.ex: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, federal laws made under it, and treaties “the supreme Law of the Land,” overriding conflicting state law.
w: The state law controls under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment reserves only undelegated powers; commerce power was delegated.
Both laws apply, and residents may choose one
When laws truly conflict, the federal law preempts the state law.
Whichever law was passed more recently controls
Timing does not matter; federal supremacy does.

alt.q: “This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land…” This excerpt is known as…
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause
alt.ex: This is the Supremacy Clause of Article VI.
w: The Necessary and Proper Clause
That clause (Article I, Section 8) lets Congress pass laws to carry out its powers.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause (Article IV) requires states to honor each other's acts and judgments.
The Commerce Clause
That clause (Article I, Section 8) gives Congress power over interstate and foreign trade.

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Maryland's tax on the Second Bank of the United States was struck down mainly because…
alt.a: A state may not tax a valid federal institution
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall reasoned that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy” and that federal supremacy bars states from burdening federal operations.
w: No power of Congress supported creating the bank
The Court held the bank valid as an implied power under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
Only Congress may levy taxes of any kind at all
States may tax; taxing is a concurrent power.
The tax violated the Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns respect among the states, not state taxes on federal entities.

items.q: “…and the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding.” This part of Article VI means state judges must…
items.a: Apply federal law over conflicting state law
items.ex: State judges are bound by the U.S. Constitution, federal laws and treaties even when their own state's constitution or laws say otherwise.
w: Apply state law over conflicting federal law
This reverses the Supremacy Clause.
Refer every federal question to the Supreme Court
State courts decide federal questions themselves, subject to review.
Be appointed by the President and the Senate
State judges are chosen under state law.

alt.q: Which historical claim most directly conflicts with the Supremacy Clause?
alt.a: Nullification, the claim a state may void federal law
alt.ex: South Carolina's nullification of federal tariffs (1832) contradicted the Supremacy Clause, and President Jackson rejected it.
w: Judicial review, the claim courts may void laws
Judicial review is consistent with the Supremacy Clause.
Popular sovereignty, the claim power comes from the people
This principle underlies the Preamble, not a challenge to supremacy.
Federalism, the claim power is divided by level
Federalism includes federal supremacy within delegated powers.

alt.q: After Brown v. Board of Education, Arkansas officials claimed they were not bound by the ruling. In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), the Supreme Court relied mainly on…
alt.a: The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
alt.ex: The Court held that its interpretation of the Constitution in Brown was the supreme law of the land and binding on state officials.
w: The Commerce Clause of Article I
The Commerce Clause concerns Congress's power over trade.
The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
Arkansas's states'-rights argument was rejected, not relied on.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause governs respect among states, not federal-state conflict.

items.q: A Florida court orders a person to pay $20,000 in damages. The person moves to Georgia to avoid paying. Which clause requires Georgia's courts to enforce the Florida judgment?
items.a: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
items.ex: Article IV, Section 1 requires each state to give full faith and credit to the “judicial Proceedings of every other State.”
w: The Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause protects out-of-state citizens from discrimination, not judgments.
The Supremacy Clause
That clause settles federal-state conflicts, not state-to-state ones.
The Extradition Clause
That clause returns people fleeing criminal charges; this is a civil judgment.

alt.q: A couple married in Alabama moves to Oregon, which recognizes their marriage. Which constitutional provision most directly supports this recognition?
alt.a: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
alt.ex: Full Faith and Credit requires states to respect the “public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings” of other states, such as marriage records.
w: Article IV's Republican Guarantee Clause
That clause promises a republican form of government.
Article VI's Supremacy Clause
That clause makes federal law supreme over state law.
Article I's Commerce Clause
That clause gives Congress power over trade.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of the Full Faith and Credit Clause?
alt.a: To make states respect each other's laws and rulings
alt.ex: It keeps the states from acting like foreign countries toward each other's official acts and court judgments.
w: To make states treat visitors like their own citizens
That is the purpose of the Privileges and Immunities Clause.
To make state laws yield to valid federal laws
That is the purpose of the Supremacy Clause.
To make states return people who flee criminal charges
That is the purpose of the Extradition Clause.

items.q: “Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State.” Which situation best illustrates this clause?
items.a: Nevada enforcing a child-support order issued in Utah
items.ex: A child-support order is a judicial proceeding, so other states must give it full faith and credit.
w: Nevada letting Utah residents buy land on equal terms
Equal treatment of out-of-staters is Privileges and Immunities.
Nevada sending a fugitive back to Utah for trial
Returning fugitives is the Extradition Clause.
Nevada following a federal law over its own statute
Federal law prevailing over state law is the Supremacy Clause.

alt.q: This clause appears in which article of the Constitution?
alt.a: Article IV, on interstate relations
alt.ex: Full Faith and Credit is Article IV, Section 1, the article on interstate relations.
w: Article I, on the powers of Congress
Article I creates Congress and lists its powers.
Article III, on the federal courts
Article III creates the judiciary.
Article VI, on federal supremacy
Article VI contains the Supremacy Clause, oaths and debts.

alt.q: The Full Faith and Credit Clause and the Privileges and Immunities Clause share which main goal?
alt.a: Uniting the states as one nation, not rivals
alt.ex: Both Article IV clauses keep states from treating one another and one another's citizens as foreign.
w: Strengthening the President's power over the states
Neither clause involves the President.
Protecting people from searches by state police
Search protections come from the Fourth Amendment.
Letting each state ignore the others' laws
Both clauses do the opposite.

items.q: “To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes…” Congress relied on this power to pass which law, upheld in Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964)?
items.a: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
items.ex: The Court upheld the Act's ban on discrimination in public accommodations because such discrimination burdened interstate travel and commerce.
w: The Voting Rights Act of 1965
That law enforced the Fifteenth Amendment's voting protections.
The Pendleton Act of 1883
That law created merit-based civil service hiring.
The Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990
That law was struck down as beyond the commerce power in U.S. v. Lopez (1995).

alt.q: A motel serving mostly interstate travelers refuses to rent rooms to Black guests. Congress's power to ban this discrimination was upheld under…
alt.a: The Commerce Clause
alt.ex: In Heart of Atlanta Motel v. U.S. (1964), the Court held that racial discrimination by businesses serving travelers affected interstate commerce.
w: The Equal Protection Clause
That clause limits state action; the motel was a private business.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns states honoring one another's acts and rulings.
The Emoluments Clause
That clause bars officials from taking unapproved payments or gifts.

alt.q: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) is a key Commerce Clause case because the Court held that…
alt.a: Congress's commerce power covers navigation between states
alt.ex: Chief Justice Marshall read “commerce” broadly to include navigation and struck down New York's steamboat monopoly as it conflicted with a federal license.
w: States may grant monopolies over interstate waterways
The Court struck down New York's monopoly.
Congress may not regulate trade within any state's borders
The ruling expanded, not restricted, federal power.
Commerce means only the buying and selling of goods
Marshall rejected this narrow definition.

items.q: In United States v. Lopez (1995), the Supreme Court struck down a federal ban on guns in school zones mainly because…
items.a: Congress overstepped its interstate commerce power
items.ex: The Court held that carrying a gun near a school is not economic activity substantially affecting interstate commerce, the first such limit since 1937.
w: The ban violated the Second Amendment right to bear arms
The case was decided on Commerce Clause grounds, not the Second Amendment.
The ban conflicted with the Supremacy Clause of Article VI
Supremacy concerns valid federal law over state law; the law here was invalid.
Congress has no power to regulate any firearms at all
Congress regulates firearms in commerce; Lopez was narrower.

alt.q: Which case was the first in nearly sixty years to limit Congress's power under the Commerce Clause?
alt.a: United States v. Lopez (1995)
alt.ex: Lopez ended a long line of decisions since 1937 that had upheld nearly every use of the commerce power.
w: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Gibbons expanded the commerce power.
Heart of Atlanta Motel v. U.S. (1964)
Heart of Atlanta upheld the Civil Rights Act under the commerce power.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
McCulloch concerned implied powers and a national bank.

alt.q: Congress makes it a federal crime to have a gun within 1,000 feet of a school, arguing that school violence harms the economy. The strongest objection, as in Lopez, is that…
alt.a: Gun possession is not commerce Congress can regulate
alt.ex: Lopez held that simple possession near a school is not commercial activity, so the commerce power could not reach it.
w: The law is an unconstitutional bill of attainder
A bill of attainder punishes named persons without trial; this law is general.
The law violates the Full Faith and Credit Clause of Article IV
That clause concerns interstate respect for records and judgments.
The law is an ex post facto law punishing past acts
The law applies only to future conduct.

items.q: “…no Person holding any Office of Profit or Trust under them, shall, without the Consent of the Congress, accept of any present, Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever, from any King, Prince, or foreign State.” The main purpose of this clause is to…
items.a: Keep foreign powers from buying officials' loyalty
items.ex: The Foreign Emoluments Clause (Article I, Section 9) guards against corruption and divided loyalty by requiring congressional consent for foreign gifts or titles.
w: Stop Congress from giving its own members an immediate raise
Congressional pay changes are limited by the Twenty-seventh Amendment.
Stop the states from granting titles of nobility
States are barred from granting titles by Article I, Section 10.
Stop the President from making treaties alone
The treaty power requires Senate consent under Article II.

alt.q: A foreign monarch offers a U.S. ambassador a valuable gift and an honorary title. Under the Constitution, the ambassador may accept only if…
alt.a: Congress consents to the gift and the title
alt.ex: The Foreign Emoluments Clause bars federal officeholders from accepting foreign presents or titles “without the Consent of the Congress.”
w: The President approves it in a written order
The clause gives the consent power to Congress, not the President.
The Senate ratifies it by a two-thirds vote
Two-thirds Senate votes are for treaties, not gifts.
The Supreme Court finds no conflict of interest
Courts do not pre-approve gifts to officials.

alt.q: Which clause forbids the President from receiving any payment from the United States or the states beyond the fixed salary?
alt.a: The Domestic Emoluments Clause
alt.ex: Article II, Section 1 says the President “shall not receive within that Period any other Emolument from the United States, or any of them.”
w: The Foreign Emoluments Clause
That clause (Article I, Section 9) concerns gifts from foreign states.
The Origination Clause
That clause requires revenue bills to start in the House.
The Take Care Clause of Article II
That clause requires the President to see that laws are faithfully executed.

items.q: As used in the Constitution, the word “emolument” best means…
items.a: A payment or other benefit gained from an office
items.ex: An emolument is compensation or advantage from an office; both Emoluments Clauses limit such benefits to prevent corruption.
w: A formal charge of misconduct against an officer
That is an impeachment.
A title of nobility granted by a foreign ruler
Titles are listed separately from emoluments in the clause.
A law punishing a person without a trial
That is a bill of attainder.

alt.q: “…he shall not receive within that Period any other Emolument from the United States, or any of them.” This provision is meant to keep the President…
alt.a: Independent of extra pay from Congress or the states
alt.ex: Fixing the President's salary and barring other federal or state emoluments prevents Congress or the states from rewarding or pressuring the President.
w: Loyal to the political party that first nominated them
The Constitution does not mention parties.
Free from paying any federal income taxes
The clause does not address taxes.
Unable to accept titles from foreign kings
Foreign gifts and titles fall under the Foreign Emoluments Clause.

alt.q: Both Emoluments Clauses reflect the framers' concern with…
alt.a: Corruption and divided loyalty in officeholders
alt.ex: Having seen European courts bribe diplomats, the framers limited officials' outside payments from foreign and domestic sources.
w: Protecting the rights of people accused of crimes
Rights of the accused appear in the Fifth and Sixth Amendments.
Balancing the power of large and small states
That was the focus of the Great Compromise.
Expanding federal power over interstate trade
That is the Commerce Clause.

items.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the Constitution's two Due Process Clauses?
items.a: The Fifth limits the federal government; the Fourteenth limits the states
items.ex: The Fifth Amendment (1791) restrains federal action; the Fourteenth (1868) says “nor shall any State deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.”
w: The Fifth limits the states; the Fourteenth limits the federal government
This reverses the two clauses.
Both apply only to criminal trials held in federal courts
Due process covers civil and administrative actions at both levels.
The Fifth protects only property; the Fourteenth protects only liberty
Both protect life, liberty and property.

alt.q: A state agency revokes a teacher's license with no notice and no hearing. Which clause would the teacher most likely invoke?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause
alt.ex: Because a state acted, the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of fair procedure before taking liberty or property applies.
w: The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause
The Fifth Amendment's clause restrains the federal government.
Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause bars discrimination against out-of-state citizens.
The Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause
That clause defines who is a citizen.

alt.q: The Supreme Court has applied most of the Bill of Rights to the states through which provision?
alt.a: The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause
alt.ex: Through selective incorporation (e.g., Gitlow 1925, Mapp 1961, Gideon 1963), the Court has read “liberty” in this clause to include most Bill of Rights guarantees.
w: The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers of states
The Tenth Amendment protects state powers, not individual rights against states.
The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause
The Fifth Amendment limits only the federal government.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
Supremacy settles conflicts between laws; incorporation came through due process.

items.q: “…nor shall any State deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law…” In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), the Court used this clause to require states to…
items.a: Provide lawyers to poor felony defendants
items.ex: Gideon incorporated the Sixth Amendment right to counsel against the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
w: Exclude illegally seized evidence from trials
That was Mapp v. Ohio (1961), applying the exclusionary rule.
Warn suspects of their rights before questioning
That was Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
Allow students to wear political armbands
That was Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), a free-speech case.

alt.q: Which idea best explains how the Bill of Rights came to limit state governments?
alt.a: Selective incorporation via the Fourteenth Amendment
alt.ex: Case by case, the Court has held that the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause makes most Bill of Rights protections binding on states.
w: Judicial review under Marbury v. Madison
Marbury established the power to void laws, not incorporation.
Federal supremacy as declared in McCulloch v. Maryland
McCulloch addressed implied powers and state taxation of a federal bank.
Reserved powers under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment protects state power rather than limiting it.

alt.q: The core idea of “due process of law” is best described as…
alt.a: Government must use fair steps before taking rights
alt.ex: Due process requires fair, established legal procedures, such as notice and a hearing, before depriving anyone of life, liberty or property.
w: Government must treat similarly situated people alike
That describes equal protection.
Government may use only powers the Constitution lists
That describes enumerated powers and limited government.
Government must win the people's consent in elections
That describes popular sovereignty.

items.q: “…nor deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.” In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Court relied on this clause to hold that…
items.a: State-segregated public schools are inherently unequal
items.ex: Brown held that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, violating the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
w: Separate facilities are legal if they are equal
That was the “separate but equal” rule of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which Brown rejected for schools.
Segregated interstate buses burden commerce
Bus segregation was challenged in other cases, not Brown.
Organized school prayer violates the Establishment Clause
That was Engel v. Vitale (1962).

alt.q: A state bars women from attending its public military college. The strongest constitutional challenge would cite…
alt.a: The Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: In United States v. Virginia (1996), the Court held that excluding women from the Virginia Military Institute violated equal protection.
w: The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause
The Fifth Amendment limits the federal government; this is a state school.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns states honoring each other's acts and judgments.
Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause
That clause protects out-of-state citizens, not women as a group.

alt.q: In public education, Brown v. Board of Education overturned which earlier case?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
alt.ex: Plessy had upheld “separate but equal”; Brown held it has no place in public education.
w: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
Dred Scott, denying Black citizenship, was overturned by the Fourteenth Amendment.
Korematsu v. United States (1944)
Korematsu upheld Japanese American internment.
Shaw v. Reno (1993)
Shaw concerned racial gerrymandering and came after Brown.

items.q: Under the Fourteenth Amendment, what does the Equal Protection Clause require of the states?
items.a: It requires states to apply laws impartially to all people
items.ex: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) forbids any state to “deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.”
w: It requires states to honor other states' court rulings
That is the Full Faith and Credit Clause.
It requires states to follow fair procedures before punishing
That is the Due Process Clause.
It requires states to treat out-of-state visitors like residents
That is Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause.

alt.q: Because the Fourteenth Amendment speaks only of states, equal protection limits on the federal government come mainly from…
alt.a: The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause
alt.ex: In Bolling v. Sharpe (1954), the companion to Brown, the Court found equal protection principles in the Fifth Amendment to end segregation in D.C. schools.
w: The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
The Tenth reserves powers to states and the people.
The Ninth Amendment's retained rights
The Ninth protects unlisted rights but was not the basis.
Article IV's Republican Guarantee Clause
That clause promises states republican government.

alt.q: In Baker v. Carr (1962), voters challenged state legislative districts with very unequal populations. The later “one person, one vote” rule rests on…
alt.a: The Equal Protection Clause
alt.ex: Baker let courts hear apportionment claims under equal protection, and Reynolds v. Sims (1964) required districts of roughly equal population.
w: Article IV's Guarantee Clause
The Court has treated Guarantee Clause claims as political questions it will not decide.
The Seventeenth Amendment
That amendment provides for direct election of senators.
The Commerce Clause
The Commerce Clause concerns trade, not voting districts.

items.q: “To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers…” In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court relied on this clause to uphold…
items.a: Congress's creation of a national bank
items.ex: Marshall held that the bank was a legitimate means of carrying out powers to tax, borrow and regulate commerce, even though banks are not listed.
w: A state's tax on a federal bank branch
McCulloch struck down Maryland's tax under the Supremacy Clause.
A federal ban on guns near schools
That law was struck down in United States v. Lopez (1995).
The Court's own power of judicial review
Judicial review came from Marbury v. Madison (1803).

alt.q: The Necessary and Proper Clause is often called the “Elastic Clause” because it…
alt.a: Stretches Congress's powers to meet new needs
alt.ex: By allowing laws needed to carry out listed powers, the clause lets federal power expand to new situations through implied powers.
w: Stretches state powers when Congress fails to act
The clause concerns Congress's powers, not the states'.
Stretches the President's term during emergencies
Terms are fixed; no clause extends them.
Stretches the Constitution through easy amendment
Amendments follow the demanding Article V process.

alt.q: Anti-Federalists feared the Necessary and Proper Clause mainly because they believed it would…
alt.a: Let Congress claim almost unlimited power
alt.ex: Critics such as Brutus warned the clause, with the Supremacy Clause, would let Congress swallow up the states.
w: Let states veto any federal law
The clause expands federal power; it gives states no veto.
Weaken Congress compared with the President
Anti-Federalists feared a too-strong Congress under this clause.
Keep Congress from collecting taxes
Congress's taxing power is expressly listed in Article I, Section 8.

items.q: Congress creates the Federal Aviation Administration to regulate air travel between states, though airplanes are never mentioned in the Constitution. Which combination best justifies this?
items.a: The Commerce Clause with the Necessary and Proper Clause
items.ex: Regulating interstate travel is part of the commerce power, and the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress create agencies to carry it out.
w: The Supremacy Clause together with the Tenth Amendment
Supremacy settles conflicts and the Tenth reserves powers; neither grants new federal power.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause with the Guarantee Clause
These Article IV clauses concern relations among states, not federal agencies.
The Emoluments Clause with Article II
Emoluments rules limit gifts to officials.

alt.q: In McCulloch v. Maryland, the Court read the word “necessary” to mean…
alt.a: Useful or appropriate, not strictly indispensable
alt.ex: Marshall rejected Maryland's strict reading and held that Congress may choose any appropriate means plainly adapted to a legitimate end.
w: Absolutely essential, with no other possible option
This strict reading was Maryland's argument, which the Court rejected.
Approved first by a majority of the states
The Court required no state approval.
Listed explicitly elsewhere in Article I
If listed, a power would be expressed, not implied.

alt.q: Thomas Jefferson opposed the first Bank of the United States (1791) because he read the Necessary and Proper Clause…
alt.a: Strictly, allowing only essential laws
alt.ex: Jefferson's strict construction clashed with Hamilton's loose construction, which held the bank was a useful means to carry out listed powers.
w: Loosely, allowing any useful law
That was Hamilton's position, defending the bank.
As applying only to state governments
The clause applies to Congress.
As a grant of power to the President alone
The clause empowers Congress.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Federalists during the ratification debate of 1787–1788?
items.a: Backers of ratification and a stronger central government
items.ex: Federalists such as Hamilton, Madison and Jay argued the new Constitution would fix the Articles' weaknesses while protecting liberty.
w: Opponents who feared a strong and distant central government
That describes the Anti-Federalists.
Supporters of keeping the Articles with only small changes
Revising the Articles was closer to the Anti-Federalist view.
Members of Jefferson's Democratic-Republican Party
That party formed in the 1790s, after ratification.

alt.q: Which writers produced The Federalist Papers under the pen name “Publius”?
alt.a: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
alt.ex: The 85 essays appeared in New York newspapers in 1787–1788; Hamilton wrote most, Madison about 29 and Jay five.
w: Patrick Henry, George Mason and Richard Henry Lee
These were prominent Anti-Federalists from Virginia.
Thomas Jefferson, John Adams and Benjamin Franklin
Jefferson and Adams were abroad; none of the three wrote the essays.
Robert Yates, Mercy Otis Warren and George Clinton
These were Anti-Federalists from New York and Massachusetts.

alt.q: The Federalist Papers were first published mainly to…
alt.a: Persuade New York to ratify the Constitution
alt.ex: The essays ran in New York newspapers to win over a state where opposition was strong.
w: Persuade Britain to recognize American independence
Britain recognized independence in the Treaty of Paris (1783).
Persuade Congress to add a bill of rights
Hamilton argued in No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary.
Persuade Virginia to give up western lands
Western land cessions happened under the Articles.

items.q: Which group of leaders is most closely associated with the Anti-Federalist cause?
items.a: Patrick Henry, George Mason and Mercy Otis Warren
items.ex: Henry and Mason led opposition in Virginia, and Warren wrote against ratification as “A Columbian Patriot.”
w: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
These were the Federalist authors of The Federalist Papers.
George Washington, Benjamin Franklin and James Wilson
All three supported ratification.
John Marshall, John Adams and Roger Sherman
All three were Federalists or supported the Constitution.

alt.q: George Mason refused to sign the Constitution in 1787 mainly because it…
alt.a: Contained no declaration or bill of rights
alt.ex: Mason, author of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), began his written objections by noting there was no declaration of rights.
w: Gave the small states too much power in the House
The House is based on population, favoring large states.
Created a presidency that was much too weak
Anti-Federalists feared the presidency was too strong.
Abolished the state legislatures entirely
The Constitution kept the state legislatures.

alt.q: Patrick Henry, who refused to attend the Philadelphia Convention, opposed ratification in Virginia chiefly because he believed the Constitution…
alt.a: Endangered the states and individual liberty
alt.ex: Henry warned that the consolidated government, lacking a bill of rights, would swallow the states and threaten liberty.
w: Left the national government too weak to act
That was the Federalists' complaint about the Articles.
Failed to create any national court system
Article III created a Supreme Court, which Anti-Federalists feared.
Made the President an elected rather than hereditary office
Henry did not favor a hereditary executive.

items.q: Which argument was most typical of the Anti-Federalists?
items.a: A large republic would endanger liberty and states
items.ex: Anti-Federalists, drawing on Montesquieu, believed republics must be small and that a distant national government would threaten liberty.
w: A large republic best controls the effects of faction
That is Madison's Federalist argument in Federalist No. 10.
A bill of rights is unnecessary and even dangerous
That is Hamilton's Federalist argument in Federalist No. 84.
A single energetic executive ensures good government
That is Hamilton's Federalist argument in Federalist No. 70.

alt.q: “In a republic, the manners, sentiments, and interests of the people should be similar. If this be not the case, there will be a constant clashing of opinions…” This argument from Brutus No. 1 claims that…
alt.a: A republic as large as the U.S. could not succeed
alt.ex: Brutus (October 1787) argued that a vast, diverse nation could not be governed as a free republic.
w: A large republic would best control faction
This is Madison's opposite argument in Federalist No. 10.
A republic needs a strong executive to settle disputes
Brutus feared, rather than favored, strong national power.
A bill of rights would protect minority opinions
This passage concerns size and diversity, not a bill of rights.

alt.q: Which document is the best-known Anti-Federalist essay warning against a consolidated national government?
alt.a: Brutus No. 1
alt.ex: Brutus No. 1 (1787), published in New York, argued that the Constitution would create one consolidated government.
w: Federalist No. 10
Federalist No. 10 is Madison's pro-ratification essay on factions.
Federalist No. 51
Federalist No. 51 is Madison's pro-ratification essay on checks and balances.
Common Sense
Common Sense (1776) by Thomas Paine argued for independence.

items.q: “Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens…” Which argument does Madison make here?
items.a: A large republic makes oppressive majorities rarer
items.ex: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that a large, diverse republic controls the effects of faction because no single faction can easily form a majority.
w: A small republic best protects the rights of minorities
That was the Anti-Federalist view Madison was answering.
Separate branches should check one another's ambition
That is Madison's argument in Federalist No. 51.
A bill of rights is needed to protect citizens' rights
That was the Anti-Federalist demand, not this passage's point.

alt.q: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argues that the causes of faction cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so the best remedy is to…
alt.a: Control their effects with a large republic
alt.ex: Since faction is “sown in the nature of man,” Madison proposed controlling its effects through representation in an extended republic.
w: Ban political parties by passing a federal law
Madison said removing causes would destroy liberty.
Give each state a veto over national laws
Madison wanted to strengthen, not weaken, the national government.
Elect a strong executive to suppress them
Federalist No. 10 relies on size and representation, not the executive.

alt.q: Which group most directly rejected this argument, insisting that free republics must be small?
alt.a: Anti-Federalists, such as Brutus
alt.ex: Brutus No. 1 argued that a republic must be small with similar interests, directly opposing Madison's extended republic.
w: Federalists, such as Hamilton
Hamilton co-wrote The Federalist and supported the extended republic.
Loyalists, such as Thomas Hutchinson
Loyalists sided with Britain during the Revolution.
Framers who backed the Virginia Plan
Virginia Plan supporters wanted a strong national government.

items.q: “For why declare that things shall not be done which there is no power to do?” In Federalist No. 84, Alexander Hamilton used this question to argue that…
items.a: A bill of rights was unneeded in the Constitution
items.ex: Hamilton argued that because Congress had only enumerated powers, listing restrictions was unnecessary and could even be dangerous.
w: The President should not hold a veto over Congress
Hamilton defended the veto elsewhere; No. 84 is about a bill of rights.
Congress should list every right it may not violate
This is the opposite of Hamilton's argument.
The Supreme Court should not review acts of Congress
Hamilton defended judicial review in Federalist No. 78.

alt.q: Which amendment answered the concern that listing some rights might imply that unlisted rights were unprotected?
alt.a: The Ninth Amendment
alt.ex: The Ninth Amendment says the enumeration of certain rights “shall not be construed to deny or disparage others retained by the people.”
w: The Tenth Amendment
The Tenth reserves powers, not rights, to the states or the people.
The First Amendment
The First protects religion, speech, press, assembly and petition.
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth (1868) limits the states through due process and equal protection.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the Federalist position on a bill of rights in 1787–1788?
alt.a: Unneeded, since Congress held only listed powers
alt.ex: Federalists argued that a government of enumerated powers had no authority to violate rights in the first place.
w: Essential, since Congress held unlimited powers
That reflects Anti-Federalist fears.
Needed only to restrain the state governments
Federalists did not argue this.
Needed to protect slavery in the Southern states
The ratification debate over a bill of rights did not turn on this.

items.q: Why did Federalists promise to add a bill of rights after ratification?
items.a: To win votes in divided states like Massachusetts and Virginia
items.ex: Federalists accepted recommended amendments to secure ratification; Madison then introduced the amendments in 1789, and they were ratified in 1791.
w: To satisfy a demand made by the British government
Britain played no role in ratification.
Because Article VII required one before the Constitution took effect
Article VII required only nine state conventions.
To give the national government more power over the states
A bill of rights limits, rather than expands, national power.

alt.q: Which leader, once doubtful that a bill of rights was needed, introduced the proposed amendments in the First Congress in 1789?
alt.a: James Madison
alt.ex: Madison kept his ratification-campaign promise and drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights (ratified 1791).
w: Alexander Hamilton
Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary.
George Mason
Mason demanded a bill of rights but did not serve in the First Congress.
Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson urged a bill of rights by letter but was minister to France.

alt.q: The “Massachusetts Compromise” of February 1788 helped secure ratification by…
alt.a: Ratifying while recommending amendments for later
alt.ex: Massachusetts ratified and attached recommended amendments; other states, including Virginia and New York, followed this model.
w: Making ratification depend on a second convention
Conditional ratification was rejected in favor of recommendations.
Giving Massachusetts extra seats in the Senate
Every state receives two senators.
Delaying a vote until a bill of rights was adopted
Massachusetts ratified before any bill of rights existed.

items.q: At a 1788 ratifying convention, a delegate warns that the Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause will let Congress swallow up the state governments. This delegate is most likely…
items.a: An Anti-Federalist opposing ratification
items.ex: Anti-Federalists feared these clauses would create a consolidated government and destroy state sovereignty.
w: A Federalist defending ratification
Federalists defended these clauses as needed for an effective government.
A delegate seeking stronger national power
This delegate fears, not seeks, national power.
A delegate favoring an end to the states
The delegate wants to protect the states.

alt.q: Which features of the Constitution did Anti-Federalists most often cite as threats to the states?
alt.a: The Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses
alt.ex: Brutus and others argued these clauses gave Congress nearly unlimited power and made federal law override the states.
w: The ban on religious tests for federal office
This was not a central Anti-Federalist complaint about state power.
Equal representation of the states in the Senate
Equal Senate votes protected the states' role.
The rule requiring nine states to ratify
This concerned adoption, not ongoing federal power.

alt.q: The Tenth Amendment is best understood as a response to which concern?
alt.a: Anti-Federalist fears of national power
alt.ex: The Tenth Amendment reassured critics that powers not delegated remained with the states or the people.
w: Federalist fears of disorder like Shays' Rebellion
That concern led to a stronger national government, not the Tenth.
Small-state fears about representation in the House
That was settled by the Great Compromise.
Southern fears about ending the slave trade
That was addressed by Article I, Section 9.

items.q: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” Madison used this argument in Federalist No. 51 to defend…
items.a: Checks and balances among separate branches
items.ex: Federalist No. 51 argues each branch must have the means and motive to resist encroachment by the others.
w: A large republic to control the effects of faction
That is the argument of Federalist No. 10.
Life tenure for judges as the least dangerous branch
That is Hamilton's argument in Federalist No. 78.
A single executive with energy and unity
That is Hamilton's argument in Federalist No. 70.

alt.q: Federalist No. 51 argues that liberty in the American “compound republic” is protected because power is divided…
alt.a: Between two levels and among the branches
alt.ex: Madison described a “double security”: power split between national and state governments and then among separate departments.
w: Only among the three national branches
This omits the division between national and state governments.
Only between the states and the nation
This omits the separation of branches.
Among the people, the states and the churches
Churches play no role in Madison's scheme.

alt.q: Which famous line comes from Federalist No. 51?
alt.a: “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.”
alt.ex: Madison used this line to argue that government must be controlled by internal checks as well as by the people.
w: “These are the times that try men's souls.”
Thomas Paine wrote this in The American Crisis (1776).
“Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition…”
Hamilton wrote this in Federalist No. 70.
“the power to tax involves the power to destroy”
John Marshall wrote this in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).

items.q: What is generally considered the Anti-Federalists' most lasting contribution to American government?
items.a: Pressure that produced the Bill of Rights
items.ex: Although they lost the ratification fight, Anti-Federalist demands produced the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791.
w: Defeat of the Constitution in most of the states
All thirteen states eventually ratified.
Creation of the Electoral College system
The Electoral College was designed at the 1787 Convention.
Writing of the essays in The Federalist Papers
Federalists Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote those essays.

alt.q: North Carolina and Rhode Island did not ratify until 1789 and 1790. Their delay best shows that…
alt.a: Concerns about rights and state power persisted
alt.ex: North Carolina ratified in November 1789 after amendments were proposed, and Rhode Island in May 1790, under pressure.
w: The Constitution needed unanimous approval to begin
Article VII required only nine states.
Federalists controlled every state convention
Anti-Federalists controlled those two states' decisions.
Most states opposed adding a bill of rights
Most states had recommended amendments.

alt.q: Which state ratified the Constitution last, in May 1790, after the Bill of Rights had been proposed?
alt.a: Rhode Island
alt.ex: Rhode Island, which had boycotted the Convention, ratified on May 29, 1790.
w: North Carolina
