w: the Articles of Confederation
The Articles were an agreement among states, not individuals forming a government.
the Magna Carta
The Magna Carta limited an existing king's power.
the English Bill of Rights
The English Bill of Rights limited the Crown in favor of Parliament.

items.q: Which statement best describes the English Bill of Rights (1689)?
items.a: It limited the Crown's power and protected Parliament's rights
items.ex: After the Glorious Revolution, William and Mary accepted limits: no taxes or peacetime standing army without Parliament, free elections, the right to petition, and no cruel and unusual punishments.
w: It forced King John to accept written limits on his royal power
That was the Magna Carta (1215).
It declared the American colonies independent from England
That was the Declaration of Independence (1776).
It served as a written constitution for the colonies
It was an act of Parliament for England, not a colonial constitution.

alt.q: "That levying money for or to the use of the Crown by pretence of prerogative, without grant of Parliament... is illegal." This provision of the English Bill of Rights (1689) influenced the American principle that —
alt.a: only the elected legislature may levy taxes
alt.ex: Colonists built on this to argue "no taxation without representation"; the Constitution gives the taxing power to Congress (Article I, Section 8).
w: only the president may command the army
This provision concerns taxing, not military command.
only the federal courts may declare laws invalid
This concerns taxing power, not judicial review.
only the states may coin money
The Constitution gives coinage to Congress, and this clause concerns taxes.

alt.q: After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, William and Mary accepted a document stating that the Crown could not suspend laws, raise taxes, or keep a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. This document was —
alt.a: the English Bill of Rights
alt.ex: Enacted in 1689, it limited the monarchy and influenced the U.S. Bill of Rights.
w: the Magna Carta
The Magna Carta dates from 1215 under King John.
the Petition of Right of 1628
The Petition of Right (1628) was presented to Charles I.
the Mayflower Compact
The Mayflower Compact (1620) was a settlers' agreement.

items.q: "That excessive bail ought not to be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted." This line from the English Bill of Rights (1689) was adopted almost word for word in which amendment?
items.a: The Eighth Amendment
items.ex: The Eighth Amendment (1791) repeats this language, which had also passed through the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776).
w: The Sixth Amendment
The Sixth guarantees a speedy, public jury trial and counsel.
The Fifth Amendment
The Fifth covers due process, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination.
The Fourth Amendment
The Fourth protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.

alt.q: A judge sets bail at $10 million for a person accused of shoplifting. The defendant's lawyer argues the bail is unconstitutional. The protection the lawyer relies on traces back to —
alt.a: the English Bill of Rights of 1689
alt.ex: The Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive bail copies the English Bill of Rights.
w: the Mayflower Compact of 1620
The Compact concerns self-government, not bail.
the Magna Carta of 1215
The Magna Carta is the root of due process, not the excessive-bail ban.
Thomas Paine's Common Sense of 1776
Common Sense argued for independence, not criminal procedure.

alt.q: Which pair correctly matches a provision of the English Bill of Rights (1689) with the part of the U.S. Constitution it influenced?
alt.a: No cruel and unusual punishment — Eighth Amendment
alt.ex: The English ban on excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments became the Eighth Amendment.
w: Right to petition the king — Second Amendment
The right to petition influenced the First Amendment.
Protestants may have arms — Third Amendment
The arms provision influenced the Second Amendment.
Free election of members of Parliament — Fourth Amendment
Free elections are not the subject of the Fourth Amendment.

items.q: What was the main purpose of Thomas Paine's Common Sense (January 1776)?
items.a: To persuade ordinary colonists to support independence
items.ex: Written in plain language, Common Sense attacked monarchy and argued for separation from Britain; it sold widely and swayed public opinion.
w: To explain formally to foreign nations why the colonies left
That was the purpose of the Declaration of Independence (July 1776).
To argue for ratifying the new federal Constitution
That was the purpose of The Federalist Papers (1787–1788).
To urge colonists to reconcile with the king and Parliament
Paine argued against reconciliation.

alt.q: "...there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island." This argument for independence appeared in —
alt.a: Thomas Paine's Common Sense
alt.ex: Paine used plain, common-sense reasoning in 1776 to argue that America should be independent of Britain.
w: Jefferson's Declaration of Independence
The Declaration argues from natural rights and grievances, not this comparison.
Madison's Federalist No. 14
No. 14 (1787) defends a large republic, not independence.
John Locke's Second Treatise
Locke wrote in 1689 about government generally, not American independence.

alt.q: Which feature made Common Sense especially influential in early 1776?
alt.a: Its plain language reached ordinary readers
alt.ex: Paine wrote for farmers and artisans rather than lawyers, helping turn public opinion toward independence months before July 1776.
w: Its legal arguments convinced Parliament
Parliament was not persuaded; the pamphlet was aimed at colonists.
Its plan of government became the Articles
The Articles were drafted by John Dickinson and Congress.
Its author was a leading member of Congress
Paine was a recent immigrant writer, not a member of Congress.

items.q: "For as in absolute governments the King is law, so in free countries the law ought to be King; and there ought to be no other." In Common Sense, Thomas Paine uses this idea to argue that —
items.a: America should reject monarchy and be ruled by law
items.ex: Paine attacked hereditary monarchy and argued that in a free America, law—not a king—should rule.
w: America should choose a king who obeys the law
Paine argued against having any king at all.
Parliament should be supreme over the British king
Paine rejected British rule entirely, including Parliament.
each colony should crown its own governor
Paine called for a republic, not local monarchs.

alt.q: In Common Sense, Thomas Paine attacked which institution as contrary to reason and the source of British oppression?
alt.a: Hereditary monarchy
alt.ex: Paine ridiculed kingship and hereditary succession, arguing that "the law ought to be King" in a free country.
w: Representative assemblies
Paine supported representative government.
Written constitutions
Paine proposed a written continental charter.
Trial by jury
Paine did not attack jury trials.

alt.q: A colonist in early 1776 reads a pamphlet arguing that kings are unnecessary, that hereditary rule is absurd, and that "the law ought to be King." Which pamphlet is it?
alt.a: Thomas Paine's Common Sense
alt.ex: Published in January 1776, Common Sense attacked monarchy and urged independence.
w: John Dickinson's Letters from a Farmer
Dickinson's letters (1767–1768) opposed the Townshend duties but did not reject monarchy.
James Otis's Rights of the British Colonies
Otis's 1764 pamphlet argued for colonists' rights within the empire.
The Olive Branch Petition
This 1775 petition asked King George III for reconciliation.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Virginia Declaration of Rights (June 1776)?
items.a: Mason's list of rights that shaped later bills of rights
items.ex: Adopted June 12, 1776, Mason's declaration influenced the Declaration of Independence's preamble and Madison's Bill of Rights.
w: Thomas Jefferson's list of grievances against King George III
That describes the Declaration of Independence.
James Madison's plan for a new national government in 1787
That describes the Virginia Plan (1787).
Patrick Henry's speech urging Virginia to arm itself for war
That was Henry's "Give me liberty" speech (1775).

alt.q: "That all men are by nature equally free and independent and have certain inherent rights..." This line, adopted in Virginia in June 1776, most directly influenced the opening of —
alt.a: the Declaration of Independence
alt.ex: Weeks later, Jefferson's draft echoed Mason's words: "all men are created equal" with "unalienable Rights."
w: the Articles of Confederation
The Articles begin with a league of states, not a statement of natural rights.
the Mayflower Compact
The Compact (1620) came long before 1776.
the English Bill of Rights of 1689
The English Bill of Rights (1689) came long before 1776.

alt.q: George Mason refused to sign the U.S. Constitution in 1787 mainly because —
alt.a: it lacked a bill of rights like the one he wrote
alt.ex: Mason, author of the Virginia Declaration of Rights, objected that the Constitution had no declaration of rights.
w: it gave small states too little power in Congress
Small states won equal Senate representation.
it created no executive to enforce national laws
The Constitution created a president in Article II.
it ended the foreign slave trade immediately
The slave trade was protected until 1808.

items.q: "That the freedom of the press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty, and can never be restrained but by despotic governments." This 1776 statement from the Virginia Declaration of Rights later influenced which part of the U.S. Constitution?
items.a: The First Amendment
items.ex: Section 12 of Mason's declaration was a model for the First Amendment's protection of the press.
w: The Fourth Amendment
The Fourth concerns searches and seizures.
The Ninth Amendment
The Ninth protects unlisted rights.
The Tenth Amendment
The Tenth reserves powers to the states or the people.

alt.q: Which document, written by George Mason in 1776, served as a major model for the Bill of Rights that James Madison proposed in 1789?
alt.a: The Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: Mason's declaration protected press freedom, religious exercise, jury trial, and barred excessive bail—rights Madison carried into the amendments.
w: The English Bill of Rights
This 1689 act also influenced the Bill of Rights, but Mason did not write it.
The Massachusetts Declaration of Rights
John Adams drafted this in 1779 for the 1780 state constitution.
The Declaration of Independence
Jefferson wrote it; it lists grievances, not enforceable rights.

alt.q: Members of the First Congress compare Madison's proposed amendments with a 1776 state document that already protected a free press, religious exercise, and jury trials. Which document were they most likely consulting?
alt.a: The Virginia Declaration of Rights
alt.ex: Madison, a Virginian, drew heavily on Mason's Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776).
w: The Northwest Ordinance
The 1787 ordinance protected rights in a territory, not as a 1776 state document.
The Massachusetts State Constitution
Massachusetts adopted its constitution in 1780, not 1776.
The Articles of Confederation
The Articles contained no bill of rights.

items.q: "We hold these truths to be self-evident; that all men and women are created equal..." This line from the Declaration of Sentiments (1848) was written to —
items.a: apply the Declaration of Independence's ideals to women
items.ex: Adopted at Seneca Falls, New York, on July 19–20, 1848, it copied the 1776 Declaration's form, adding "and women."
w: apply the Declaration of Independence's ideals to the enslaved
Frederick Douglass made this argument in his 1852 Fourth of July speech.
protest Britain's taxation of the American colonies
That was a grievance of the 1776 Declaration.
argue that states could leave the Union at will
Secessionists made this argument in 1860–1861.

alt.q: Who was the principal author of the Declaration of Sentiments, adopted at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848?
alt.a: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
alt.ex: Stanton drafted the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence; about 100 people signed it.
w: Susan Brownell Anthony
Anthony did not attend Seneca Falls; she met Stanton in 1851.
Sojourner Truth
Truth is known for her 1851 "Ain't I a Woman?" speech in Ohio.
Lucretia Mott
Mott co-organized the convention, but Stanton was the principal author.

alt.q: A reform document lists "repeated injuries and usurpations" by one group against another and closes with resolutions demanding change, deliberately echoing 1776. Adopted at Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848, it is called —
alt.a: the Declaration of Sentiments
alt.ex: It mirrors the Declaration of Independence: "The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman."
w: the Emancipation Proclamation
Lincoln's 1863 order freed enslaved people in Confederate-held areas.
the Gettysburg Address
Lincoln's 1863 speech honored Union dead.
the Nineteenth Amendment
The 1920 amendment barred sex discrimination in voting.

items.q: The Declaration of Sentiments charged, "He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise." Which later amendment achieved the goal of this grievance?
items.a: The Nineteenth Amendment
items.ex: The Nineteenth Amendment (1920) barred denying the vote "on account of sex," 72 years after Seneca Falls.
w: The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote on account of race.
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth (1868) defined citizenship and equal protection; its Section 2 even used the word "male."
The Twenty-sixth Amendment
The Twenty-sixth (1971) set the voting age at 18.

alt.q: Which demand in the Declaration of Sentiments (1848) was the only resolution not adopted unanimously at the Seneca Falls Convention?
alt.a: The right of women to vote
alt.ex: The ninth resolution, on the elective franchise, passed narrowly after Stanton and Frederick Douglass argued for it.
w: The right of women to own property
Property rights were among the grievances but were not the contested resolution.
The right of women to attend college
Education was among the grievances but was not the contested resolution.
The right of women to keep wages
Control of wages was among the grievances but was not the contested resolution.

alt.q: A historian notes that a goal first demanded at Seneca Falls in 1848 took 72 years to win nationally. Which goal and amendment are meant?
alt.a: Women's suffrage; Nineteenth Amendment
alt.ex: The Seneca Falls demand for the vote (1848) was achieved by the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
w: Abolition of slavery; Thirteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) came 17 years after Seneca Falls.
Equal protection; Fourteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) came 20 years later.
Voting at age 18; Twenty-sixth Amendment
The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971) was not a Seneca Falls demand.

items.q: After losing the election of 1800, President John Adams appointed a justice of the peace whose commission was never delivered. The appointee asked the Supreme Court to order the new Secretary of State to deliver it. Which case arose from this dispute?
items.a: Marbury v. Madison
items.ex: Marbury v. Madison (1803) began when William Marbury, a last-minute Adams appointee, sought a writ of mandamus against Madison; Chief Justice John Marshall used the case to establish judicial review.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
1819 case on the national bank and a state tax, not an undelivered commission.
United States v. Nixon
1974 case ordering President Nixon to hand over the Watergate tapes.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 case denying Black citizenship and striking down the Missouri Compromise.

alt.q: Which case first established that federal courts may declare an act of Congress unconstitutional and therefore void?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) the Court struck down Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, the first time it voided an act of Congress, establishing judicial review.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
Upheld an act of Congress (the bank charter) and struck down a state tax.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Struck down the Missouri Compromise in 1857, but Marbury had already set the precedent.
Gibbons v. Ogden
1824 Marshall Court case defining Congress's power over interstate commerce.

alt.q: "It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is." In which case did Chief Justice John Marshall write this?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison
alt.ex: This line from Marbury v. Madison (1803) is the classic statement of judicial review; the Court later quoted it in United States v. Nixon (1974).
w: McCulloch v. Maryland
Also by Marshall, but known for 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.'
United States v. Nixon
Quoted this Marbury line in 1974; it did not originate it.
Gibbons v. Ogden
Marshall's 1824 opinion on the Commerce Clause and steamboat licenses.

items.q: Which principle did Marbury v. Madison establish?
items.a: Judicial review of laws for constitutionality
items.ex: Marbury (1803) held that a law conflicting with the Constitution is void and that courts decide such conflicts, establishing judicial review.
w: Implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Established by McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
Executive privilege limited by due process
The holding of United States v. Nixon (1974).
Selective incorporation of the Bill of Rights
Developed in 20th-century cases such as Gideon and Mapp.

alt.q: In Marbury v. Madison, why did the Court refuse to order Madison to deliver the commission, even though it said Marbury had a right to it?
alt.a: The statute granting that power violated Article III
alt.ex: Marshall held that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 unconstitutionally expanded the Court's original jurisdiction beyond Article III, so the Court could not issue the writ.
w: Marbury's appointment was never confirmed by the Senate
False: the Senate had confirmed him; only delivery was missing.
Delivering commissions was a political question for Congress
Marshall held delivery was a ministerial legal duty courts could review, not a political matter.
The President held an absolute executive privilege over it
Absolute executive privilege was rejected in United States v. Nixon (1974).

alt.q: Chief Justice Marshall concluded in 1803 that "a law repugnant to the constitution is void." Which idea does this statement express?
alt.a: Courts may void laws that conflict with the Constitution
alt.ex: This Marbury v. Madison reasoning is the basis of judicial review: the Constitution is supreme over ordinary statutes, and courts enforce that supremacy.
w: States may void federal laws they find unconstitutional
That is nullification (Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions), which Marbury did not endorse.
Congress may pass laws needed to carry out its powers
That is the Necessary and Proper Clause, interpreted in McCulloch.
The President may refuse to enforce unconstitutional laws
Marbury gave the power of review to the courts, not the President.

items.q: Marbury v. Madison and McCulloch v. Maryland were both written by Chief Justice John Marshall. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Marbury set up judicial review; McCulloch upheld implied powers
items.ex: Marbury (1803) established judicial review; McCulloch (1819) upheld the national bank under implied powers and barred Maryland's tax on it.
w: Marbury upheld implied powers; McCulloch set up judicial review
Reverses the two holdings.
Marbury voided a state tax; McCulloch voided a federal statute
Reversed: Marbury voided part of a federal statute; McCulloch voided a state tax.
Marbury upheld the national bank; McCulloch ordered a commission delivered
Mixes up the facts of the two cases.

alt.q: Which pairing correctly matches a Marshall Court case with the law it held unconstitutional?
alt.a: Marbury: part of the Judiciary Act of 1789
alt.ex: Marbury (1803) voided Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789; McCulloch (1819) voided Maryland's tax on the Second Bank of the United States.
w: Marbury: Maryland's tax on the national bank
That tax was struck down in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
McCulloch: the charter of the Second Bank
McCulloch upheld the bank's charter as a valid implied power.
Marbury: the Judiciary Act of 1801's new judgeships
That act was repealed by Congress in 1802, not voided in Marbury.

alt.q: A student writes: 'Marshall's Court first claimed the power to strike down federal laws, and sixteen years later used federal supremacy to stop a state from taxing a federal institution.' Which cases are described, in order?
alt.a: Marbury v. Madison, then McCulloch v. Maryland
alt.ex: Marbury (1803) established judicial review; McCulloch (1819) used the Supremacy Clause to bar Maryland's tax on the national bank.
w: McCulloch v. Maryland, then Marbury v. Madison
Correct cases in the wrong order: Marbury came first.
Marbury v. Madison, then Gibbons v. Ogden
Gibbons (1824) concerned interstate commerce, not a state tax on a federal bank.
Fletcher v. Peck, then McCulloch v. Maryland
Fletcher (1810) voided a state law under the Contract Clause; it did not establish review of federal laws.

items.q: In 1818 a state taxed a local branch of the Second Bank of the United States, and the branch's cashier refused to pay. Which case resulted?
items.a: McCulloch v. Maryland
items.ex: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819): the Court unanimously held that Congress could charter the bank and that Maryland could not tax it.
w: Marbury v. Madison
1803 case about an undelivered judicial commission that established judicial review.
Gibbons v. Ogden
1824 case about steamboat licenses and the Commerce Clause.
United States v. Lopez
1995 case limiting the Commerce Clause in a school gun law.

alt.q: Which case held that Congress may create a national bank under its implied powers and that a state may not tax that bank?
alt.a: McCulloch v. Maryland
alt.ex: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Marshall read the Necessary and Proper Clause broadly and used the Supremacy Clause to strike Maryland's tax.
w: Marbury v. Madison
Established judicial review in 1803; it did not involve the bank.
Gibbons v. Ogden
Defined 'commerce' broadly in 1824; it did not involve a bank tax.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 case on slavery in the territories and Black citizenship.

alt.q: Chief Justice Marshall reasoned "that the power to tax involves the power to destroy." What did the Court conclude from this reasoning?
alt.a: Maryland could not tax the Bank of the United States
alt.ex: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Marshall reasoned that a state tax could destroy a federal institution, which the Supremacy Clause forbids.
w: Congress could not tax banks chartered by the states
Reverses the case: the issue was a state taxing a federal bank.
Congress lacked power to create a national bank
That was Maryland's losing argument; the Court upheld the bank.
States could tax federal banks at equal rates
The Court barred the state tax entirely, not only unequal ones.

items.q: Which constitutional provisions were central to McCulloch v. Maryland?
items.a: Necessary and Proper Clause and Supremacy Clause
items.ex: Marshall read 'necessary' broadly, as useful or conducive rather than absolutely necessary, to uphold the bank, and used the Supremacy Clause to strike Maryland's tax (1819).
w: Commerce Clause and the Tenth Amendment's reserved powers
Central to United States v. Lopez (1995), not McCulloch.
Article III original jurisdiction and the Judiciary Act
Central to Marbury v. Madison (1803).
General Welfare Clause and the Full Faith and Credit Clause
Neither was the basis of McCulloch's holding.

alt.q: Congress creates a federal agency that is not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution, reasoning that it helps carry out the power to regulate commerce. Which doctrine from McCulloch v. Maryland best supports this?
alt.a: Implied powers drawn from the Necessary and Proper Clause
alt.ex: McCulloch (1819) held that Congress may use means not listed in the Constitution if they are appropriate to carry out an enumerated power.
w: Reserved powers kept by the states under the Tenth Amendment
Reserved powers limit federal action; they do not authorize it.
Concurrent powers shared equally by states and the nation
Concurrent powers (like taxing) were not the basis for creating the bank.
Inherent powers held by the President in foreign affairs
McCulloch concerned Congress's powers, not presidential foreign-affairs power.

alt.q: "Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and all means which are appropriate ... are constitutional." Which idea does this passage support?
alt.a: A broad reading of Congress's implied powers
alt.ex: Marshall's line in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) is the classic statement of loose construction of the Necessary and Proper Clause.
w: A strict reading limited to enumerated powers
That was the Jeffersonian view Marshall rejected.
The states' reserved power to tax federal banks
The same case held Maryland could not tax the bank.
The courts' power to void unconstitutional laws
That is judicial review from Marbury v. Madison (1803).

items.q: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) and United States v. Lopez (1995) both concerned the reach of federal power. Which statement correctly contrasts them?
items.a: McCulloch expanded federal power; Lopez set a limit on it
items.ex: McCulloch upheld broad implied powers; Lopez struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act as beyond the Commerce Clause.
w: McCulloch limited federal power; Lopez expanded federal power
Reverses the two outcomes.
Both cases struck down federal laws as exceeding Article I
McCulloch upheld the federal bank and struck a state tax.
Both cases upheld federal laws under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Lopez struck down the federal law.

alt.q: A student confuses McCulloch v. Maryland with United States v. Lopez. Which holding belongs only to Lopez?
alt.a: Congress exceeded its Commerce Clause power
alt.ex: Lopez (1995) held that carrying a gun near a school is not economic activity that Congress may regulate under the Commerce Clause.
w: A state could not tax a federal institution
That was McCulloch's holding on Maryland's bank tax.
Congress may use means not listed in the Constitution
That is McCulloch's implied-powers holding.
Federal law is supreme over conflicting state law
McCulloch applied the Supremacy Clause; Lopez did not turn on it.

alt.q: Which pairing correctly matches each case to the clause it mainly interpreted?
alt.a: McCulloch – Necessary and Proper; Lopez – Commerce
alt.ex: McCulloch (1819) interpreted the Necessary and Proper Clause; Lopez (1995) interpreted the Commerce Clause.
w: McCulloch – Commerce; Lopez – Necessary and Proper
Reverses the two clauses.
McCulloch – Supremacy; Lopez – Second Amendment
Lopez was a Commerce Clause case, not a gun-rights case.
McCulloch – Tenth Amendment; Lopez – Due Process
McCulloch rejected the Tenth Amendment argument; Lopez did not rest on due process.

items.q: An enslaved man who had lived for years in a free state and in a free federal territory sued in federal court for freedom after returning to Missouri. Which case arose?
items.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
items.ex: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled 7–2 that Scott was not a citizen and could not sue.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
1896 case upholding segregated railroad cars.
Prigg v. Pennsylvania
1842 case on fugitive slave recovery, not a freedom suit by residence.
Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case striking down school segregation.

alt.q: Which case held that people of African descent could not be U.S. citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories?
alt.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
alt.ex: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) denied Black citizenship and declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Upheld 'separate but equal' in 1896; it did not deny citizenship.
McCulloch v. Maryland
1819 case on the national bank and implied powers.
Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case ending school segregation.

alt.q: Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote that Black Americans "had no rights which the white man was bound to respect." This statement comes from which case?
alt.a: Dred Scott v. Sandford
alt.ex: Taney's majority opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) contains this line; the 14th Amendment (1868) overturned its citizenship ruling.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Its majority, by Justice Henry Billings Brown, upheld segregation in 1896.
Korematsu v. United States
1944 case upholding Japanese American exclusion.
Brown v. Board of Education
1954 opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren ending school segregation.

items.q: Which constitutional change most directly overturned the Dred Scott decision's ruling on citizenship?
items.a: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868)
items.ex: The 14th Amendment (1868) declares that all persons born or naturalized in the United States are citizens, reversing Dred Scott's citizenship holding.
w: The Thirteenth Amendment (1865)
It abolished slavery but did not define citizenship.
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870)
It barred race-based denial of the vote; it did not define citizenship.
The Emancipation Proclamation (1863)
An executive order, not a constitutional change, and it addressed slavery in Confederate-held areas.

alt.q: Which part of the Dred Scott ruling most intensified sectional conflict before the Civil War?
alt.a: It declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional
alt.ex: By holding that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, Dred Scott (1857) voided the Missouri Compromise and angered the North.
w: It upheld the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery
The Court struck the Compromise down.
It required Northern states to return fugitive slaves
That was the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, a law of Congress.
It struck down the Kansas-Nebraska Act's popular sovereignty
The Court did not rule on the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

alt.q: On what constitutional basis did Chief Justice Taney argue that Congress could not ban slavery in the federal territories?
alt.a: The Fifth Amendment's protection of property
alt.ex: Taney treated enslaved people as property and held that banning slavery in the territories deprived owners of property without due process (1857).
w: The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers of states
Taney's territorial holding rested on property rights, not reserved powers.
The Commerce Clause's limits on federal power
The commerce power was not the basis of the ruling.
Article IV's Full Faith and Credit Clause
That clause concerns honoring other states' records, not slavery.

items.q: Dred Scott v. Sandford and Plessy v. Ferguson are often confused. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Dred Scott denied Black citizenship; Plessy upheld segregation
items.ex: Dred Scott (1857) said Black Americans could not be citizens; Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal' segregation.
w: Dred Scott upheld segregation; Plessy denied Black citizenship
Reverses the two holdings.
Dred Scott ended slavery in territories; Plessy ended segregation
Both cases went the other way.
Both cases were overturned by the Thirteenth Amendment
Dred Scott was overturned by the 13th and 14th Amendments; Plessy by Brown (1954).

alt.q: Which case came after the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified and so had to interpret its Equal Protection Clause?
alt.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
alt.ex: Plessy (1896) interpreted the 14th Amendment (1868) to allow segregation; Dred Scott (1857) came before that amendment existed.
w: Dred Scott v. Sandford
Decided in 1857, before the 14th Amendment was written.
Prigg v. Pennsylvania
Decided in 1842 on the Fugitive Slave Clause.
Marbury v. Madison
Decided in 1803 on judicial review.

alt.q: A history student writes: 'This decision ruled that Congress could not keep slavery out of federal territories, helping push the nation toward civil war.' Which case is described, and what reversed its key holdings?
alt.a: Dred Scott; reversed by the 13th and 14th Amendments
alt.ex: Dred Scott (1857) was undone by constitutional amendments: the 13th (1865) ended slavery and the 14th (1868) made Black Americans citizens.
w: Plessy; reversed by Brown v. Board of Education
Plessy upheld segregation; it did not involve the territories.
Dred Scott; reversed by Brown v. Board of Education
Brown overturned Plessy, not Dred Scott.
Plessy; reversed by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments
Plessy came after these amendments and was overturned by Brown.

items.q: A man who was one-eighth African American sat in a railroad car reserved for white passengers in Louisiana, refused to move, and was arrested under a state law. Which case resulted?
items.a: Plessy v. Ferguson
items.ex: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld Louisiana's Separate Car Act 7–1, creating the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case that rejected 'separate but equal' in schools.
Dred Scott v. Sandford
1857 case denying Black citizenship.
Korematsu v. United States
1944 case on Japanese American exclusion.

items.q: New York's Board of Regents wrote a short, nondenominational prayer that public school students could recite voluntarily each morning. Parents sued. Which case resulted?
items.a: Engel v. Vitale
items.ex: Engel v. Vitale (1962), 6–1, held that the Regents' prayer violated the Establishment Clause.
w: Wisconsin v. Yoder
1972 Free Exercise case on Amish schooling.
Abington School District v. Schempp
1963 case striking down school Bible reading.
Lemon v. Kurtzman
1971 case on state aid to religious schools.

alt.q: Which case held that a state-written prayer in public schools violates the Establishment Clause even when participation is voluntary?
alt.a: Engel v. Vitale
alt.ex: Justice Hugo Black wrote for the Court in Engel v. Vitale (1962).
w: Wisconsin v. Yoder
Granted Amish families an exemption under Free Exercise.
Abington School District v. Schempp
Struck down Bible reading, not a state-written prayer.
Lemon v. Kurtzman
Created a three-part test for government aid to religion.

alt.q: "...it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers for any group of the American people to recite as a part of a religious program carried on by government." This statement reflects which clause?
alt.a: The Establishment Clause
alt.ex: Justice Black wrote this in Engel v. Vitale (1962) under the First Amendment's Establishment Clause.
w: The Free Exercise Clause
Protects individuals' practice of religion; it was the basis of Yoder.
The Free Speech Clause
Protects expression generally, not the issue here.
The Equal Protection Clause
A 14th Amendment clause on equal treatment.

items.q: Why did the Court in Engel v. Vitale strike down the Regents' prayer even though students could remain silent or leave?
items.a: Government itself wrote and sponsored the prayer
items.ex: Engel (1962) held that a government-composed prayer is an establishment of religion regardless of voluntariness.
w: It favored one Christian denomination over others
The prayer was deliberately nondenominational.
It forced students to violate their own faith
Coercion of belief is a Free Exercise concern; the prayer was voluntary.
It took instructional time away from lessons
Instructional time was not the constitutional issue.

alt.q: What is the lasting impact of Engel v. Vitale?
alt.a: Public schools may not lead official prayers
alt.ex: Engel (1962) bars school-sponsored prayer; students may still pray privately.
w: Students may not pray on their own at school
A common misconception; private student prayer is protected.
Religious clubs are banned from public schools
Student religious clubs are allowed under the Equal Access Act (1984).
Public schools must teach about every religion
Engel imposed no curriculum requirement.

alt.q: A public school principal begins each day by reading a prayer over the loudspeaker and invites students to join. Which principle is most clearly at issue?
alt.a: Government establishment of religion
alt.ex: Under Engel v. Vitale (1962), school-led prayer violates the Establishment Clause.
w: Students' free exercise of religion
Free exercise protects students' own practice; the issue is government sponsorship.
School officials' freedom of speech
A principal speaking for the school acts as government.
The right to peaceably assemble at school
Assembly is not at issue in a school-led prayer.

items.q: Engel v. Vitale (1962) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) both involved religion and schools. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: Engel turned on establishment; Yoder on free exercise
items.ex: Engel struck down a state-written prayer (Establishment); Yoder exempted Amish teens from compulsory schooling (Free Exercise).
w: Engel turned on free exercise; Yoder on establishment
Reverses the two clauses.
Both upheld the state's power over school religion
Both ruled against the state.
Engel involved Amish families; Yoder a school prayer
Reverses the facts.

alt.q: Which outcome pairing is correct?
alt.a: Engel: school prayer struck; Yoder: Amish exemption granted
alt.ex: Engel (1962) struck down the Regents' prayer; Yoder (1972) let Amish parents end schooling after eighth grade.
w: Engel: school prayer upheld; Yoder: Amish exemption denied
Both outcomes are reversed.
Engel: Amish exemption granted; Yoder: school prayer struck
Swaps the facts of the cases.
Engel: Bible reading upheld; Yoder: Amish exemption denied
Bible reading was struck in Schempp (1963); Yoder granted the exemption.

alt.q: Two disputes: (1) a state writes a prayer for public school students; (2) a state forces Amish teens to attend high school against their faith. Which clauses apply, in order?
alt.a: Establishment Clause; Free Exercise Clause
alt.ex: (1) is Engel v. Vitale (Establishment); (2) is Wisconsin v. Yoder (Free Exercise).
w: Free Exercise Clause; Establishment Clause
Reverses the clauses.
Free Speech Clause; Equal Protection Clause
Neither dispute turns on these clauses.
Establishment Clause; Due Process Clause
Yoder was decided under the Free Exercise Clause.

items.q: A man charged in Florida with breaking and entering asked for a lawyer, but the judge refused because state law provided counsel only in capital cases. The defendant handled their own defense, was convicted, and appealed. Which case?
items.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
items.ex: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), 9–0, held that states must provide counsel to defendants who cannot afford one.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Concerned warnings before police questioning (1966).
Betts v. Brady
1942 case that Gideon overruled; it had denied a general right to appointed counsel.
Strickland v. Washington
1984 case setting the standard for ineffective assistance of counsel.

alt.q: Which case required states to provide lawyers to felony defendants who cannot afford them?
alt.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
alt.ex: Justice Hugo Black's unanimous opinion in Gideon (1963) incorporated the Sixth Amendment right to counsel.
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Requires warnings about counsel during questioning, not trial counsel.
Betts v. Brady
Held the opposite in 1942 and was overruled by Gideon.
Strickland v. Washington
Concerned the quality, not the provision, of counsel.

alt.q: "...any person haled into court, who is too poor to hire a lawyer, cannot be assured a fair trial unless counsel is provided for him." Which case?
alt.a: Gideon v. Wainwright
alt.ex: Justice Black wrote this in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963).
w: Miranda v. Arizona
Concerned custodial interrogation, not trial counsel.
Powell v. Alabama
1932 Scottsboro case requiring counsel in that capital case only.
Strickland v. Washington
Set the test for ineffective counsel in 1984.

items.q: Gideon v. Wainwright applied which right to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment?
items.a: Sixth Amendment right to the assistance of counsel
items.ex: Gideon (1963) held the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and binds the states.
w: Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination
The basis of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches
The basis of Mapp v. Ohio (1961).
Eighth Amendment ban on excessive bail
Not involved in Gideon.

alt.q: A defendant charged with a felony in state court says they cannot afford a lawyer. Under Gideon, what must happen?
alt.a: The court must appoint counsel at public expense
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) requires appointed counsel for indigent felony defendants unless they knowingly waive the right.
w: The defendant must be read Miranda warnings first
Miranda governs police questioning, not court proceedings.
The defendant may be tried only if they waive a jury
Jury waiver is unrelated to the right to counsel.
The court may appoint counsel only in capital cases
That was Florida's pre-Gideon rule.

alt.q: Which development is a direct result of Gideon v. Wainwright?
alt.a: Expansion of public defender systems in the states
alt.ex: To meet Gideon's 1963 requirement, states built or expanded public defender offices.
w: Police reading suspects their rights before questioning
A result of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
Exclusion of evidence from warrantless home searches
A result of Mapp v. Ohio (1961).
Bans on mandatory prayer in public classrooms
A result of Engel v. Vitale (1962).

items.q: Both Gideon v. Wainwright and Miranda v. Arizona involve a right to a lawyer. What is the key difference?
items.a: Gideon covers trial; Miranda covers police questioning
items.ex: Gideon (1963) guarantees counsel at trial; Miranda (1966) requires warnings, including the right to counsel, before custodial interrogation.
w: Gideon covers police questioning; Miranda covers trial
Reverses the two cases.
Gideon covers searches; Miranda covers jury selection
Searches are Mapp; neither case concerns jury selection.
Gideon covers federal courts; Miranda covers state courts
Gideon applied the right to state courts.

alt.q: Which situation would be governed by Gideon rather than Miranda?
alt.a: A poor defendant goes to trial without a lawyer
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) concerns appointed counsel at trial for those who cannot afford one.
w: A suspect in custody is questioned without warnings
Governed by Miranda (1966).
Police search a car without a warrant or consent
A Fourth Amendment search issue (Mapp).
A suspect confesses before being told they may stay silent
Governed by Miranda (1966).

alt.q: Which amendments are most associated with Gideon and Miranda, respectively?
alt.a: Sixth Amendment; Fifth Amendment
alt.ex: Gideon applied the Sixth Amendment right to counsel; Miranda rests mainly on the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
w: Fifth Amendment; Sixth Amendment
Reverses the amendments.
Fourth Amendment; Fifth Amendment
The Fourth Amendment is Mapp's, not Gideon's.
Sixth Amendment; Fourth Amendment
Miranda is not a search case.

items.q: A suspect arrested in 1963 confessed after two hours of police questioning, but officers never said the suspect could remain silent or have a lawyer. The conviction was overturned. Which case?
items.a: Miranda v. Arizona
items.ex: Miranda v. Arizona (1966), 5–4, required warnings before custodial interrogation.
w: Mapp v. Ohio
1961 case on illegally seized evidence.
Gideon v. Wainwright
1963 case on appointed counsel at trial.
Escobedo v. Illinois
1964 case on a suspect denied access to a lawyer they had requested.

alt.q: Which case requires police to warn suspects in custody of their rights before interrogation?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: Chief Justice Earl Warren's opinion in Miranda (1966) created the familiar warnings.
w: Mapp v. Ohio
Applied the exclusionary rule to searches.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Required counsel for poor defendants at trial.
Escobedo v. Illinois
A 1964 precursor that did not set out the full warnings.

alt.q: "He must be warned prior to any questioning that he has the right to remain silent, that anything he says can be used against him in a court of law..." Which case?
alt.a: Miranda v. Arizona
alt.ex: This is the core holding of Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
w: Mapp v. Ohio
Concerns searches and seizures, not warnings.
Gideon v. Wainwright
Concerns appointed counsel at trial.
Escobedo v. Illinois
Did not set out these warnings.

items.q: Miranda v. Arizona is based mainly on which constitutional protection?
items.a: Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination
items.ex: Miranda (1966) held that custodial interrogation without warnings violates the Fifth Amendment privilege.
w: Fourth Amendment protection from unreasonable searches
The basis of Mapp v. Ohio.
Sixth Amendment right to a speedy and public trial
Concerns trials, not interrogation.
Eighth Amendment ban on cruel and unusual punishment
Concerns punishment, not questioning.

alt.q: Police arrest a suspect, place them in an interrogation room, and question them without any warnings. The suspect confesses. Under Miranda, what is the usual result?
alt.a: The confession cannot be used to prove guilt at trial
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) bars the prosecution from using unwarned custodial statements as evidence of guilt.
w: The arrest is void and the suspect must be released
The arrest remains valid; only the statement is excluded.
The confession is allowed if a lawyer is appointed later
Later counsel does not cure the missing warnings.
The entire case must be dismissed with prejudice
Other lawfully obtained evidence can still be used.

alt.q: When do Miranda warnings apply?
alt.a: When a suspect is in custody and being interrogated
alt.ex: Miranda (1966) applies to custodial interrogation, not casual or voluntary conversations.
w: Whenever an officer speaks with any person on the street
Non-custodial questioning does not require warnings.
Only after formal charges are filed in court
Miranda applies before charges, during custody.
Only when a suspect asks for a lawyer by name
Warnings are required whether or not the suspect asks.

items.q: A student mixes up Mapp v. Ohio and Miranda v. Arizona. Which statement is correct?
items.a: Mapp excludes illegally seized items; Miranda, unwarned confessions
items.ex: Mapp (1961) is a Fourth Amendment search case; Miranda (1966) is a Fifth Amendment interrogation case.
w: Mapp excludes unwarned confessions; Miranda, illegally seized items
Reverses the two cases.
Both require a lawyer to be appointed for poor defendants
That is Gideon v. Wainwright.
Both apply only to federal agents, not state police
Both cases apply to state police.

alt.q: Three defendants: (A) evidence came from a warrantless home search; (B) no lawyer at a felony trial; (C) a confession without warnings. Which cases match A, B, C?
alt.a: Mapp; Gideon; Miranda
alt.ex: A = Mapp v. Ohio (1961); B = Gideon v. Wainwright (1963); C = Miranda v. Arizona (1966).
w: Miranda; Gideon; Mapp
Swaps A and C.
Mapp; Miranda; Gideon
Swaps B and C.
Gideon; Mapp; Miranda
Swaps A and B.

alt.q: Which protection did Miranda add that Gideon did not cover?
alt.a: A lawyer during custodial police questioning
alt.ex: Gideon (1963) guaranteed counsel at trial; Miranda (1966) extended the right to have counsel present during custodial interrogation.
w: A lawyer at trial for poor felony defendants
That is Gideon's own holding.
Exclusion of evidence from illegal searches
That is Mapp v. Ohio.
A jury trial for all serious state crimes
That is Duncan v. Louisiana (1968).

items.q: Several public school students wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War and were suspended under a policy adopted just before the protest. Which case?
items.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
items.ex: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), 7–2, held the suspensions violated the First Amendment.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
1988 case on a school-sponsored newspaper.
Texas v. Johnson
1989 case on flag burning at a protest.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
1986 case allowing discipline for a lewd assembly speech.

alt.q: Which case held that students keep free speech rights at school unless their expression would substantially disrupt the school?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
alt.ex: Justice Abe Fortas wrote the majority in Tinker (1969), setting the substantial-disruption test.
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
Allowed censorship of school-sponsored speech.
Texas v. Johnson
Protected flag burning outside the school setting.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
Allowed punishment of lewd student speech.

alt.q: "It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." Which case?
alt.a: Tinker v. Des Moines
alt.ex: Justice Fortas wrote this in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969).
w: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
Limited student press rights in 1988.
Texas v. Johnson
Known for the 'bedrock principle' against banning offensive ideas.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
Upheld discipline for a lewd speech.

items.q: What standard did Tinker set for when a school may restrict student expression?
items.a: When it would materially and substantially disrupt school
items.ex: Tinker (1969) requires a showing of material and substantial interference with school operations, not mere fear.
w: When it poses a clear and present danger to the nation
The Schenck (1919) test for wartime speech.
When it appears in a school-sponsored student newspaper
The Hazelwood (1988) context.
When any teacher, parent, or classmate finds the message offensive
Tinker rejected suppression based on discomfort.

alt.q: A student wears a T-shirt with a political slogan; no classes are disrupted, but the principal fears future trouble and suspends the student. Under Tinker, the suspension is most likely
alt.a: unconstitutional, since fear of disruption is not enough
alt.ex: Tinker (1969) held that 'undifferentiated fear or apprehension of disturbance' does not justify suppressing student speech.
w: constitutional, since schools may ban all political messages
Tinker protected political speech in school.
constitutional, since the shirt is conduct, not speech
Tinker treated armbands as symbolic speech.
unconstitutional, since schools may never limit any speech
Too broad: schools may limit disruptive, lewd, or school-sponsored speech.

alt.q: The Tinker armbands were treated as symbolic speech. Which amendment protected them?
alt.a: The First Amendment, applied to states through the 14th
alt.ex: Tinker (1969) applied First Amendment free speech protection to a public school through the 14th Amendment.
w: The Fourth Amendment, applied to schools through the 14th
The Fourth concerns searches, not speech.
The Ninth Amendment's protection of unlisted rights
Free speech is listed in the First Amendment.
The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause alone
The Fifth binds the federal government; the ruling rested on the First.

items.q: Tinker v. Des Moines, Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier, and Texas v. Johnson all involve expression. Which pairing is correct?
items.a: Tinker–armbands; Hazelwood–school paper; Johnson–flag burning
items.ex: Tinker (1969): armbands; Hazelwood (1988): school-sponsored newspaper; Texas v. Johnson (1989): flag burning.
w: Tinker–school paper; Hazelwood–armbands; Johnson–flag burning
Swaps Tinker and Hazelwood.
Tinker–flag burning; Hazelwood–school paper; Johnson–armbands
Swaps Tinker and Johnson.
Tinker–armbands; Hazelwood–flag burning; Johnson–school paper
Swaps Hazelwood and Johnson.

alt.q: How does Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier limit Tinker v. Des Moines?
alt.a: Schools may edit school-sponsored papers for teaching goals
alt.ex: Hazelwood (1988) lets educators control school-sponsored speech when reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns.
w: Schools may ban any personal student speech they find offensive
Tinker still protects non-disruptive personal speech.
Schools may punish speech only if it causes violence
Neither case requires violence.
Schools may restrict personal speech without disruption
That would contradict Tinker, which still governs personal speech.

alt.q: A student wears an armband protesting a war (A), and another student's article is pulled from the school-run newspaper by the principal (B). Which cases apply to A and B?
alt.a: Tinker; Hazelwood
alt.ex: Personal symbolic speech falls under Tinker (1969); school-sponsored publications fall under Hazelwood (1988).
w: Hazelwood; Tinker
Reverses the matches.
Tinker; Texas v. Johnson
Johnson concerned flag burning at a public protest.
Texas v. Johnson; Hazelwood
The armband case is Tinker, not Johnson.

items.q: In 1971 the Nixon administration went to court to stop two newspapers from publishing a classified Defense Department study of U.S. involvement in Vietnam. Which case?
items.a: New York Times v. United States
items.ex: In New York Times v. United States (1971), the 'Pentagon Papers' case, the Court ruled 6–3 against prior restraint.
w: New York Times v. Sullivan
1964 libel case requiring 'actual malice' for public officials.
United States v. Nixon
1974 case on the Watergate tapes.
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
1988 case allowing a principal to censor a school paper.

alt.q: Which case held that the government failed to justify blocking newspapers from printing a classified study on national security grounds?
alt.a: New York Times v. United States
alt.ex: The per curiam opinion in NYT v. United States (1971) found the government had not met its heavy burden for prior restraint.
w: New York Times v. Sullivan
Concerned libel suits by public officials.
United States v. Nixon
Concerned executive privilege and the Watergate tapes.
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier
Upheld censorship of a school-sponsored paper.

alt.q: Justice Hugo Black wrote, "Only a free and unrestrained press can effectively expose deception in government." His concurrence supported which ruling?
alt.a: Newspapers could publish the Pentagon Papers
alt.ex: Black wrote this concurring in New York Times v. United States (1971).
w: A principal could censor a school newspaper
That was Hazelwood (1988), decided long after Black's death.
The President had to turn over the Watergate tapes
That was United States v. Nixon (1974).
Antiwar leaflets could be punished in wartime
That was Schenck (1919).

items.q: New York Times v. United States is a leading case on which First Amendment doctrine?
items.a: Limits on prior restraint of the press
items.ex: NYT v. U.S. (1971) held that prior restraint carries a heavy presumption against its constitutionality.
w: The clear and present danger test for speech
From Schenck v. United States (1919).
Protection of symbolic speech such as armbands
From Tinker (1969) and Texas v. Johnson (1989).
Actual malice in libel of public officials
From New York Times v. Sullivan (1964).

alt.q: A federal agency asks a judge to order a news website not to publish a leaked report, claiming harm to national security but offering no evidence of direct, immediate harm. Under NYT v. United States, the judge should most likely
alt.a: deny the order, since prior restraint is presumed invalid
alt.ex: NYT v. U.S. (1971) requires the government to overcome a heavy presumption against prior restraint.
w: grant the order, since national security concerns always prevail
The Court rejected a vague 'security' claim.
grant the order, since leaked documents lack protection
The Pentagon Papers were leaked, yet publication was allowed.
deny the order, since the press may never be restrained
Too broad: the Court left room for extreme, proven harms.

alt.q: "Any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." What does this passage mean?
alt.a: Government must meet a very high bar to block publication
alt.ex: The NYT v. U.S. per curiam (1971) quoted this rule to reject blocking the Pentagon Papers.
w: Government may block publication if a court approves it first
Court approval does not remove the heavy presumption.
The press must get approval before printing secrets
That would be prior restraint, which the rule disfavors.
Publishers are liable for false statements about officials
That concerns libel (NYT v. Sullivan), not prior restraint.

items.q: New York Times v. United States (1971) and United States v. Nixon (1974) both involved the Nixon administration. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
items.a: NYT: press could publish; Nixon: President had to release tapes
items.ex: NYT v. U.S. rejected prior restraint of the Pentagon Papers; U.S. v. Nixon (8–0) rejected an absolute executive privilege.
w: NYT: President had to release tapes; Nixon: press could publish
Reverses the two cases.
Both upheld executive privilege over national security
Both ruled against the administration.
NYT: press was blocked; Nixon: tapes stayed confidential
Both outcomes are reversed.

alt.q: New York Times v. United States (1971) is often confused with New York Times v. Sullivan (1964). What did Sullivan decide?
alt.a: Public officials must prove actual malice to win libel suits
alt.ex: Sullivan (1964) required public officials to prove a falsehood was made knowingly or recklessly.
w: The government could not block the Pentagon Papers
That was NYT v. United States (1971).
Reporters must reveal their confidential sources to grand juries
That issue arose in Branzburg v. Hayes (1972).
Prior restraint is allowed in wartime emergencies
Sullivan did not address prior restraint.

alt.q: The government tried to stop a newspaper from printing leaked classified documents (A). Decades earlier, a man was jailed after distributing antidraft leaflets (B). How did the Court rule in A and B?
alt.a: A: publication allowed; B: conviction upheld
alt.ex: A is NYT v. U.S. (1971), which allowed publication; B is Schenck (1919), which upheld the conviction.
w: A: publication blocked; B: conviction upheld
The Court refused to block publication in A.
A: publication allowed; B: conviction reversed
Schenck's conviction was upheld 9–0.
A: publication blocked; B: conviction reversed
Both outcomes are reversed.

items.q: Amish parents in a Midwestern state refused to send their children to school after eighth grade, saying high school conflicted with their religious way of life, and were fined under a compulsory-attendance law. Which case?
items.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
items.ex: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972), 7–0, held that the parents' free exercise rights outweighed the state's interest.
w: Engel v. Vitale
1962 Establishment Clause case on school prayer.
Employment Division v. Smith
1990 case denying a religious exemption from a drug law.
Pierce v. Society of Sisters
1925 case letting parents choose private schools.

alt.q: Which case held that a state could not force Amish children to attend school beyond the eighth grade?
alt.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
alt.ex: Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote for the Court in Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972).
w: Engel v. Vitale
Struck down a state-written school prayer.
Employment Division v. Smith
Held neutral laws generally apply despite religious objections.
Pierce v. Society of Sisters
Struck down a law requiring public school attendance only.

alt.q: In which case did the Court rule that parents' free exercise of religion outweighed the state's interest in two more years of compulsory schooling?
alt.a: Wisconsin v. Yoder
alt.ex: Yoder (1972) found one or two more years of high school would gravely endanger Amish religious practice.
w: Engel v. Vitale
An Establishment Clause case, not free exercise.
Employment Division v. Smith
Ruled against the religious claimants in 1990.
Pierce v. Society of Sisters
Rested on parental liberty under due process, not free exercise.

items.q: Wisconsin v. Yoder was decided under which clause?
items.a: The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment
items.ex: Yoder (1972) protected the Amish families' free exercise of religion.
w: The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment
The basis of Engel v. Vitale (1962).
The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
Not the basis of the ruling.
The Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment
The case concerned religious practice, not speech.

alt.q: What principle does Wisconsin v. Yoder illustrate?
alt.a: Religious practice can outweigh some general state laws
alt.ex: Yoder (1972) balanced the state's interest in education against a sincere, long-established religious practice and sided with the parents.
w: Government may never require school attendance
Yoder allowed attendance laws through eighth grade.
States may write prayers if attendance is voluntary
Engel (1962) rejected this.
Religious groups must obey every neutral law without exception
Yoder granted an exception; compare Employment Division v. Smith.

alt.q: A state requires all teens to attend school until 16. A long-established religious community shows high school would undermine its faith and way of life. Under Yoder, the state should most likely
alt.a: exempt the community's children after eighth grade
alt.ex: Yoder (1972) held the state could not compel Amish children to attend school past eighth grade.
w: require attendance since the law applies to everyone
Yoder rejected applying the law to the Amish.
require the community to open its own public school
No such remedy was ordered.
exempt all children whose parents object for any reason
Yoder protected sincere religious practice, not any objection.

items.q: Which statement about Engel v. Vitale and Wisconsin v. Yoder is accurate?
items.a: Engel limited government religion; Yoder protected private religion
items.ex: Engel (1962) applied the Establishment Clause; Yoder (1972) applied the Free Exercise Clause.
w: Engel protected private religion; Yoder limited government religion
Reverses the two cases.
Both ruled that schools must allow prayer during class
Engel struck down school prayer.
Both ruled for the state against religious objectors
Both ruled against the state.

alt.q: A student says, 'Yoder is the school prayer case.' What is the best correction?
alt.a: Yoder concerned Amish schooling; Engel concerned prayer
alt.ex: Engel v. Vitale (1962) is the school prayer case; Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) concerned Amish compulsory education.
w: Yoder concerned Bible reading; Engel concerned Amish
Bible reading was Abington v. Schempp (1963).
Yoder concerned prayer at graduations; Engel at football games
Those are Lee v. Weisman (1992) and Santa Fe v. Doe (2000).
Yoder concerned a flag salute rule; Engel concerned prayer
The flag salute case was West Virginia v. Barnette (1943).

alt.q: In which pair of cases did the Court rule for the families challenging the state in both?
alt.a: Engel v. Vitale and Wisconsin v. Yoder
alt.ex: The families won in Engel (1962, prayer struck) and in Yoder (1972, Amish exemption granted).
w: Employment Division v. Smith and Wisconsin v. Yoder
The claimants lost in Smith (1990).
Engel v. Vitale and Employment Division v. Smith
The claimants lost in Smith.
Reynolds v. United States and Wisconsin v. Yoder
Reynolds (1879) upheld a ban on polygamy against a Mormon.

items.q: A pregnant Texas woman using a pseudonym challenged a state law banning abortion except to save the mother's life, and in 1973 the Court struck down the law. Which case?
items.a: Roe v. Wade
items.ex: Roe v. Wade (1973), 7–2, recognized an abortion right; it was overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022).
w: Planned Parenthood v. Casey
1992 case that reaffirmed Roe's core and adopted the undue burden test.
Griswold v. Connecticut
1965 case recognizing privacy in contraceptive use.
Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
2022 case that overruled Roe.

alt.q: Which 1973 case held that a constitutional right to privacy covered a woman's decision to have an abortion?
alt.a: Roe v. Wade
alt.ex: Justice Harry Blackmun wrote Roe v. Wade (1973); Dobbs (2022) overruled it.
w: Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Decided in 1992.
Griswold v. Connecticut
Concerned contraception in 1965.
Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
Rejected any such constitutional right in 2022.

alt.q: A 1973 opinion said the right of privacy "is broad enough to encompass a woman's decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy." What later happened to this holding?
alt.a: It was overruled by Dobbs v. Jackson in 2022
alt.ex: Roe's holding was overruled on June 24, 2022, in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization.
w: It was reaffirmed by Dobbs v. Jackson in 2022
Dobbs overruled Roe and Casey.
It was overruled by Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Casey (1992) reaffirmed Roe's central holding while dropping the trimester framework.
It was made permanent by a constitutional amendment
No amendment on abortion has been adopted.

items.q: Roe v. Wade based the abortion right on which part of the Constitution?
items.a: The Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: Roe (1973) found a privacy right in the 14th Amendment's concept of liberty; Dobbs (2022) rejected that reading.
w: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
Roe did not rest on equal protection.
The Fourth Amendment's search and seizure clause
Not the basis of Roe.
The Ninth Amendment standing alone
Roe noted the lower court's Ninth Amendment view but grounded the right in 14th Amendment liberty.

alt.q: What framework did Roe v. Wade use to balance a woman's right against state interests?
alt.a: A trimester system based on stages of pregnancy
alt.ex: Roe (1973) let states regulate more as pregnancy advanced, permitting bans after viability with life and health exceptions.
w: An undue burden test applied throughout pregnancy
Adopted by Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992).
Strict scrutiny with no state interest recognized
Roe recognized state interests in health and potential life.
A rule leaving all abortion law to the states
That is the result of Dobbs (2022).

alt.q: What is the current constitutional status of the abortion right recognized in Roe v. Wade?
alt.a: Overruled in 2022; states may now regulate or ban it
alt.ex: Dobbs (2022) held the Constitution confers no right to abortion and returned the issue to the people's elected representatives.
w: Still protected nationwide under Roe's trimester rule
Roe was overruled in 2022.
Protected under Casey's undue burden test since 1992
Casey was overruled along with Roe.
Banned nationwide by the Supreme Court in Dobbs
Dobbs did not ban abortion; it left the issue to states.

items.q: How did Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) change the law set by Roe v. Wade (1973)?
items.a: It overruled Roe and returned abortion law to the states
items.ex: Dobbs held 'Roe and Casey must be overruled' and returned the issue 'to the people's elected representatives.'
w: It upheld Roe but allowed a 15-week limit in Mississippi
That was roughly Chief Justice Roberts's concurrence, not the majority.
It banned abortion nationwide under the 14th Amendment
Dobbs did not ban abortion.
It replaced Roe's trimesters with an undue burden test
That was Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992).

alt.q: "The Constitution makes no reference to abortion, and no such right is implicitly protected by any constitutional provision..." Which case contains this statement?
alt.a: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health
alt.ex: Justice Samuel Alito wrote this in Dobbs (2022), which overruled Roe v. Wade (1973).
w: Roe v. Wade
Roe held the opposite in 1973.
Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Casey reaffirmed Roe's core holding in 1992.
Webster v. Reproductive Health Services
1989 case upholding some Missouri limits without overruling Roe.

alt.q: A state bans most abortions after 15 weeks, and the law reaches the Supreme Court in 2021–2022. What did the Court decide?
alt.a: Upheld the law and overruled Roe and Casey
alt.ex: In Dobbs (2022), the Court upheld Mississippi's 15-week law, 6–3 on the judgment, and overruled Roe and Casey 5–4.
w: Struck the law down under Roe's trimester rule
The law was upheld.
Upheld the law but kept Roe's core right
That was Chief Justice Roberts's separate view, not the Court's holding.
Struck the law down under Casey's undue burden test
Casey was overruled, and the law was upheld.

items.q: A special prosecutor subpoenaed tape recordings of Oval Office conversations for a trial of the President's aides in the Watergate scandal. The President refused, claiming executive privilege. Which case?
items.a: United States v. Nixon
items.ex: United States v. Nixon (1974), 8–0, ordered President Nixon to turn over the tapes.
w: New York Times v. United States
1971 Pentagon Papers case on prior restraint.
Clinton v. Jones
1997 case allowing a civil suit against a sitting President for prior conduct.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald
1982 case giving Presidents immunity from civil damages for official acts.

alt.q: Which case unanimously held that executive privilege is not absolute and ordered the President to produce evidence for a criminal trial?
alt.a: United States v. Nixon
alt.ex: Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote the 8–0 opinion in United States v. Nixon (1974); Justice Rehnquist did not participate.
w: New York Times v. United States
Concerned newspapers, not presidential evidence.
Clinton v. Jones
Concerned a civil lawsuit, not a criminal subpoena.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald
Expanded presidential immunity in civil cases.

alt.q: "...neither the doctrine of separation of powers nor the need for confidentiality of high-level communications, without more, can sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege..." Which case?
alt.a: United States v. Nixon
alt.ex: This passage from United States v. Nixon (1974) rejected an absolute executive privilege against a criminal subpoena.
w: Nixon v. Fitzgerald
1982 case that expanded presidential immunity from civil damages.
Clinton v. Jones
1997 case on a civil suit over pre-office conduct.
New York Times v. United States
1971 case on prior restraint of the press.

items.q: United States v. Nixon is most closely tied to which constitutional principle?
items.a: Rule of law: even the President is subject to the courts
items.ex: U.S. v. Nixon (1974) held that a President must comply with a judicial subpoena in a criminal case.
w: Popular sovereignty: the people may recall a President
The Constitution has no recall; removal is by impeachment.
Federalism: states may prosecute federal officials
The case was a federal prosecution.
Executive privilege: the President decides what to share
The Court rejected an absolute privilege.

alt.q: What was the most immediate result of United States v. Nixon?
alt.a: Nixon released the tapes and resigned weeks later
alt.ex: The ruling came on July 24, 1974; Nixon released the tapes and resigned on August 9, 1974.
w: Nixon was impeached by the House and removed by the Senate
He resigned before the full House voted on impeachment.
Congress passed a law ending executive privilege
No such law was passed; a limited privilege still exists.
Nixon was pardoned by the Supreme Court itself
President Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon; courts do not pardon.

alt.q: A future President refuses to give a federal court evidence subpoenaed for a criminal trial, citing only a general need for confidential advice. Under United States v. Nixon, a court would most likely
alt.a: order the evidence produced, as privilege is not absolute
alt.ex: U.S. v. Nixon (1974) held a generalized interest in confidentiality must yield to a specific need for evidence in a criminal trial.
w: uphold the refusal, since privilege is absolute
The Court rejected an absolute privilege.
refuse to hear the case as a political question
The Court held the dispute was justiciable.
require a vote of Congress before any evidence is released
No congressional vote is required.

items.q: United States v. Nixon (1974) quoted Marbury v. Madison (1803). Which statement correctly links the two?
items.a: Both affirm courts' power to say what the law is
items.ex: Nixon relied on Marbury's statement that it is 'the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.'
w: Both struck down acts of Congress as unconstitutional
Nixon struck down no statute.
Both involved presidential appointments not delivered
Only Marbury involved an undelivered commission.
Both held the President immune from court orders
Nixon held the opposite.

alt.q: During the Watergate crisis, which branch did what?
alt.a: Courts ordered the tapes; the House pursued impeachment
alt.ex: The Supreme Court ordered the tapes released (1974), while the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment.
w: The House ordered the tapes; courts pursued impeachment
Courts do not impeach.
The Senate ordered the tapes; courts removed the President
Courts cannot remove a President.
Courts ordered the tapes; the Senate convicted Nixon
There was no Senate trial; Nixon resigned.

alt.q: United States v. Nixon (1974) is sometimes confused with Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982). What did Fitzgerald decide?
alt.a: Presidents are immune from civil damages for official acts
alt.ex: Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) granted absolute immunity from civil damages suits based on official presidential acts.
w: Presidents must turn over tapes for criminal trials
That was United States v. Nixon (1974).
Presidents may be sued over private acts taken before office
That was Clinton v. Jones (1997).
Presidents can be indicted while in office
Fitzgerald did not address indictment.

items.q: A white applicant was twice rejected by a public medical school that reserved 16 of 100 seats for minority applicants, though their scores exceeded those of admitted minority students. Which case?
items.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
items.ex: In Bakke (1978), the Court struck down UC Davis's fixed quota and ordered Bakke admitted.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
1954 case ending school segregation.
Grutter v. Bollinger
2003 case upholding a law school's holistic use of race.
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
2023 case ending race-conscious admissions at Harvard and UNC.

alt.q: Which case struck down a fixed racial quota in admissions but allowed race to be considered as one factor among many?
alt.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) produced split 5–4 holdings, with Justice Lewis Powell casting the deciding vote on both.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Concerned segregation, not admissions preferences.
Grutter v. Bollinger
Upheld holistic admissions in 2003, building on Bakke.
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
Ruled against race-conscious admissions in 2023.

alt.q: In which 1978 case did Justice Lewis Powell's controlling opinion reject reserved seats for minorities while allowing race as a 'plus' factor?
alt.a: Regents of Univ. of California v. Bakke
alt.ex: Powell's opinion in Bakke (1978) became the model for affirmative action in admissions for decades.
w: Brown v. Board of Education
Decided in 1954 by Chief Justice Warren.
Grutter v. Bollinger
Decided in 2003, written by Justice O'Connor.
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
Decided in 2023, written by Chief Justice Roberts.

items.q: Along with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Bakke turned mainly on which constitutional clause?
items.a: The Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment
items.ex: Powell held the UC Davis quota violated the Equal Protection Clause (1978).
w: The Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
UC Davis is a state school, so the 14th Amendment applied.
The Commerce Clause of Article I
Admissions quotas were not a commerce issue.
The Privileges or Immunities Clause of the 14th Amendment
Not the basis of Bakke.

alt.q: A state university gives applicants a modest boost for race as one of many factors, with no reserved seats. Under Bakke, this approach was
alt.a: permitted, as a flexible plus rather than a quota
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) allowed race as a 'plus' factor; Students for Fair Admissions (2023) later found such programs at Harvard and UNC unconstitutional.
w: forbidden, since any use of race was unconstitutional
Bakke allowed race as one factor.
required, since quotas were needed to fix past bias
Bakke struck down quotas.
permitted, only if seats were set aside by race
Set-aside seats were exactly what Bakke struck down.

alt.q: What was the main result of Bakke?
alt.a: Racial quotas were barred, but race could still be a factor
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) struck the 16-seat quota while allowing race as one consideration in admissions.
w: All affirmative action in admissions was banned
Bakke allowed race as one factor.
Affirmative action became mandatory in every public university
Bakke required no such programs.
Schools had to admit applicants by test scores only
The Court imposed no scores-only rule.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes Bakke (1978) from Brown v. Board of Education (1954)?
items.a: Bakke addressed affirmative action; Brown, segregation
items.ex: Both applied Equal Protection to race in education, but Brown ended segregation while Bakke limited affirmative action quotas.
w: Bakke addressed segregation; Brown, affirmative action
Reverses the two cases.
Bakke addressed school prayer; Brown, segregation
School prayer was Engel v. Vitale.
Bakke addressed voting districts; Brown, admissions
Neither description is correct.

alt.q: Bakke (1978) is often contrasted with Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023). What did the later case do?
alt.a: It found race-conscious admissions programs unlawful
alt.ex: SFFA (2023) held the Harvard and UNC programs violated equal protection, largely ending the race-as-a-factor approach Bakke allowed.
w: It reaffirmed Bakke's use of race as one plus factor
SFFA rejected those programs.
It required racial quotas to fix past discrimination
Quotas remain unconstitutional.
It required all public colleges to adopt racial quotas for admissions
SFFA did the opposite.

alt.q: A medical school (A) holds 16 seats only for minority applicants; a law school (B) considers race individually alongside many factors with no seats reserved. Under Bakke's reasoning, which is true?
alt.a: A is unconstitutional; B may be permissible
alt.ex: Bakke (1978) struck the fixed quota (like A) but allowed race as one factor (like B); Grutter (2003) later upheld a program like B.
w: A is permissible; B is unconstitutional
Reverses Bakke's reasoning.
Both are required by Brown v. Board
Brown required neither.
Both are unconstitutional under Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy concerned segregation and was overturned for schools by Brown.

items.q: A Missouri high school principal removed two pages from the school-sponsored student newspaper because articles on teen pregnancy and divorce were inappropriate. Students sued. Which case?
items.a: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
items.ex: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988), 5–3, upheld the principal's action.
w: Tinker v. Des Moines
1969 case protecting students' personal armbands.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
1986 case on a lewd student assembly speech.
New York Times v. United States
1971 case rejecting prior restraint of national newspapers.

alt.q: Which case held that educators may control the content of school-sponsored student publications for legitimate teaching reasons?
alt.a: Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier
alt.ex: Justice Byron White wrote for the Court in Hazelwood (1988).
w: Tinker v. Des Moines
Protected personal student expression.
Bethel School District v. Fraser
Allowed discipline for lewd speech.
New York Times v. United States
Concerned prior restraint of the national press.
