The 1957 act dealt with voting rights and created the Civil Rights Commission.
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) sets minimum wages and maximum hours.
The Americans with Disabilities Act
The ADA (1990) bans disability discrimination.

items.q: A public school district that receives federal money still runs separate schools for Black and white students in 1966. Which part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 lets federal agencies cut off its funds?
items.a: Title VI, banning bias in federally funded programs
items.ex: Title VI bars discrimination by race, color or national origin in any program receiving federal financial assistance; the threat of losing funds sped school desegregation after Brown.
w: Title II, banning bias in places of public accommodation
Title II covers hotels, restaurants and theaters, not schools' funding.
Title VII, banning bias by employers against workers
Title VII covers employment.
Title I, setting uniform rules for voter registration
Title I of the 1964 act dealt with voting procedures.

alt.q: "No person in the United States shall, on the ground of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance." Where is this found?
alt.a: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
alt.ex: This is the core sentence of Title VI (1964); Title IX (1972) later copied its structure to ban sex discrimination in federally funded education.
w: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972
Title IX uses similar wording but covers sex in education programs.
Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
Section 2 bars voting practices that deny or abridge the vote on account of race or color.
Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968
Title VIII (the Fair Housing Act) covers housing.

alt.q: What protection did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 add for people in programs that receive federal grants?
alt.a: A ban on race-based exclusion from those programs
alt.ex: Title VI bars exclusion or discrimination by race, color or national origin in federally funded programs and allows agencies to cut off funds.
w: A ban on poll taxes in state and local elections
Poll taxes in federal elections were banned by the 24th Amendment; in state elections by Harper v. Virginia (1966).
A requirement of racial hiring quotas for recipients
The 1964 act does not require quotas; Title VII expressly does not require preferential treatment.
A ban on discrimination in the sale of houses
Housing discrimination was banned by the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

items.q: Which law provides: "No voting qualification or prerequisite to voting, or standard, practice, or procedure shall be imposed or applied by any State or political subdivision to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color"?
items.a: The Voting Rights Act
items.ex: This is Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, signed by Lyndon Johnson on August 6, 1965, to enforce the Fifteenth Amendment.
w: The Fifteenth Amendment
The 15th Amendment (1870) says the vote shall not be denied 'on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude'; the excerpt is statutory language enforcing it.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The 24th Amendment (1964) bans poll taxes in federal elections.
The Civil Rights Act of 1957
The 1957 act let the Justice Department sue to protect voting but did not contain this section.

alt.q: Which constitutional amendment was the Voting Rights Act of 1965 primarily designed to enforce?
alt.a: The Fifteenth Amendment
alt.ex: The 15th Amendment (1870) bars denying the vote on account of race; Section 2 of that amendment gave Congress enforcement power, which the VRA used.
w: The Nineteenth Amendment
The 19th Amendment (1920) protects voting regardless of sex.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment
The 26th Amendment (1971) set the voting age at 18.
The Seventeenth Amendment
The 17th Amendment (1913) provided for direct election of senators.

alt.q: Which event in March 1965, when state troopers beat marchers on a bridge in Alabama, pushed Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act?
alt.a: Bloody Sunday in Selma
alt.ex: On March 7, 1965, troopers attacked voting-rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma; televised images built support for the VRA.
w: The March on Washington
The 1963 March on Washington supported the civil rights bill that became the 1964 act.
The Montgomery bus boycott
The 1955-56 boycott challenged bus segregation.
The Greensboro sit-ins
The 1960 Greensboro sit-ins challenged lunch-counter segregation.

items.q: In 1970 a Mississippi county covered by a 1965 federal law wants to move its polling places. Before doing so it must get approval from the U.S. Attorney General or a federal court in D.C. What is this requirement called?
items.a: Preclearance
items.ex: Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act required jurisdictions identified by the Section 4(b) coverage formula to 'preclear' any change in voting rules with federal authorities.
w: Judicial review
Judicial review is a court's power to strike down unconstitutional laws (Marbury v. Madison).
Redistricting
Redistricting is redrawing district lines; it was one kind of change that needed preclearance.
Incorporation
Incorporation applies Bill of Rights protections to the states through the 14th Amendment.

alt.q: In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), what did the Supreme Court decide about the Voting Rights Act?
alt.a: Its formula for picking covered places was outdated
alt.ex: The Court struck down Section 4(b)'s coverage formula as based on decades-old data, leaving Section 5 preclearance with no jurisdictions to apply to; Section 2 remains in force.
w: Its ban on racial discrimination in voting was void
Section 2's nationwide ban was not struck down.
Its preclearance rule had to cover every state
The Court did not extend preclearance; it disabled it.
Its protections applied to federal elections only
The VRA applies to state and local elections too.

alt.q: Which tool of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 most directly removed a common barrier used to keep Black citizens from registering?
alt.a: Suspending literacy tests in covered areas
alt.ex: The VRA suspended literacy tests in covered jurisdictions and sent federal examiners to register voters; later amendments banned such tests nationwide.
w: Banning poll taxes in all federal elections
That was the 24th Amendment (1964), not the VRA.
Lowering the voting age to eighteen
That was the 26th Amendment (1971).
Creating the Commission on Civil Rights
That was the Civil Rights Act of 1957.

items.q: Which statement best describes the effect of the Voting Rights Act of 1965?
items.a: Black registration in the South rose sharply within a few years
items.ex: With literacy tests suspended and federal examiners on site, Black registration soared; in Mississippi it rose from about 7% in 1964 to about 60% by 1967.
w: Black voter registration fell as states switched to poll taxes
The 24th Amendment and court rulings blocked poll taxes; registration rose.
It had little effect until the Supreme Court enforced it in 2013
The 2013 Shelby County ruling limited the act; its effects came in the 1960s.
It extended the right to vote to women in the Southern states
Women's suffrage was secured by the 19th Amendment (1920).

alt.q: In Mississippi about 7% of eligible Black adults were registered to vote in 1964, and about 60% in 1967. Which measure best explains this change?
alt.a: The Voting Rights Act
alt.ex: The VRA suspended literacy tests and sent federal registrars into covered states such as Mississippi, causing the sharp rise.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1957
The 1957 act relied on slow lawsuits and produced little change.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment
The 24th Amendment ended poll taxes only in federal elections and did not address literacy tests.
The Fair Housing Act of 1968
The Fair Housing Act concerns housing and came after 1967.

alt.q: Which President signed the Voting Rights Act after urging Congress in a televised March 1965 speech to pass it?
alt.a: Lyndon B. Johnson
alt.ex: Johnson addressed Congress on March 15, 1965, after Selma, and signed the VRA on August 6, 1965.
w: John F. Kennedy
Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963.
Dwight D. Eisenhower
Eisenhower signed the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960.
Richard M. Nixon
Nixon signed a 1970 extension of the VRA, not the original act.

items.q: Which statement best describes the difference between Medicare and Medicaid, both created in 1965?
items.a: Medicare covers older Americans; Medicaid covers low-income people
items.ex: The Social Security Amendments of 1965 (signed July 30, 1965) created Medicare, federal health insurance for people 65+, and Medicaid, a joint federal-state program for people with low incomes.
w: Medicare covers low-income people; Medicaid covers older Americans
This reverses the two programs.
Medicare covers veterans; Medicaid covers federal civil servants
Veterans' care is through the VA; federal workers have their own plans.
Medicare covers children; Medicaid covers only the disabled
Medicare is mainly for those 65+; Medicaid covers many low-income groups, including children.

alt.q: A 70-year-old retiree is hospitalized for surgery in 1967, and the federal government pays most of the hospital bill through a program funded by payroll taxes. Which program is this?
alt.a: Medicare
alt.ex: Medicare (1965) is federal health insurance for people 65 and older; its hospital coverage (Part A) is funded by payroll taxes.
w: Medicaid
Medicaid is for low-income people and is run jointly by states and the federal government.
Head Start
Head Start is a preschool program for low-income children.
Job Corps
Job Corps (1964) is a job-training program for young people; it does not pay hospital bills.

alt.q: A low-income family with two young children gets health coverage through a program their state runs and the federal government helps pay for. Which program is this?
alt.a: Medicaid
alt.ex: Medicaid (1965) is a joint federal-state program covering eligible low-income people; states administer it with federal matching funds.
w: Medicare
Medicare is a federal program mainly for people 65 and older.
Social Security
Social Security pays retirement, survivor and disability cash benefits.
Job Corps
Job Corps is a job-training program for young people.

items.q: Which statement best describes the primary goal of Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs?
items.a: To end poverty and racial injustice using federal power
items.ex: Johnson's Great Society (1964-1966) included the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, and civil rights laws.
w: To end the Depression through relief, recovery and reform
Relief, recovery and reform were FDR's New Deal goals in the 1930s.
To shrink federal spending and return programs to states
That describes Reagan-era 'New Federalism,' not the Great Society.
To break up monopolies and make food and drugs safer
Trust-busting and food safety laws belong to the Progressive Era.

alt.q: Which group of laws belongs to Lyndon Johnson's Great Society?
alt.a: Medicare, Head Start and school aid (ESEA)
alt.ex: Medicare (1965), Head Start (1965) and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965) were core Great Society programs.
w: Social Security, the Wagner Act and the FLSA
These are FDR's New Deal laws (1935-1938).
The Meat Inspection, Pure Food and Hepburn Acts
These are Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal laws (1906).
The PATRIOT Act, No Child Left Behind, Part D
These are George W. Bush-era laws (2001-2003).

alt.q: Lyndon Johnson declared an "unconditional war on poverty" in 1964. Which law launched programs such as the Job Corps and VISTA as part of that effort?
alt.a: The Economic Opportunity Act
alt.ex: The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 created the Office of Economic Opportunity, Job Corps, VISTA and Community Action programs.
w: The Social Security Act
The Social Security Act was a 1935 New Deal law.
The Fair Labor Standards Act
The FLSA (1938) set minimum wage and hours.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The Civil Rights Act banned discrimination; it did not create anti-poverty job programs.

items.q: In 1970 a landlord refuses to rent an apartment to a family because the family is Jewish. Which law most directly prohibits this?
items.a: The Fair Housing Act of 1968
items.ex: Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 bans discrimination in selling, renting and financing housing based on race, color, religion or national origin (sex added 1974; disability and familial status 1988).
w: Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title II covers public accommodations such as hotels and restaurants, not apartment rentals.
Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title VII covers employment.
Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
Section 2 covers voting.

alt.q: Which event in April 1968 helped push Congress to pass the Fair Housing Act within a week?
alt.a: The assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
alt.ex: King was killed on April 4, 1968; Johnson urged quick passage and signed the Civil Rights Act of 1968 on April 11.
w: The assassination of Senator Robert F. Kennedy
RFK was shot in June 1968, after the act passed.
The Tet Offensive launched in South Vietnam
The Tet Offensive (January 1968) affected war policy, not housing law.
The Watts uprising in Los Angeles
The Watts riots occurred in 1965.

alt.q: A 1968 law's housing title begins: "It is the policy of the United States to provide, within constitutional limitations, for fair housing throughout the United States." Which practice was this law mainly aimed at?
alt.a: Refusing to sell or rent homes due to race
alt.ex: This opens Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Fair Housing Act), which outlawed discrimination in sales, rentals and financing of housing.
w: Refusing to serve diners at lunch counters
Lunch-counter segregation was addressed by Title II of the 1964 act.
Using literacy tests to block registration
Literacy tests were addressed by the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Paying women less than men for the same work
Unequal pay by sex was addressed by the Equal Pay Act of 1963.

items.q: In 1975 a bank refuses to make home loans in any neighborhood where most residents are Black. Which law makes this practice, known as redlining, illegal?
items.a: The Fair Housing Act of 1968
items.ex: The Fair Housing Act (1968) bans discrimination in the financing of housing as well as in sales and rentals, which covers redlining.
w: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title VII covers employment discrimination.
Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Title II covers public accommodations.
The Civil Rights Act of 1875
The 1875 act was struck down in 1883 and covered inns and transport.

alt.q: Which activities are covered by the Fair Housing Act of 1968?
alt.a: Selling, renting and financing homes
alt.ex: Title VIII of the 1968 act bans discrimination in the sale, rental and financing of dwellings.
w: Hiring, promoting and firing workers
That is Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Serving guests in hotels and diners
That is Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Registering voters and running polls
That is the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

alt.q: Which category was not protected when the Fair Housing Act was first passed in 1968 but was added by Congress in 1974?
alt.a: Sex
alt.ex: The original act covered race, color, religion and national origin; sex was added in 1974, and disability and familial status in 1988.
w: Race
Race was protected from the start in 1968.
Religion
Religion was protected from the start in 1968.
Color
Color was protected from the start in 1968.

items.q: In August 1964 Congress stated that it "approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression." What did this resolution do?
items.a: It gave Johnson broad power to escalate the war in Vietnam
items.ex: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution passed on August 7, 1964 (House 416-0, Senate 88-2) after reported attacks on U.S. destroyers; Johnson used it to justify major escalation without a declaration of war. Congress repealed it in January 1971.
w: It formally declared war on North Vietnam under Article I
Congress never declared war in Vietnam; the resolution was an authorization, not a declaration.
It required the President to withdraw troops within 60 days
That deadline comes from the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
It ended U.S. combat in Vietnam after the Paris Peace Accords
The Paris Peace Accords came in January 1973.

alt.q: Which document contains the words "to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression"?
alt.a: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
alt.ex: This 1964 joint resolution became the legal basis Johnson cited for escalating U.S. involvement in Vietnam.
w: The War Powers Resolution
The War Powers Resolution (1973) limits, rather than expands, the President's ability to deploy troops.
The Formosa Resolution of 1955
The 1955 Formosa Resolution authorized Eisenhower to defend Taiwan; it said nothing about attacks on U.S. forces in Southeast Asia.
The 2002 Iraq War Resolution
The 2002 resolution authorized force against Iraq, nearly four decades later.

alt.q: Critics later called the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution a "blank check." Which concern does that label express?
alt.a: Congress gave away its war power without declaring war
alt.ex: The open-ended authorization let Johnson and Nixon fight a major war without Congress using its Article I power to declare war, which later led to the War Powers Resolution.
w: Congress spent unlimited money without passing any budget
The label refers to war-making authority, not spending.
The President signed a treaty without the Senate's consent
The resolution was not a treaty; it passed both houses.
The Supreme Court approved the war without hearing a case
The Supreme Court never ruled on the war's constitutionality.

items.q: Which requirement is part of the War Powers Resolution of 1973?
items.a: The President must notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying
items.ex: The War Powers Resolution requires a report within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities and withdrawal within 60 days (plus 30 for withdrawal) unless Congress declares war or authorizes the action; it passed over Nixon's veto on November 7, 1973.
w: The President must get a declaration of war before any deployment
The resolution allows deployments first, then sets reporting and time limits.
The Senate must approve every deployment by a two-thirds vote
Two-thirds Senate approval applies to treaties, not deployments.
The Supreme Court must review any deployment lasting over 90 days
The resolution gives no role to the courts.

alt.q: A President sends troops into hostilities abroad and reports to Congress. Sixty days pass with no declaration of war or other authorization. Under the War Powers Resolution, what must happen?
alt.a: The President must begin withdrawing the forces
alt.ex: After 60 days without congressional authorization, forces must be removed, with up to 30 more days allowed for safe withdrawal.
w: The President may keep them there as Commander in Chief
The resolution was written to prevent open-ended deployments without Congress.
The Supreme Court must decide whether troops can stay
The resolution gives the decision to Congress, not the courts.
The states must vote on whether to continue the mission
States have no role in authorizing military action.

alt.q: How did the War Powers Resolution become law in 1973?
alt.a: Congress overrode President Nixon's veto
alt.ex: Nixon vetoed it as an unconstitutional limit on his powers; both houses overrode the veto on November 7, 1973.
w: Nixon signed it after the Vietnam cease-fire
Nixon vetoed the resolution.
The Court ordered it in a Watergate case
Courts cannot order Congress to pass laws; U.S. v. Nixon concerned tapes.
Ford issued it as an executive order
Ford took office in August 1974, after it became law.

items.q: "It is the purpose of this joint resolution to fulfill the intent of the framers of the Constitution of the United States and insure that the collective judgment of both the Congress and the President will apply to the introduction of United States Armed Forces into hostilities." Which principle does this most directly reflect?
items.a: Checks and balances over the use of military force
items.ex: The War Powers Resolution (1973) aimed to restore Congress's check on war-making by requiring the 'collective judgment' of both branches.
w: Federalism dividing power between nation and states
The excerpt concerns two branches of the national government, not the states.
Judicial review of military orders by federal courts
The excerpt mentions Congress and the President, not the courts.
Popular election of the commander of the armed forces
The excerpt concerns how war decisions are made, not elections.

alt.q: Which law begins with the purpose of ensuring "that the collective judgment of both the Congress and the President will apply to the introduction of United States Armed Forces into hostilities"?
alt.a: The War Powers Resolution
alt.ex: This is Section 2(a) of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, passed over Nixon's veto.
w: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
The 1964 Tonkin Resolution expanded presidential power rather than requiring shared judgment.
The Iraq War Resolution
The 2002 Iraq Resolution authorized force against Iraq; it is not the 1973 framework law.
The National Security Act
The National Security Act (1947) created the NSC and CIA and reorganized the military.

alt.q: Which experience most directly led Congress to pass the War Powers Resolution in 1973?
alt.a: Years of undeclared war in Vietnam
alt.ex: Frustration with the Vietnam War, fought under the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution without a declaration, drove Congress to reassert its war powers.
w: The attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941
Pearl Harbor led to a formal declaration of war in 1941.
The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962
The 1962 crisis ended without war and did not prompt this law.
The Watergate break-in of 1972
Watergate was a domestic political scandal, not about war powers.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Clean Air Act of 1970?
items.a: It set national air quality standards that states had to help meet
items.ex: Signed by Nixon on December 31, 1970, the Clean Air Act authorized national air quality standards and emission limits for cars and factories, enforced by the new EPA, with states writing implementation plans.
w: It set national limits on water pollution discharged by factories
That was the Clean Water Act of 1972.
It created a federal list to protect endangered plants and animals
That was the Endangered Species Act of 1973.
It left all air pollution rules entirely up to the state governments
The 1970 act did the opposite, creating national standards.

alt.q: Which federal agency, created by President Nixon in 1970, enforces the Clean Air Act's standards?
alt.a: The Environmental Protection Agency
alt.ex: Nixon created the EPA by reorganization plan in December 1970; it sets and enforces national air quality standards.
w: The Department of the Interior
Interior manages public lands and national parks.
The Department of Transportation
The Department of Transportation (1966) oversees highways, aviation and rail; it does not set air quality standards.
The Department of Health, Education, and Welfare
Before 1970 federal air pollution programs sat in HEW; Nixon moved them to the new EPA.

alt.q: Under the Clean Air Act, a state writes a plan to cut smog from factories and cars so its cities meet federal standards; if the plan is weak, federal regulators can impose their own. Which concept does this illustrate?
alt.a: Cooperative federalism
alt.ex: The Clean Air Act sets national standards but relies on state implementation plans, with a federal backstop: a classic example of cooperative federalism.
w: Dual (layer-cake) federalism
Dual federalism describes separate, non-overlapping state and federal spheres.
State nullification
Nullification is a state claiming power to void a federal law.
Judicial activism
Judicial activism refers to courts' approach to rulings, not program design.

items.q: Which statement best describes the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001?
items.a: It expanded surveillance powers to fight terrorism
items.ex: Signed by George W. Bush on October 26, 2001, it expanded wiretap and records-search powers (roving wiretaps, delayed-notice searches, Section 215 business records), raising Fourth Amendment privacy concerns.
w: It created a new cabinet department for homeland security
That was the Homeland Security Act of 2002.
It authorized military force against those behind 9/11
That was the Authorization for Use of Military Force (September 18, 2001).
It banned cruel treatment of detainees in U.S. custody
That was the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005.

alt.q: After 2001 federal agents get a court order to tap any phone a terrorism suspect uses, rather than one line, and delay telling a person their home was searched. Critics argue these tools strain which amendment?
alt.a: The Fourth Amendment
alt.ex: The PATRIOT Act's roving wiretaps and 'sneak and peek' delayed-notice warrants raised concerns under the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.
w: The Fifth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment covers self-incrimination, double jeopardy and due process.
The Sixth Amendment
The Sixth Amendment covers rights at criminal trial, such as counsel and jury.
The Eighth Amendment
The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishment.

alt.q: Which law, passed weeks after the September 11 attacks, authorized "roving" wiretaps and expanded access to business records in terrorism investigations?
alt.a: The USA PATRIOT Act
alt.ex: The USA PATRIOT Act (October 26, 2001) expanded surveillance tools, including roving wiretaps and Section 215 orders for business records.
w: The Homeland Security Act
The Homeland Security Act (2002) created the Department of Homeland Security.
The USA FREEDOM Act
The USA FREEDOM Act (2015) narrowed, rather than created, these surveillance powers.
The Intelligence Reform Act
The 2004 Intelligence Reform Act created the Director of National Intelligence; it came three years later.

items.q: Supporters and critics of the USA PATRIOT Act mainly debated which tension in American government?
items.a: National security versus personal privacy
items.ex: Supporters said expanded surveillance was needed to prevent terrorism; critics said it weakened Fourth Amendment privacy and due process protections.
w: States' rights versus national supremacy
The PATRIOT Act debate was not mainly about state versus federal power.
Free trade versus protective tariffs on imports
Trade policy was not the issue.
Majority rule versus voting rights
The act did not deal with elections or voting.

alt.q: In 2015 Congress ended the PATRIOT Act's bulk collection of Americans' phone records and replaced it with a narrower system. Which law did this?
alt.a: The USA FREEDOM Act
alt.ex: After Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures, the USA FREEDOM Act (2015) ended NSA bulk collection under Section 215.
w: The Homeland Security Act
The Homeland Security Act (2002) created DHS.
The Intelligence Reform Act
The 2004 Intelligence Reform Act created the Director of National Intelligence.
The Privacy Act
The Privacy Act (1974) regulates how federal agencies handle personal records.

alt.q: A city council member argues that letting the FBI obtain library records without telling patrons sacrifices too much privacy for too little safety. Which law is the member criticizing?
alt.a: The USA PATRIOT Act
alt.ex: Section 215 of the PATRIOT Act let investigators obtain 'tangible things,' including library records, drawing protests from librarians and civil liberties groups.
w: The Freedom of Information Act
FOIA (1966) gives the public access to government records.
The Privacy Act of 1974
The Privacy Act limits, rather than expands, government use of personal records.
The War Powers Resolution
The War Powers Resolution limits military deployments.

items.q: Which set of provisions best describes the Affordable Care Act of 2010?
items.a: No denials for preexisting conditions; dependents covered to 26
items.ex: Signed by Barack Obama on March 23, 2010, the ACA barred denial for preexisting conditions, let young adults stay on parents' plans to 26, created marketplaces with subsidies, expanded Medicaid, and included an individual mandate.
w: Health insurance for everyone 65 and older, funded by payroll taxes
That describes Medicare (1965).
A single government-run insurer that replaces all private health plans
The ACA kept private insurance; a single-payer system was not enacted.
Prescription drug coverage added to Medicare for older Americans
That was Medicare Part D, created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003.

alt.q: In 2014 a 24-year-old graduate stays on a parent's health plan, and a neighbor with diabetes buys a policy on a state marketplace without being denied for that condition. Which law made both possible?
alt.a: The Affordable Care Act of 2010
alt.ex: The ACA (2010) extended dependent coverage to age 26 and barred insurers from denying coverage for preexisting conditions starting in 2014.
w: The Social Security Amendments of 1965
Those created Medicare and Medicaid.
The Medicare Modernization Act
That 2003 law created Medicare Part D drug coverage.
The Health Insurance Portability Act
HIPAA (1996) limited some preexisting-condition exclusions in group plans but did not create marketplaces or age-26 coverage.

alt.q: Which ACA feature was most controversial because it required most Americans to obtain health insurance or pay a penalty?
alt.a: The individual mandate
alt.ex: The individual mandate required most people to have coverage or pay a penalty; Congress reduced the penalty to $0 starting in 2019.
w: The employer mandate
The employer mandate applied to large employers, not individuals.
The public option
A government-run 'public option' was dropped from the final bill.
The Medicaid expansion
The expansion widened eligibility for low-income adults; it did not require anyone to buy insurance.

items.q: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), how did the Supreme Court rule on the Affordable Care Act?
items.a: It upheld the mandate as a tax but made Medicaid expansion optional
items.ex: Chief Justice Roberts found the mandate exceeded the Commerce Clause but was valid under the taxing power; threatening states' existing Medicaid funds was unconstitutionally coercive, so expansion became optional.
w: It upheld the mandate under the Commerce Clause and full expansion
The Court rejected the Commerce Clause basis and limited the Medicaid expansion.
It struck down the mandate but kept the rest of the law in force
The mandate was upheld as a tax.
It struck down the entire law as beyond Congress's enumerated powers
Most of the law survived; only the Medicaid penalty was limited.

alt.q: After 2012 some states decline to expand Medicaid under the ACA, and the federal government cannot take away their existing Medicaid funds. Which ruling and principle explain this?
alt.a: NFIB v. Sebelius; Congress can't coerce states with funds
alt.ex: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the Court held that threatening all of a state's Medicaid money to force expansion was unconstitutionally coercive.
w: U.S. v. Lopez; Congress may not ban guns near local schools
Lopez (1995) limited the Commerce Clause; it did not involve Medicaid.
McCulloch v. Maryland; states may not tax federal banks
McCulloch (1819) concerned implied powers and state taxation of the national bank.
King v. Burwell; ACA tax credits apply in every state
King (2015) upheld subsidies on federal exchanges, not Medicaid funding.

alt.q: Under which power did the Supreme Court uphold the ACA's individual mandate in 2012?
alt.a: The power to lay and collect taxes
alt.ex: Roberts's majority treated the mandate's penalty as a tax within Congress's Article I taxing power.
w: The power to regulate interstate commerce
The Court said the Commerce Clause cannot compel people to buy a product.
The Necessary and Proper Clause alone
The Court held the Necessary and Proper Clause could not support the mandate by itself.
The Supremacy Clause of Article VI
The Supremacy Clause makes federal law supreme; it is not a source of power to create a mandate.

items.q: Article 1 of a treaty states that the British king "acknowledges the said United States... to be free sovereign and Independent States." Which treaty is this?
items.a: The Treaty of Paris of 1783
items.ex: Signed September 3, 1783 and negotiated by Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay, it ended the Revolutionary War, recognized independence and set the western boundary at the Mississippi River.
w: The Treaty of Ghent of 1814
The Treaty of Ghent ended the War of 1812, restoring prewar boundaries.
The Treaty of Paris of 1898
The 1898 treaty ended the Spanish-American War.
The Jay Treaty of 1794
The Jay Treaty settled later disputes with Britain, such as British forts in the Northwest.

alt.q: Which territorial result came from the Treaty of Paris of 1783?
alt.a: U.S. land reached west to the Mississippi
alt.ex: Britain recognized U.S. boundaries running west to the Mississippi River, north to roughly the Great Lakes, and south to Spanish Florida.
w: U.S. land reached west to the Rocky Mountains
Lands to the Rockies came with the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
Spain ceded all of Florida to the U.S.
Spain ceded Florida in the Adams-Onís Treaty (1819).
Britain ceded all of Canada to the new U.S.
Canada remained British.

alt.q: Which three Americans negotiated the treaty that ended the American Revolution?
alt.a: Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay
alt.ex: Franklin, Adams and Jay negotiated the Treaty of Paris (1783); Henry Laurens also joined late in the talks.
w: Thomas Jefferson, James Madison and John Marshall
Jefferson was in Congress; none of these men negotiated the 1783 treaty.
George Washington, Henry Knox and Alexander Hamilton
These men led the army and the later Washington administration.
Robert Livingston, James Monroe and John Q. Adams
Livingston and Monroe negotiated the Louisiana Purchase; John Quincy Adams negotiated the Treaty of Ghent and the Adams-Onís Treaty.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results of the Treaty of Paris of 1898?
items.a: Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, the Philippines
items.ex: Signed December 10, 1898, it ended the Spanish-American War; the U.S. paid $20 million for the Philippines, and the Senate ratified it 57-27 in February 1899.
w: Spain ceded Florida and gave up its claims to the Oregon Country
That was the Adams-Onís Treaty (1819).
Mexico ceded California and the Southwest to the United States
That was the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848).
Britain recognized U.S. independence and its western lands
That was the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

alt.q: Article I of a treaty reads: "Spain relinquishes all claim of sovereignty over and title to Cuba." Which conflict did this treaty end?
alt.a: The Spanish-American War
alt.ex: This is the Treaty of Paris of 1898; Cuba then came under U.S. occupation until 1902.
w: The Mexican-American War
That war ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848).
The War of 1812
That war ended with the Treaty of Ghent (1814).
The Philippine-American War
That war (1899-1902) began after the treaty, when Filipinos resisted U.S. rule.

alt.q: Why was the Senate debate over the 1898 Treaty of Paris so heated?
alt.a: Critics opposed ruling colonies like the Philippines
alt.ex: Anti-imperialists, including the Anti-Imperialist League, argued that ruling the Philippines without consent violated American principles; the treaty passed with one vote to spare.
w: Critics opposed paying France for the Louisiana territory
That was the 1803 Louisiana Purchase debate.
Critics opposed giving Texas back to the Mexican government
The 1898 treaty did not involve Texas or Mexico.
Critics opposed Cuba's independence from Spanish rule
Congress had already pledged, in the Teller Amendment, not to annex Cuba.

items.q: A President's diplomats sign a peace treaty ending a war. Before it takes effect for the United States, what does the Constitution require?
items.a: Approval by two-thirds of the senators present
items.ex: Article II, Section 2 gives the President power to make treaties "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate... provided two thirds of the Senators present concur."
w: Approval by a majority of both houses of Congress
That is how bills and joint resolutions pass; treaties need only the Senate.
Approval by three-fourths of the state legislatures
That is the ratification rule for constitutional amendments.
A ruling by the Supreme Court that it is valid
The Court does not pre-approve treaties.

alt.q: The Senate approved the 1898 Treaty of Paris 57-27 in February 1899, just one vote more than needed. Which constitutional rule made the margin so tight?
alt.a: Treaties need consent of two-thirds of senators present
alt.ex: With 84 senators voting, 56 votes were needed for two-thirds; the treaty got 57.
w: Treaties need a majority vote in both the House and Senate
The House plays no formal role in ratifying treaties.
Treaties need a three-fourths vote of the entire Senate
The requirement is two-thirds of senators present.
Treaties need approval by special state conventions
State conventions were used to ratify the Constitution itself, not treaties.

alt.q: Which statement best describes the treaty-making power under the Constitution?
alt.a: A shared power of the President and the Senate
alt.ex: The President negotiates and signs treaties; the Senate must consent by a two-thirds vote (Article II, Section 2), an example of checks and balances.
w: An exclusive power held by the President alone
Treaties require Senate consent.
A shared power of the House and the Senate
The House has no formal role in treaty ratification.
A reserved power kept by the individual states
Article I, Section 10 forbids states from entering treaties.

items.q: Which statement best describes President Jefferson's dilemma over the Louisiana Purchase in 1803?
items.a: The Constitution did not clearly let him acquire foreign land
items.ex: Jefferson, a strict constructionist, doubted the Constitution allowed buying territory and drafted an amendment, but he acted through the treaty power; the Senate ratified the $15 million treaty in October 1803.
w: Congress had already declared war on France over the territory
The U.S. was not at war with France in 1803; the Quasi-War had ended in 1800.
Spain still held New Orleans and refused to sell it to anyone
Spain had secretly returned Louisiana to France in 1800.
The Senate had rejected every treaty he had submitted to it
The Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase treaty by a wide margin.

alt.q: Jefferson's purchase of Louisiana is often cited as a time when he set aside which of his own principles?
alt.a: Strict construction of the Constitution
alt.ex: Jefferson believed the federal government had only expressly granted powers, and no clause clearly authorized acquiring territory; he bought Louisiana anyway.
w: Loose construction of the Constitution
Loose construction was Hamilton's view; Jefferson acted more like a loose constructionist here.
Judicial review of acts passed by Congress
Judicial review was the issue in Marbury v. Madison (1803), not the purchase.
Separation of church and state
The purchase raised no religion question.

alt.q: In 1803 Kentucky farmers depend on shipping crops down the Mississippi through New Orleans, which France now controls. Which action secured their access permanently?
alt.a: Buying Louisiana from France for $15 million
alt.ex: The Louisiana Purchase put New Orleans and the whole Mississippi under U.S. control.
w: Gaining Florida from Spain in the Adams-Onís Treaty
That 1819 treaty concerned Florida and the western border.
Signing Pinckney's Treaty for a right of deposit
Pinckney's Treaty (1795) gave only a temporary right of deposit, which Spain suspended in 1802.
Declaring war on France in the Quasi-War
The Quasi-War (1798-1800) was an undeclared naval conflict.

items.q: Which statement best describes the significance of the Louisiana Purchase?
items.a: It roughly doubled the land area of the United States
items.ex: The 1803 purchase of about 828,000 square miles from France roughly doubled the nation's size and gave it the Mississippi River and New Orleans.
w: It gave the United States its first coastline on the Pacific
The Pacific coast came with the Oregon Treaty (1846) and the Mexican Cession (1848).
It ended all Spanish claims to land east of the Mississippi
Spain gave up Florida in the Adams-Onís Treaty (1819).
It settled the northern border between the U.S. and Canada
The northern border was set by later agreements with Britain (1818, 1842, 1846).

alt.q: From which nation, and under whose leadership, did the United States buy Louisiana in 1803?
alt.a: France under Napoleon
alt.ex: Napoleon sold Louisiana after failing to retake Saint-Domingue (Haiti) and needing money for war with Britain.
w: Spain under King Ferdinand VII
Spain under Ferdinand VII ceded Florida in 1819.
Britain under King George III
Britain did not own Louisiana.
Mexico under Santa Anna
Santa Anna sold land in the Gadsden Purchase (1853).

alt.q: Which expedition did Jefferson send in 1804 to explore the newly purchased territory and reach the Pacific?
alt.a: The Lewis and Clark expedition
alt.ex: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led the Corps of Discovery (1804-1806) up the Missouri River to the Pacific.
w: The Frémont western surveys
John C. Frémont's expeditions were in the 1840s.
The Hernando de Soto expedition
De Soto was a 16th-century Spanish explorer.
The Henry Hudson voyages
Hudson explored the Northeast in the early 1600s.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Adams-Onís Treaty, signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821?
items.a: Spain ceded Florida, and a border with New Spain was set
items.ex: Negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams and Spanish minister Luis de Onís, it transferred Florida, drew a boundary to the Pacific, and had the U.S. give up its claim to Texas and assume up to $5 million in citizens' claims.
w: Spain let Americans ship goods duty-free through New Orleans
That right of deposit came from Pinckney's Treaty (1795).
Britain and the U.S. agreed to share the Oregon Country
Joint occupation of Oregon came from the Convention of 1818 with Britain.
Mexico ceded Texas and California after losing a war
That was the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848).

alt.q: Which American negotiated the 1819 treaty in which Spain ceded Florida to the United States?
alt.a: John Quincy Adams
alt.ex: As Monroe's Secretary of State, Adams negotiated with Luis de Onís; the treaty bears both names.
w: Andrew Jackson
Jackson's 1818 invasion of Florida pressured Spain, but he did not negotiate the treaty.
James Monroe
Monroe was President; his Secretary of State conducted the negotiations.
Robert Livingston
Livingston helped negotiate the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.

alt.q: What did the United States give up in the Adams-Onís Treaty in exchange for Florida and a defined border?
alt.a: Its claim to Texas as part of Louisiana
alt.ex: The U.S. renounced its claim that Texas was included in the Louisiana Purchase; Spain gave up claims to the Pacific Northwest.
w: Its claim to the Oregon Country in the Northwest
Spain, not the U.S., gave up claims north of the 42nd parallel.
Its right to use the port of New Orleans
New Orleans was already U.S. territory after 1803.
Its trade with Spain's Caribbean colonies
The treaty did not end U.S. trade with Spanish colonies.

items.q: In 1818 General Andrew Jackson chased Seminole raiders into Spanish Florida and seized Spanish forts. How did this affect talks with Spain?
items.a: It exposed how weakly Spain held Florida
items.ex: Jackson's raid demonstrated Spain's weakness; Secretary of State John Quincy Adams defended it and used it to press Spain into the 1819 Adams-Onís Treaty.
w: It led Spain to declare war on the U.S.
Spain did not go to war; it negotiated instead.
It made Congress return Louisiana to Spain
Louisiana was never returned to Spain.
It ended all talks until after the Civil War
The treaty was signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821.

alt.q: Which other name for the Adams-Onís Treaty reflects that it drew a U.S.-Spanish boundary all the way to the Pacific?
alt.a: The Transcontinental Treaty
alt.ex: Because its boundary line ran from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific along rivers and the 42nd parallel, it is also called the Transcontinental Treaty.
w: The Oregon Boundary Treaty
The Oregon Treaty (1846) split the Oregon Country with Britain at the 49th parallel.
The Northwest Ordinance
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) organized the Northwest Territory.
The Gadsden Purchase Treaty
The Gadsden Purchase (1853) bought land from Mexico for a southern railroad route.

alt.q: Which territory did Spain transfer to the United States under the treaty that John Quincy Adams negotiated in 1819?
alt.a: Florida
alt.ex: Spain ceded East and West Florida under the Adams-Onís Treaty, signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821.
w: Louisiana
Louisiana was bought from France in 1803.
Texas
The U.S. gave up its claim to Texas in this treaty.
Oregon
Spain gave up claims to Oregon, but the U.S. shared that region with Britain; Spain did not transfer it.

items.q: A President told Congress in 1823 that "the American continents... are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers." Which policy is this?
items.a: The Monroe Doctrine
items.ex: James Monroe announced it in his annual message of December 2, 1823; Secretary of State John Quincy Adams was its chief author.
w: The Roosevelt Corollary
Theodore Roosevelt's 1904 corollary claimed a U.S. 'international police power' in Latin America.
The Truman Doctrine
The Truman Doctrine (1947) pledged support to nations resisting communism.
Washington's Farewell Address
Washington's 1796 address warned against permanent alliances; it said nothing about colonization of the Americas.

alt.q: Monroe's 1823 message said the American continents were "not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers." Which principle does this state?
alt.a: No new European colonies in the Americas
alt.ex: This line is the non-colonization principle of the Monroe Doctrine; the message also warned against European intervention in the hemisphere.
w: Containment of Soviet communist expansion
Containment was Cold War policy (Truman Doctrine, 1947).
Isolation from all foreign trade and ties
The doctrine did not cut off trade; it warned Europe away from the Americas.
Collective security through binding alliances
Collective security alliances like NATO came after 1945.

alt.q: Which official, as Secretary of State, was the chief author of the policy announced in Monroe's 1823 message?
alt.a: John Quincy Adams
alt.ex: Adams insisted the U.S. act alone rather than jointly with Britain, and drafted the key principles.
w: Speaker Henry Clay
Clay was Speaker of the House and a champion of Latin American independence.
James Madison
Madison was a former President who advised Monroe to accept a joint statement with Britain.
Thomas Jefferson
Jefferson, also retired, advised Monroe but did not draft the message.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Monroe Doctrine's main message to Europe?
items.a: Keep out of the Americas; the U.S. will stay out of Europe
items.ex: Monroe warned against new colonization or intervention in the Western Hemisphere, while saying the U.S. would not take part in Europe's own wars.
w: Join the U.S. in a defensive alliance against the Russian Empire
Monroe proposed no alliance; Adams rejected even a joint statement with Britain.
Help the U.S. end the Atlantic slave trade by naval force
Ending the slave trade was not part of the doctrine.
Share control of Latin American trade with the United States
The doctrine aimed to keep European powers out, not to share influence.

alt.q: Monroe wrote that "we should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety." Whom does "their" refer to?
alt.a: European monarchies
alt.ex: Monroe was warning the European powers, especially the monarchies of the Holy Alliance, not to restore Spanish rule or extend their system in the Americas.
w: Latin American republics
The doctrine aimed to protect the newly independent Latin American republics.
Native American nations
The message concerns European powers, not Native nations.
Southern slaveholding states
The message concerns foreign powers, not U.S. states.

alt.q: In the 1860s France installed an emperor in Mexico while the U.S. was fighting the Civil War. After the war, U.S. pressure helped force French troops out. Which policy did U.S. leaders invoke?
alt.a: The Monroe Doctrine
alt.ex: Secretary of State William Seward pressed France to withdraw, relying on the Monroe Doctrine's opposition to European intervention; Maximilian's regime fell in 1867.
w: The Open Door Policy
The Open Door (1899-1900) concerned trade access in China.
The Good Neighbor Policy
FDR's Good Neighbor Policy (1930s) renounced U.S. intervention in Latin America.
Dollar diplomacy
Taft's dollar diplomacy (1909-1913) used investment to gain influence.

items.q: How did the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 change the Monroe Doctrine?
items.a: It asserted a U.S. right to police Latin American nations
items.ex: Theodore Roosevelt said 'chronic wrongdoing' could force the U.S. to exercise 'an international police power,' turning a warning to Europe into a justification for U.S. intervention (e.g., Dominican Republic, 1905).
w: It barred any U.S. military action in the Western Hemisphere
That is closer to FDR's Good Neighbor Policy of the 1930s.
It opened Latin America to new colonies from European powers
The corollary was meant to keep Europeans out.
It ended all U.S. involvement in Latin American affairs
It expanded U.S. involvement.

alt.q: A President declared in 1904 that wrongdoing in the hemisphere might force the United States "to the exercise of an international police power." Which policy is this?
alt.a: The Roosevelt Corollary
alt.ex: Theodore Roosevelt's corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (December 1904) justified U.S. intervention in Latin American countries.
w: The Monroe Doctrine
The original 1823 doctrine warned Europe away; it did not claim a police power for the U.S.
The Good Neighbor Policy
FDR's policy rejected intervention.
The Open Door Policy
The Open Door concerned trade in China.

alt.q: Which President expanded the Monroe Doctrine in 1904 to justify U.S. intervention in Latin American countries' affairs?
alt.a: Theodore Roosevelt
alt.ex: Theodore Roosevelt announced the corollary in his 1904 annual message, in line with his 'big stick' diplomacy.
w: William McKinley
McKinley led the U.S. in the Spanish-American War and was killed in 1901.
Woodrow Wilson
Wilson intervened in Mexico and the Caribbean but did not issue the corollary.
Franklin D. Roosevelt
FDR's Good Neighbor Policy moved away from the corollary.

items.q: The Constitution states: "The Privilege of the Writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it." Why was Lincoln's 1861 suspension controversial?
items.a: It sits in Article I, implying only Congress may suspend
items.ex: The clause appears in Article I, Section 9, among limits on Congress. Lincoln suspended the writ in April 1861 while Congress was not in session; Chief Justice Taney said only Congress could do so, and Congress authorized suspension in 1863.
w: The clause is in Article II, limiting it to wartime treaties
The clause is in Article I, not Article II, and does not mention treaties.
The clause is in the Bill of Rights as an absolute ban
It is in the original Constitution and allows suspension in rebellion or invasion.
The clause was added by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865
It was in the original 1787 Constitution.

alt.q: In 1861 Union soldiers arrest a Maryland man accused of burning railroad bridges and hold him without charges, ignoring a federal judge's order to bring him to court. Which presidential action allowed this?
alt.a: Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus
alt.ex: This was the Merryman case: Lincoln had authorized suspension along the Philadelphia-Washington line, and the Army refused Chief Justice Taney's writ.
w: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation
The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed enslaved people in rebel areas.
Lincoln's call for 75,000 militia volunteers
The April 1861 call raised troops; it did not authorize detentions.
Lincoln's blockade of Southern ports
The blockade targeted Confederate shipping.

alt.q: In Ex parte Merryman (1861), what did Chief Justice Roger Taney conclude?
alt.a: Only Congress had power to suspend habeas corpus
alt.ex: Taney, sitting as a circuit judge, held that the suspension clause's placement in Article I gave the power to Congress; Lincoln did not comply.
w: The President may suspend habeas corpus in any war
That was Lincoln's view, which Taney rejected.
Civilians may never be tried in any federal court
Taney's ruling concerned detention without charges, not civilian trials.
Maryland had no right to remain in the Union
The case did not address Maryland's status.

items.q: Defending his actions to Congress on July 4, 1861, Lincoln asked: "are all the laws, but one, to go unexecuted, and the government itself go to pieces, lest that one be violated?" Which action was he defending?
items.a: Suspending the writ of habeas corpus
items.ex: Lincoln argued that preserving the Union justified suspending habeas corpus, and that the Constitution did not say which branch could suspend it in an emergency.
w: Freeing slaves in the rebelling states
The Emancipation Proclamation came in 1862-63.
Admitting West Virginia as a new state
West Virginia was admitted in 1863.
Drafting men into the Union army
The federal draft began under the Enrollment Act of 1863.

alt.q: Lincoln asked Congress: "are all the laws, but one, to go unexecuted, and the government itself go to pieces, lest that one be violated?" Which argument does this question make?
alt.a: Saving the Union justified breaking one legal limit
alt.ex: Lincoln reasoned that strictly obeying one provision (habeas corpus) should not cause the collapse of the whole government and all its laws.
w: Only Congress may decide when liberties are suspended
That was Taney's position in Merryman, which Lincoln was rebutting.
Courts must approve each wartime arrest in advance
Lincoln was defending arrests made without court approval.
States may ignore federal laws they think unjust
That is nullification, which Lincoln rejected.

alt.q: In Ex parte Milligan (1866), what did the Supreme Court decide about wartime power?
alt.a: Civilians can't be tried by the military if courts are open
alt.ex: Milligan, an Indiana civilian, had been sentenced by a military commission; the Court held this unconstitutional because civilian courts were functioning.
w: The President may suspend habeas corpus without asking Congress
Milligan limited wartime military power; it did not endorse unilateral suspension.
States may never leave the Union for any reason
That was Texas v. White (1869).
Enslaved people may not sue in federal courts
That was Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).

items.q: The proclamation declared that "all persons held as slaves within any State or designated part of a State, the people whereof shall then be in rebellion against the United States, shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free." Which statement best describes its scope?
items.a: It covered only Confederate-held areas, not loyal states
items.ex: Issued January 1, 1863 (after a preliminary proclamation on September 22, 1862), it did not cover the loyal border states or Union-held areas; slavery everywhere ended with the 13th Amendment (1865).
w: It freed all enslaved people across the entire United States
Nationwide abolition came with the 13th Amendment in 1865.
It freed enslaved people only in the loyal border states
It did the reverse: the border states were excluded.
It freed enslaved people once each state's voters agreed
No state vote was required; it was a war measure.

alt.q: Under which authority did Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation?
alt.a: His war power as Commander in Chief
alt.ex: Lincoln issued it "as a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion," relying on his Article II military powers.
w: A statute passed by two-thirds of Congress
It was an executive proclamation, not a law of Congress.
The Supreme Court's ruling in Dred Scott
Dred Scott (1857) protected slavery in the territories.
The Thirteenth Amendment's enforcement clause
The 13th Amendment was ratified in December 1865.

alt.q: In 1863 an enslaved person in Kentucky, a slave state loyal to the Union, hears about the Emancipation Proclamation. What did the proclamation do for this person?
alt.a: Nothing directly; Kentucky was not in rebellion
alt.ex: The proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion; slavery in Kentucky ended with the 13th Amendment in December 1865.
w: It freed them immediately on January 1, 1863
Kentucky was excluded because it had not seceded.
It freed them once Kentucky's legislature agreed
No state approval process was part of the proclamation.
It made them a citizen, though not yet free
Citizenship came with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment.

items.q: Which statement best describes an important effect of the Emancipation Proclamation?
items.a: It made ending slavery a Union war aim and let Black men enlist
items.ex: The proclamation turned the war into a fight against slavery, discouraged Britain and France from recognizing the Confederacy, and opened the Union army and navy to about 180,000 Black soldiers.
w: It ended the Civil War by forcing an immediate Southern surrender
The war continued until April 1865.
It granted citizenship and voting rights to all freedpeople
Citizenship and voting came with the 14th (1868) and 15th (1870) Amendments.
It led Britain and France to recognize the Confederacy at once
It made European recognition of the Confederacy less likely.

alt.q: The Emancipation Proclamation stated that "such persons of suitable condition, will be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts, positions, stations, and other places, and to man vessels of all sorts in said service." What change does this announce?
alt.a: Black men could enlist in Union forces
alt.ex: This part of the proclamation opened military service to freed and Black men; about 180,000 served in the U.S. Colored Troops.
w: Freedpeople could vote in federal elections
Voting rights came with the 15th Amendment (1870).
Former Confederates could rejoin the army
The excerpt concerns people freed by the proclamation.
Northern men could be drafted into service
The draft came from the Enrollment Act of 1863.

alt.q: Why did Lincoln wait until after the Battle of Antietam in September 1862 to announce emancipation?
alt.a: So it would not seem a desperate act after defeats
alt.ex: Secretary of State Seward advised waiting for a victory; the Union success at Antietam let Lincoln issue the preliminary proclamation on September 22, 1862.
w: Because Congress had just passed the 13th Amendment
Congress passed the 13th Amendment in January 1865.
Because the border states had asked for emancipation
The border states opposed emancipation and were excluded.
Because the Supreme Court had approved the plan
The Court did not review the proclamation in advance.

items.q: In February 1942 a President authorized military commanders "to prescribe military areas... from which any or all persons may be excluded." How was this order primarily used?
items.a: To move Japanese Americans from the West Coast to camps
items.ex: Executive Order 9066 (February 19, 1942) named no group, but it was used to remove about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them U.S. citizens, to incarceration camps.
w: To hold German prisoners of war in Midwestern camps
POWs were held under the laws of war, not under EO 9066.
To keep Black workers out of defense plants in war zones
FDR's EO 8802 (1941) actually banned discrimination in defense industries.
To evacuate coastal cities ahead of a Japanese invasion
No general civilian evacuation took place; the order targeted one ancestry group.

alt.q: Which executive action authorized military commanders "to prescribe military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate Military Commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded"?
alt.a: Executive Order 9066
alt.ex: Franklin Roosevelt signed EO 9066 on February 19, 1942; it led to the forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans.
w: Executive Order 9981
EO 9981 (1948) desegregated the armed forces.
Executive Order 8802
EO 8802 (1941) banned discrimination in defense industries.
Executive Order 10730
EO 10730 (1957) sent troops to Little Rock.

alt.q: What justification did Executive Order 9066 give for creating military exclusion areas?
alt.a: Protection against espionage and sabotage
alt.ex: The order begins: "Whereas the successful prosecution of the war requires every possible protection against espionage and against sabotage."
w: Punishment of crimes already committed
No crimes were charged; the order was preventive.
Enforcement of existing immigration quotas
Most of those removed were U.S.-born citizens.
Compliance with a Supreme Court order
No court ordered the removal; Korematsu came later, in 1944.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the federal government later addressed Executive Order 9066?
items.a: Congress apologized and paid $20,000 to each living survivor
items.ex: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (signed by Reagan) apologized and paid reparations; a 1983 federal commission blamed "race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership."
w: The Supreme Court struck down the order while the war continued
Korematsu (1944) upheld the exclusion; Ex parte Endo only barred detaining loyal citizens.
Congress passed a law making internment legal in future wars
Congress did the opposite, apologizing for it.
Roosevelt withdrew the order one week after he issued it
Removal and incarceration lasted until 1945-46.

alt.q: In Korematsu v. United States (1944), how did the Supreme Court treat the exclusion order based on Executive Order 9066?
alt.a: It upheld the order as a wartime necessity
alt.ex: In a 6-3 decision, the Court upheld Fred Korematsu's conviction for violating the exclusion order; the Court repudiated Korematsu in Trump v. Hawaii (2018).
w: It struck the order down as racial discrimination
The majority upheld it; Justices Murphy, Jackson and Roberts dissented.
It ruled the order applied only to noncitizens
Korematsu himself was a U.S. citizen.
It said a declaration of war was required first
War had already been declared in December 1941.

alt.q: In 1990 a Japanese American who spent the war years in a camp in Wyoming receives a letter of apology and a check from the federal government. Which law provided this?
alt.a: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988
alt.ex: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 granted a formal apology and $20,000 to each surviving person incarcerated; payments began in 1990.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The 1964 act banned discrimination in public accommodations and employment.
The Immigration Act of 1952
The McCarran-Walter Act (1952) allowed Japanese immigrants to naturalize.
The Evacuation Claims Act of 1948
The 1948 Japanese American Evacuation Claims Act repaid some property losses; it offered no apology and no $20,000 payments.

items.q: "It is hereby declared to be the policy of the President that there shall be equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services without regard to race, color, religion or national origin." Which action does this begin?
items.a: Truman's 1948 order to desegregate the military
items.ex: Executive Order 9981 (July 26, 1948) created the Fahy Committee to carry out the policy; the last all-Black Army units were abolished by 1954.
w: Roosevelt's 1941 order banning bias in defense plants
That was EO 8802, which covered defense industries, not the armed services.
Eisenhower's 1957 order sending troops to Little Rock
That was EO 10730.
Kennedy's 1961 order on affirmative action in hiring
That was EO 10925, which covered federal contractors.

alt.q: Why did Truman desegregate the military by executive order rather than through legislation?
alt.a: Southern senators could block civil rights bills
alt.ex: Southern Democrats could filibuster civil rights bills, so Truman used his authority as Commander in Chief to act alone.
w: The Supreme Court ordered him to act alone
No court ordered military desegregation.
The Constitution bars Congress from military rules
Article I gives Congress power to make rules for the armed forces.
Military rules can only be changed by treaty
Treaties govern relations with other nations.

alt.q: A Black soldier who enlisted in 1951 serves in an integrated unit in Korea, though their father served in an all-Black unit in World War II. Which executive action best explains the difference?
alt.a: Executive Order 9981
alt.ex: Truman's EO 9981 (1948) began military desegregation, which accelerated during the Korean War.
w: Executive Order 9066
EO 9066 (1942) led to the incarceration of Japanese Americans.
Executive Order 8802
EO 8802 (1941) covered defense industries, not the armed forces.
Executive Order 11246
EO 11246 (1965) covered federal contractors.

items.q: Which statement best describes President Eisenhower's action at Little Rock Central High School in 1957?
items.a: He sent federal troops to carry out a court desegregation order
items.ex: After Gov. Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to block nine Black students, Eisenhower issued EO 10730 (September 24, 1957), federalized the Guard and sent the 101st Airborne to escort the Little Rock Nine.
w: He ordered the school closed until Arkansas agreed to integrate
It was Faubus who closed Little Rock's high schools in 1958-59.
He signed a law requiring every state to integrate its schools
No such law was passed; he enforced a federal court order under Brown.
He asked the Supreme Court to delay integration in Arkansas
Arkansas officials sought delay; the Court refused in Cooper v. Aaron (1958).

alt.q: "Mob rule cannot be allowed to override the decisions of our courts." In which 1957 crisis did a President say this to explain his use of troops?
alt.a: School integration in Little Rock
alt.ex: Eisenhower said this in his September 24, 1957 address explaining why he sent troops to Little Rock, Arkansas.
w: Integration of Ole Miss in Mississippi
Kennedy sent troops to the University of Mississippi in 1962.
The Montgomery bus boycott in Alabama
The 1955-56 boycott did not involve federal troops.
The Freedom Rides through the Deep South
The Freedom Rides were in 1961; Kennedy sent federal marshals.

alt.q: Which constitutional principle did Eisenhower's action at Little Rock most directly uphold?
alt.a: Federal supremacy over state resistance
alt.ex: By enforcing a federal court order against a governor's defiance, Eisenhower upheld the Supremacy Clause and the authority of Brown v. Board.
w: States' rights to run their own schools
Faubus claimed states' rights; Eisenhower overrode him.
Separation of church and state
Religion was not at issue.
Congress's power to declare war
No war was involved; troops enforced a court order.

items.q: Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus used the state National Guard to block nine Black students from entering Central High School in 1957. Which Supreme Court ruling were the students trying to exercise?
items.a: Brown v. Board of Education
items.ex: Brown (1954) held segregated public schools unconstitutional; Little Rock's school board adopted a gradual plan under it, which Faubus resisted.
w: Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal' and was overturned by Brown.
Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg
Swann (1971) approved busing to desegregate schools, long after 1957.
Sweatt v. Painter
Sweatt (1950) integrated a Texas law school; it did not reach public schools.

alt.q: In Cooper v. Aaron (1958), arising from the Little Rock crisis, what did the Supreme Court hold?
alt.a: State officials must obey the Court's constitutional rulings
alt.ex: The Court unanimously refused Little Rock's request to delay integration and held that state officials cannot nullify Brown v. Board.
w: States may delay school integration to prevent public disorder
The Court rejected delay based on hostility or unrest.
Federal troops may not be used inside a state's schools
The Court did not limit Eisenhower's use of troops.
Separate schools are allowed if facilities are equal
That was Plessy's rule, rejected by Brown.

alt.q: What did Eisenhower do with the Arkansas National Guard in September 1957?
alt.a: Put it under federal control
alt.ex: Executive Order 10730 federalized the Arkansas National Guard, removing it from Faubus's control, alongside the 101st Airborne.
w: Disbanded it permanently
The Guard was not disbanded.
Left it under the governor
Leaving it under Faubus would have kept the students blocked.
Sent it to guard the capitol
Federalized Guard units helped protect the students at the school.

items.q: Which statement best describes Executive Order 10925, issued by John F. Kennedy in 1961?
items.a: It required federal contractors to take affirmative action
items.ex: EO 10925 (March 6, 1961) was the first to use the phrase 'affirmative action,' requiring government contractors to hire and treat workers without regard to race, creed, color or national origin; it created the President's Committee on Equal Employment Opportunity.
w: It ordered the armed services to end racial segregation in units
That was Truman's EO 9981 (1948).
It banned discrimination by hotels, restaurants and theaters
That was Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
It required racial quotas in admissions at public universities
It concerned contractor employment; quotas in admissions were struck down in Bakke (1978).

alt.q: A 1961 executive order required that "the contractor will take affirmative action to ensure that applicants are employed, and that employees are treated during employment, without regard to their race, creed, color, or national origin." Which President issued it?
alt.a: John F. Kennedy
alt.ex: This is from Kennedy's Executive Order 10925 (March 6, 1961), the first use of 'affirmative action' in this sense.
w: Lyndon B. Johnson
Johnson issued EO 11246 in 1965; as Vice President he chaired Kennedy's committee.
Dwight D. Eisenhower
Eisenhower left office in January 1961.
Harry S. Truman
Truman issued EO 9981 in 1948 on the military.

alt.q: Which group was most directly required to act under Kennedy's Executive Order 10925?
alt.a: Firms holding federal contracts
alt.ex: EO 10925 applied to businesses doing work under government contracts, using federal purchasing power to fight discrimination.
w: All private firms with 15 workers
That is Title VII's coverage (15+ employees since a 1972 amendment; 25 in the original 1964 act).
Public schools getting federal aid
That is Title VI's coverage under the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
State officials running elections
That is the Voting Rights Act's focus.

items.q: How did Lyndon Johnson's Executive Order 11246 (1965) build on earlier affirmative action orders?
items.a: It gave the Labor Department power to enforce contractor rules
items.ex: EO 11246 (September 24, 1965) required federal contractors to take affirmative action and made the Secretary of Labor responsible for enforcement (later the OFCCP); EO 11375 (1967) added sex. It was revoked in January 2025 by EO 14173.
w: It extended affirmative action to all private employers nationwide
It covered only federal contractors and subcontractors.
It ended affirmative action requirements for federal contractors
It strengthened them; revocation came only in 2025.
It applied affirmative action to voter registration in the South
Voting was handled by the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

alt.q: Which category did Johnson add to federal contractor nondiscrimination rules in 1967 by amending his 1965 order?
alt.a: Sex
alt.ex: Executive Order 11375 (1967) amended EO 11246 to bar sex discrimination by federal contractors.
w: Age
Age discrimination was addressed by the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967, a statute.
Disability
Contractor disability rules came from the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.
Veteran status
Protections for veterans at federal contractors came from the Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974.

alt.q: A construction firm with a large federal highway contract in 1970 is told it must set goals for hiring minority workers or risk losing the contract. Which executive action is being enforced?
alt.a: Executive Order 11246
alt.ex: The Labor Department enforced EO 11246 through plans such as Nixon's 1969 Philadelphia Plan, which set minority hiring goals for federal construction contractors.
w: Executive Order 9981
EO 9981 desegregated the military.
Executive Order 9066
EO 9066 led to Japanese American incarceration.
Executive Order 10730
EO 10730 sent troops to Little Rock.

items.q: Which statement best describes the "bully pulpit," a phrase coined by Theodore Roosevelt?
items.a: The President's use of the office to rally public opinion
items.ex: TR called the White House a 'bully pulpit' ('bully' meaning excellent) and used speeches and publicity to build support for his Square Deal.
w: The President's power to veto bills that Congress has passed
The veto is a formal Article I, Section 7 power, not persuasion.
The President's power to remove cabinet officers at will
Removal power is a formal executive power.
The President's duty to report on the state of the Union
Article II, Section 3 requires the report; the bully pulpit is the broader use of the office to persuade.

alt.q: In 1902 Theodore Roosevelt publicly pressured coal mine owners and striking miners into arbitration, winning public support. Which presidential tool does this best illustrate?
alt.a: The bully pulpit
alt.ex: With no law requiring arbitration, Roosevelt used public pressure and the prestige of his office to settle the anthracite coal strike.
w: The pocket veto
A pocket veto lets a bill die after Congress adjourns.
Executive privilege
Executive privilege shields internal communications from disclosure.
The pardon power
The pardon power forgives federal crimes.

alt.q: Theodore Roosevelt promoted conservation, consumer protection and control of corporations. What was this domestic program called?
alt.a: The Square Deal
alt.ex: TR's Square Deal centered on the 'three Cs': conservation, control of corporations and consumer protection.
w: The New Deal
The New Deal was Franklin Roosevelt's 1930s program.
The Fair Deal
The Fair Deal was Truman's postwar program.
The New Freedom
The New Freedom was Woodrow Wilson's 1912 program.

items.q: In a 1933 radio talk, a President told listeners: "I can assure you that it is safer to keep your money in a reopened bank than under the mattress." What was the main purpose of such talks?
items.a: To explain policy directly to the public and build trust
items.ex: FDR's first fireside chat (March 12, 1933) explained the bank holiday; he gave about 30 such radio talks through 1944.
w: To announce declarations of war after Congress voted
Declarations are made by Congress; the chats were about explaining policy.
To deliver the annual State of the Union message to Congress
The State of the Union is a formal report to Congress.
To campaign for reelection against a rival candidate
The chats were policy talks, not campaign speeches.

alt.q: What were Franklin Roosevelt's informal radio talks to the nation called?
alt.a: Fireside chats
alt.ex: FDR's fireside chats (1933-1944) used radio to speak directly to Americans in their homes.
w: Front-porch speeches
McKinley ran a 'front-porch campaign' in 1896.
Kitchen debates
The 'Kitchen Debate' was Nixon versus Khrushchev in 1959.
Hundred Days talks
The Hundred Days was FDR's first burst of legislation in 1933.

alt.q: In March 1933, after a nationwide bank holiday, a family listens as the President calmly explains on the radio how banks will reopen; within weeks deposits exceed withdrawals. Which practice does this illustrate?
alt.a: FDR's use of fireside chats
alt.ex: FDR's first fireside chat (March 12, 1933) helped restore confidence; when banks reopened, deposits outpaced withdrawals.
w: TR's use of antitrust lawsuits
TR's trust-busting was in the 1900s and used courts, not radio.
Hoover's voluntary business pledges
Hoover relied on voluntary cooperation from business, 1929-1933.
LBJ's televised addresses to Congress
LBJ's addresses came in the 1960s, on television.

items.q: In a 1964 commencement speech, a President said, "The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all." How did this speech use the bully pulpit?
items.a: It rallied public support for a broad antipoverty agenda
items.ex: Lyndon Johnson's May 22, 1964 University of Michigan speech named the Great Society; he later used a March 15, 1965 address to Congress to push the Voting Rights Act.
w: It announced a declaration of war against North Vietnam
Congress never declared war on North Vietnam.
It explained a veto of a civil rights bill from Congress
Johnson signed civil rights bills; he did not veto them.
It ordered troops to desegregate a Southern university
Kennedy sent troops to Ole Miss (1962); this speech gave no orders.

alt.q: Which President called his domestic program the "Great Society" and used speeches to the public and Congress to push Medicare and voting rights?
alt.a: Lyndon B. Johnson
alt.ex: LBJ named the Great Society in 1964 and used televised addresses to win passage of laws such as Medicare and the Voting Rights Act (1965).
w: John F. Kennedy
Kennedy's program was called the New Frontier.
Franklin D. Roosevelt
FDR's program was the New Deal.
Harry S. Truman
Truman's program was the Fair Deal.

alt.q: Days after the violence at Selma in 1965, Lyndon Johnson told Congress on national television, "Their cause must be our cause too." Which law was he urging Congress to pass?
alt.a: The Voting Rights Act
alt.ex: In his March 15, 1965 'We Shall Overcome' address, Johnson called for a voting rights bill; it became law on August 6, 1965.
w: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
The 1964 act had already passed the year before.
The Fair Housing Act
Fair housing was enacted in 1968.
The Economic Opportunity Act
The antipoverty law passed in 1964.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the Constitution divides war powers?
items.a: Congress declares war; the President commands the armed forces
items.ex: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress power to declare war and raise and support armies; Article II, Section 2 makes the President Commander in Chief. Congress has formally declared war in only five conflicts, the last being World War II.
