w: The President declares war; Congress commands the armed forces
This reverses the two roles.
The Senate declares war; the House pays for the armed forces
Both houses must pass a declaration of war.
Congress declares war; the Supreme Court approves deployments
The courts have no role in approving deployments.

alt.q: Since 1945 U.S. forces have fought in Korea, Vietnam, the Persian Gulf and Iraq. Which statement about these conflicts is accurate?
alt.a: None began with a formal declaration of war
alt.ex: Congress has not declared war since 1942; later conflicts relied on UN resolutions, presidential action, or congressional authorizations such as the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and AUMFs.
w: Each began with a formal declaration of war
No declaration was made for any of them.
Each rested only on a United Nations treaty
Vietnam and the 2003 Iraq War did not rest on UN authorization alone.
None ever received any vote from Congress
Congress passed the Tonkin Resolution (1964) and authorizations for Iraq (1991, 2002).

alt.q: At the Constitutional Convention, Madison and Elbridge Gerry moved to change Congress's power to "make" war to "declare" war, "leaving to the Executive the power to repel sudden attacks." What does this change suggest?
alt.a: The President could defend the nation in an emergency
alt.ex: Madison's notes (August 17, 1787) show the framers kept the decision to start war with Congress while letting the President defend against sudden attack.
w: The President alone could decide to start any war abroad
The change kept the power to begin war with Congress.
Congress would command troops after a declaration
Command belongs to the President as Commander in Chief.
States would defend themselves without federal help
The change concerned the federal branches, not the states.

items.q: During the Korean War, President Truman ordered the government to seize the nation's steel mills to prevent a strike. In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), what did the Supreme Court rule?
items.a: The seizure was invalid because Congress had not authorized it
items.ex: In a 6-3 decision, the Court held that neither the Commander in Chief power nor executive power allowed the seizure without a law; Justice Jackson's concurrence said presidential power is weakest when acting against Congress's will.
w: The seizure was valid under the President's Commander in Chief power
The Court rejected that argument; the mills were not a theater of war.
The seizure was valid because Congress had declared war on Korea
Congress never declared war in Korea.
The case was dismissed as a political question for the branches
The Court decided the case on the merits.

alt.q: Which principle does Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) best illustrate?
alt.a: Limits on presidential power, even in war
alt.ex: Youngstown held that the President cannot make law on his own, even during a war, without authority from Congress or the Constitution.
w: Federal supremacy over state labor laws
The case was about the President versus Congress, not states.
Freedom of the press during times of war
Press freedom was the issue in New York Times v. U.S. (1971).
Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce
The case turned on executive power, not the Commerce Clause.

alt.q: A President, citing a foreign war, orders federal officials to take over a private industry without any law from Congress allowing it. Which case would the owners most likely cite?
alt.a: Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer
alt.ex: Youngstown (1952) struck down Truman's seizure of the steel mills as beyond his powers without congressional authorization.
w: U.S. v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
Curtiss-Wright (1936) described broad presidential power in foreign affairs, which would hurt the owners' case.
Korematsu v. United States
Korematsu (1944) deferred to wartime military orders, which would not help the owners.
New York Times Co. v. United States
That 1971 case concerned prior restraint of the press.

items.q: In 1950 Truman sent U.S. troops to Korea under a UN Security Council resolution, without asking Congress for a declaration of war. What does this illustrate?
items.a: Presidents starting conflicts as commander in chief
items.ex: Korea set a precedent for major wars fought without a declaration; Truman agreed with a reporter's description of it as a 'police action.'
w: Congress using its power to declare war on a new enemy
Congress did not declare war in Korea.
The Senate using its power to ratify a peace treaty
The Korean War ended with an armistice (1953), not a ratified treaty.
The courts using judicial review to approve a war
No court approved the war.

alt.q: What term did Truman accept for the U.S. intervention in Korea in 1950, avoiding the word "war"?
alt.a: A police action
alt.ex: Truman agreed with a reporter's phrase 'police action,' reflecting that Congress never declared war.
w: A quarantine
Kennedy called the 1962 naval blockade of Cuba a 'quarantine.'
A peacekeeping mission
'Peacekeeping' describes later UN operations; Truman's own phrase for Korea was 'police action.'
A containment
Containment was the broader Cold War strategy, not a name for the Korean intervention.

alt.q: After the September 11 attacks, how did Congress authorize military action against those responsible?
alt.a: By passing an Authorization for Use of Military Force
alt.ex: The AUMF of September 18, 2001 authorized force against those who planned or aided the attacks; Congress did not declare war.
w: By formally declaring war on Afghanistan's Taliban government
No declaration of war was made.
By ratifying a new mutual defense treaty with NATO allies
NATO invoked its existing Article 5; Congress ratified no new treaty.
By amending the War Powers Resolution of 1973
The War Powers Resolution was not amended; the AUMF satisfied its terms.

items.q: The Court wrote that "neither the doctrine of separation of powers, nor the need for confidentiality of high-level communications, without more, can sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances." Which case is this?
items.a: U.S. v. Nixon
items.ex: In U.S. v. Nixon (July 24, 1974), a unanimous 8-0 Court (Chief Justice Burger; Rehnquist recused) ordered Nixon to turn over White House tapes subpoenaed by the special prosecutor.
w: Marbury v. Madison
Marbury (1803) established judicial review.
Youngstown v. Sawyer
Youngstown (1952) struck down Truman's steel seizure.
Nixon v. Fitzgerald
Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) gave presidents absolute immunity from civil damages suits over official acts; it did not involve a criminal subpoena.

alt.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in United States v. Nixon (1974)?
alt.a: Privilege isn't absolute and gives way to a criminal subpoena
alt.ex: The Court recognized a presumptive privilege rooted in the separation of powers but held that it must yield to the specific need for evidence in a criminal trial.
w: Executive privilege does not exist anywhere in the Constitution
The Court recognized that the privilege has constitutional roots.
The President is immune from all court orders while in office
The Court ordered the President to comply with the subpoena.
Congress may not impeach a President for withholding evidence
The case did not limit impeachment.

alt.q: A special prosecutor subpoenas a President's recorded conversations for use in the criminal trial of the President's aides. The President refuses, citing executive privilege. Based on precedent, what is the most likely result?
alt.a: The President must produce evidence needed for the trial
alt.ex: Under U.S. v. Nixon (1974), a generalized claim of confidentiality must yield to a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.
w: The President may withhold all of it as head of a branch
That claim of absolute privilege was rejected in 1974.
The Senate must vote on whether to release the tapes
The Senate has no role in enforcing court subpoenas.
The prosecutor must drop the case to protect secrecy
The Court put the needs of criminal justice ahead of general secrecy.

items.q: Which sequence best describes the end of the Watergate scandal in 1974?
items.a: Court ordered tapes released; Nixon resigned; Ford pardoned him
items.ex: After U.S. v. Nixon (July 24), the House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment; the 'smoking gun' tape was released August 5; Nixon resigned August 9, 1974; Ford pardoned him September 8, 1974.
w: Nixon was impeached; the Senate convicted him; Ford took office
The full House never voted, and there was no Senate trial.
Nixon was impeached; the Senate acquitted him; he finished his term
That pattern fits Andrew Johnson (1868) and Bill Clinton (1999).
Congress censured Nixon; he lost reelection; Ford pardoned him
Nixon won reelection in 1972 and resigned during his second term.

alt.q: Which statement about Richard Nixon's impeachment is accurate?
alt.a: A House committee approved articles, but he quit before a vote
alt.ex: The House Judiciary Committee approved articles for obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress in July 1974; Nixon resigned before the full House voted.
w: The full House impeached him, and then the Senate acquitted him
Nixon was never impeached by the full House.
The full House impeached him, and the Senate removed him
No President has been removed by the Senate.
The House committee rejected the articles, but he still resigned
The committee approved three articles.

alt.q: On taking the oath of office in August 1974, a new President declared, "Our long national nightmare is over." Who said this, and what had just happened?
alt.a: Gerald Ford, after Nixon resigned
alt.ex: Ford spoke at his swearing-in on August 9, 1974, the day Nixon's resignation took effect; a month later he pardoned Nixon.
w: Lyndon Johnson, after Kennedy was killed
Johnson took office in November 1963.
Jimmy Carter, after Vietnam ended
Carter took office in January 1977.
Richard Nixon, after his reelection
Nixon was the President who resigned.

items.q: Which reform was passed in response to the Watergate scandal?
items.a: The Ethics in Government Act, creating independent counsels
items.ex: Post-Watergate reforms included the 1974 Federal Election Campaign Act amendments (creating the FEC), the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 (independent counsel, financial disclosure) and the Presidential Records Act of 1978.
w: The Pendleton Act, creating a merit-based civil service
The Pendleton Act (1883) followed Garfield's assassination.
The 22nd Amendment, limiting presidents to two terms
The 22nd Amendment (1951) followed FDR's four elections.
The 25th Amendment, setting rules for presidential succession
The 25th Amendment was ratified in 1967, before Watergate, though it was used to make Ford Vice President.

alt.q: In the October 1973 "Saturday Night Massacre," what did President Nixon do?
alt.a: Had the Watergate special prosecutor fired
alt.ex: Nixon ordered Archibald Cox fired; Attorney General Elliot Richardson and his deputy William Ruckelshaus resigned rather than do it, and Robert Bork carried out the firing.
w: Fired the FBI director leading the inquiry
Nixon did not fire the FBI director.
Ordered arrests at the Watergate complex
The burglars were arrested by police on June 17, 1972.
Resigned rather than face a Senate trial
Nixon resigned in August 1974, ten months later.

alt.q: After Watergate, Congress amended federal campaign finance law in 1974. Which agency did this reform create?
alt.a: The Federal Election Commission
alt.ex: The 1974 FECA amendments set contribution limits and created the Federal Election Commission to enforce campaign finance law.
w: The Federal Communications Commission
The FCC was created in 1934 to regulate broadcasting.
The Civil Service Commission
The Civil Service Commission was created by the Pendleton Act (1883).
The Commission on Civil Rights
The Commission on Civil Rights was created in 1957.
